docs.title: What Family mruby is
docs.text:
Family mruby is a windowed GUI operating system for microcontrollers, written in Ruby and C, that runs applications written in Ruby.

It aims to be an environment where programming can be enjoyed on the machine itself, without a PC: a keyboard, a mouse and a display are all it asks for.

The editor, and the app that came out of running that code

PicoRuby runs on top of FreeRTOS. Ruby apps run at the same time as FreeRTOS tasks, each with its own memory.

docs.title: Modern and Retro
docs.text:
Modern Retro Hardware M5Stack Tab5 narya-board (a board of our own) Main chips ESP32-P4 (dual-core RISC-V) + ESP32-C6 ESP32-S3 + ESP32-WROVER Screen The built-in 1280x720 IPS panel (MIPI-DSI) NTSC composite out Framebuffer 426 x 240, scaled 3x to the panel 320 x 240 Sound Built-in speaker and a headphone jack 3.5mm line out Input USB keyboard and mouse, capacitive touch, the Tab5 Keyboard USB keyboard and mouse Network Wi-Fi and BLE through the on-board ESP32-C6 The ESP32-S3's own Wi-Fi and BLE Also Drive the screen from a browser over Wi-Fi, one GROVE port RCA video out, two GROVE ports, a battery-backed clock

The Family mruby that ran on the Narya v3 board, with its NTSC output, is what we now call Retro. Modern is defined as the variation that assumes a higher-resolution digital display, and is meant to be used more seriously as a development environment. Today it runs on the Tab5.

Choose your hardware has the details. Without either board, the same system runs in a browser tab (Studio) and as a program on a Linux PC, and small headless boards (M5Stack StickS3, AtomS3R) join the others over Asterism, the network on which machines call each other's Ruby objects and pass running apps between them.

Retro on the left (a Narya v3 board connected to a monitor), Modern on the right (an M5Stack Tab5)

docs.title: Getting the hardware
docs.text:
Modern runs on a stock M5Stack Tab5. The Tab5 Keyboard is supported as well.

Retro needs a board of its own, sold on BOOTH. The schematics, Gerber data and BOM are all public, so you can also build a compatible board yourself.

docs.title: Development Background
docs.text:
Long ago, BASIC was often the first programming language that children encountered. Despite its limitations, there were products like Family BASIC, which allowed BASIC programming not only on PCs but also on platforms such as the MSX or the Famicom (NES). Many programmers discovered the joy of programming through these environments.

Today, development environments for most programming languages are freely available and easily installable on PCs. However, because so much is possible, beginners often don't know where to start. Even reaching the point where you can make something slightly beyond "Hello World," such as a simple game, can require a surprisingly high setup cost.

Family mruby was born from the desire to create an environment where you can build small games and other applications using a scripting language on a single microcontroller -- bringing back the joy of simple, immediate programming.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Family mruby is a small multi-VM operating system on top of FreeRTOS. Several scripting VMs run side by side, one per FreeRTOS task, each with its own heap — so one app running out of memory or crashing does not take the system with it.

docs.title: One task, one VM
docs.text:
The design rule is one task = one VM. Each VM has its own stack, its own memory pool and its own allocator handle. That isolation is what makes it safe to let a user's half-finished program run next to the desktop.

User app slots 5 on Modern, the Linux builds and Studio (max_apps can lower it). 3 at a time on the ESP32-S3 boards (Retro, StickS3, AtomS3R) Heap per app Depends on the machine — see the table below Languages Ruby (PicoRuby), MicroPython, BASIC, Lua; and, as WebAssembly apps on WAMR, C, TinyGo, Rust and Zig (not on the ESP32-S3 boards; from 3.1.0) Machine Ordinary pool With large_memory = 1 Retro, StickS3, AtomS3R (ESP32-S3) 500 KB 1 MB Modern (ESP32-P4) 1 MB 2 MB Linux simulator and Linux program (64-bit) 1.5 MB 3 MB Studio (WebAssembly, 32-bit) 1.5 MB 3 MB

The pool does not grow. Everything the app has — its objects, the compiler working on its source, the files it requires — comes out of it, and an allocation fails when no single free block is large enough, not only when the total runs out. The Linux builds are 64-bit, so the same script takes about one and a half times the room there; the larger pool makes them about as tight as Modern. Studio is 32-bit with the same larger pool, so it is looser than a board: an app that fits in Studio may not fit on a board.

A separate pool is not just tidiness: memory fragmentation stays inside the app that caused it, and when an app dies its whole pool is reclaimed at once.

On Modern and the Linux and browser builds each slot has its own ordinary pool: the first three are reserved when the system starts and the rest are taken from PSRAM the first time an app lands in them. There is only one large_memory pool there, so only one such app runs at a time, and an app that does not need it should not ask for it.

The ESP32-S3 boards have three pools in all, reserved at boot: one ordinary and two large. An ordinary app takes the ordinary pool, or a free large one when that is taken; a large_memory app takes a large one. A fourth app is refused with "No free app slot". While Asterism is in use, its transfer app holds one of the large pools.

Everything resident that would otherwise be an app of its own — the clock, the network watcher, the thing that reads a sentence out loud — shares a single VM instead, the service host. A dozen small jobs then cost one task and one slot rather than a dozen.

docs.title: The kernel is compiled Ruby
docs.text:
The kernel and the desktop are written in Ruby, but they do not run on an interpreter. They are compiled ahead of time to native code — the same source, a different backend — which cut input latency substantially compared with running them on the VM. This is how the released firmware is built; the interpreted build still exists, and is what the two are checked against.

The apps you write still run on the PicoRuby VM. Only the system's own Ruby is compiled.

docs.title: Two hardware shapes
docs.text: The same OS runs on two very different arrangements. The headless boards (StickS3, AtomS3R) are the Retro arrangement's ESP32-S3 on its own, with a small LCD of their own and no desktop; the NARYA v4 board under development is the Modern arrangement on an ESP32-P4 module with HDMI out.

docs.title: Modern — one chip does everything
docs.text:
ESP32-P4  ── OS, VMs, graphics, sound, input, USB host
   │
   ├── MIPI-DSI panel (1280x720), PPA scaling from a 426x240 framebuffer
   ├── I2S codec, APU emulator
   ├── GT911 touch, Tab5 Keyboard (I2C), USB HID host
   └── ESP32-C6 (SDIO) ── Wi-Fi + BLE

Graphics and audio are local: the P4 composites the framebuffer itself and its PPA block scales it onto the panel. There is no second processor to talk to, which is why the same Ruby app is quicker to draw here.

docs.title: Retro — the work is split across two chips
docs.text:
ESP32-S3 ── OS, VMs, input, USB host, Wi-Fi/BLE
   │
   │  UART, 921600 bps, CTS/RTS flow control
   ▼
ESP32-WROVER ── graphics + audio
   ├── NTSC composite out (LovyanGFX CVBS)
   └── NES APU emulator, I2S DAC

The S3 sends drawing and sound commands over a serial link; the WROVER turns them into a composite video signal and audio. Both chips have to be flashed, and both have to be on the same version, because that link is a protocol.

docs.title: What the app sees
docs.text:
Nothing of the above. The graphics API, the audio API and the peripheral API are the same calls on both machines — one path submits them to a local renderer, the other serialises them onto a UART. An app that avoids hardcoding the screen size and branches on FmrbConst::BOARD for wiring runs unchanged on either.

Hardware is owned by the system and reached through a proxy (GPIO, I2C, RMT, files), so several VMs can use the same bus without fighting over it.

docs.title: Development targets
docs.text:
These builds come out of the same source tree:

Target What it is esp32 / Modern ESP32-P4 (M5Stack Tab5; the NARYA v4 board, in development) esp32 / Retro ESP32-S3 + ESP32-WROVER (narya-board) esp32 / Headless ESP32-S3 on its own (M5Stack StickS3, AtomS3R), one app and no desktop linux The whole system as a Linux process, with SDL2 for the screen. See Simulator Linux program The same system as one ordinary program on a Linux PC, without ESP-IDF underneath: its own window, or the whole session as the compositor. Shipped as a .deb with each release wasm The same system compiled to WebAssembly, with a cooperative FreeRTOS port, running in a browser tab. See Studio

The Linux build is not a mock: it runs the real kernel, the real desktop and the real apps, with the drivers swapped underneath. Most work can be done there before touching hardware.

docs.title: Verified Peripherals
docs.text:
This page lists USB devices that have been verified to work with actual hardware.

Devices not listed here may also work, but due to limitations in the USB driver functionality, some devices may not be recognized.

A device that is recognised but behaves wrongly

If the cursor jumps, moves on the wrong axis, or does not move while the buttons work, the device is being read with the wrong report layout. You can work out the right one on the device itself with the HID Inspector app — see HID Device Config.

Which machine these were tested on

The results below were taken on Retro (narya-board). Both machines run the same USB host driver, so a device that works on one should work on the other, but the entries here have not been re-verified on a Tab5.

On Modern you have an alternative that sidesteps USB entirely: the M5Stack Tab5 Keyboard accessory attaches to the body over I2C, and the touch panel gives you a pointer. Neither needs the USB-A port.

docs.title: Modern (M5Stack Tab5)
docs.text: Modern runs on a stock M5Stack Tab5. Everything below is the Tab5's own hardware — Family mruby only decides what it uses and what it reserves. For the full board specification, connector locations and mechanical drawings, see M5Stack's documentation.

docs.title: Overview (Modern)
docs.text: Item Details Main MCU ESP32-P4 (dual-core RISC-V) — OS, graphics, audio and input, all on one chip Radio ESP32-C6 coprocessor. Wi-Fi and BLE run at the same time Memory 32 MB PSRAM, 16 MB flash Display Built-in IPS panel, 1280 x 720, MIPI-DSI, with capacitive touch Framebuffer 426 x 240 in RGB332, scaled 3x onto the panel by the P4's PPA hardware. 640 x 360 (2x) while an app with fullscreen_hires = true is fullscreen Audio Built-in speaker and headphone jack. The speaker mutes when headphones are plugged in USB USB-A host port (keyboard, mouse, hub) and USB-C for power and flashing Expansion 1x GROVE Clock RX8130 RTC on the internal I2C bus

docs.title: Video (Modern)
docs.text:
There is no video connector: the panel is the output. The system draws into a 426 x 240 RGB332 framebuffer and the P4's PPA block scales and rotates it onto the 1280 x 720 panel, so the picture fills the screen without the CPU touching every pixel.

Unlike the NTSC output on Retro, nothing is hidden by overscan, so the margin settings (display_margin_x / display_margin_y) are 0 on this machine.

docs.title: Audio (Modern)
docs.text:
The same NES-style APU that Retro uses, but synthesised on the P4 itself and played through the built-in codec. Plugging in headphones mutes the speaker; the detection runs over the display I2C bus.

See FmrbAudio and Audio File Formats.

docs.title: GROVE (Modern)
docs.text:
One GROVE port, on GPIO53 (SDA side) and GPIO54 (SCL side).

The port is dual-purpose, the same convention as GROVE 2 on Retro: it is either an I2C bus or a serial MIDI output, whichever your app opens first. The pin manager arbitrates.

Signal GPIO Also used as Sig1 / SDA 53 MIDI TX Sig2 / SCL 54 WS2812B data, in the LED matrix demo

docs.title: Pins the system keeps (Modern)
docs.text:
Your app cannot acquire these:

GPIO Reserved for 0 / 1 Tab5 Keyboard, I2C (STM32F030 at address 0x6D) 50 Tab5 Keyboard interrupt 31 / 32 Body touch panel I2C, also the general-purpose I2C1 bus 23 Touch panel interrupt 22 LCD backlight 24 / 25 USB-Serial-JTAG — the USB-C flash and console link

The USB-A host port sits on the high-speed OTG PHY's dedicated pads, outside the GPIO matrix, so it takes no GPIO of its own.

docs.title: Storage (Modern)
docs.text:
Internal flash (16 MB) and the microSD slot. The slot is on the P4's SDMMC host (4-bit, GPIO 39-44) and appears as /mnt/sd (also /sd), FAT with long file names. There is no card-detect line, so the system assumes a card is in.

The 16 MB of flash holds the firmware and the LittleFS filesystem (/app, /home, /usr, /etc ...). In the development version the Japanese fonts (the efont faces at 12 px, 12 px bold and 16 px, about 1.3 MB) have moved out of the firmware into a partition of their own at the end of the flash, and the filesystem is about 6.7 MB instead of 8 MB. The fonts are read straight from flash, so they take no RAM; the small 8 px font stays in the firmware and stands in for all sizes if the font partition is missing. The installer writes all of it at once.

The NES APU emulator runs with 4 channels: 2 square waves + 1 triangle wave + 1 noise channel. See FmrbAudio and Audio File Formats for details.

docs.title: GROVE
docs.text:
The board has 2 GROVE connectors. Listed from left: GND, Power, Sig1, Sig2. The connections are as follows:

Connector Sig1 Sig2 Notes GROVE 1 GPIO 14/I2C1-SDA GPIO 21/I2C1-SCL For I2C / shared with RTC (RX8900, address: 0x32). 10K pull-up resistors present GROVE 2 GPIO 47 GPIO 48 General purpose. No pull-up resistors. Power source selectable

GROVE 1 shares the I2C bus with the RTC, so be careful about address conflicts.

GROVE 2 has no pull-up resistors on the signal lines, and the power supply method can be changed via pin headers, so it can be used freely for GPIO, UART, RMT, and other purposes.

docs.title: ESP32-S3 Pin Assignment
docs.text:
GPIO40 is connected to the INT pin of the RX8900 with a pull-up resistor.

JTAG functionality has not been verified. If you want to use it, you need to remove the 0-ohm resistor. See the schematics for details.

docs.text:
Bus SDA SCL Notes I2C1 GPIO 14 GPIO 21 Shared with RTC (RX8900) I2C2 GPIO 47 GPIO 48 General purpose

Use with I2C.new(unit: "ESP32_I2C0", ...) etc. (see Hardware Control > I2C).

docs.title: RTC (Real-Time Clock)
docs.text:
The board includes an RX8900 RTC IC (I2C address 0x32, via I2C1). Time is maintained by a battery.

i2c = I2C.new(unit: "ESP32_I2C0")
rtc = RX8900.new(i2c)
rtc.sync_system_clock

See RX8900 API for details.

docs.title: Headless boards (M5Stack StickS3, AtomS3R)
docs.text:
Small stock boards with an ESP32-S3, flashed from the same installer. They have no desktop: each runs one app on its own small screen and joins an Asterism network over Wi-Fi.

StickS3 AtomS3R Chip ESP32-S3 ESP32-S3 (8 MB flash, 8 MB PSRAM) Screen 240 x 135 128 x 128 Firmware fmruby-core-sticks3 fmruby-core-atoms3r

The app they start is Welcome: the version, the Wi-Fi state, the address and what to do next. Wi-Fi is set from the Family mruby Console over BLE: hold the button while powering on to enter setup mode (a board with no Wi-Fi settings at all starts in it by itself). After that, apps are sent and started over Wi-Fi, the same file and app endpoints as on the other boards. Limits are in Limitations.

docs.title: NARYA v4 (in development)
docs.text: A board of our own with an ESP32-P4 module and HDMI out, running Modern. It is used for development and is not sold; the installer has no firmware for it, and FmrbConst::BOARD reads "naryav4" on it. When this page says Modern it means the Tab5.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Most of the network features are not access-controlled. They were built for a hobby machine on a home network, and they assume everyone who can reach the device is welcome to use it. The exception is the Wi-Fi remote control on release builds (what the Web Installer writes, since 3.1.0): it stays closed until the owner opens it and pairs a PC.

Remote desktop Release builds: closed until the owner turns on Remote control in Config, and then open only to paired PCs, which send a token. The traffic is plain HTTP, so the screen, the input and the token itself can be read on the network. Development builds: no authentication; anyone on the same network can watch the screen and send keyboard and mouse input. → Remote Desktop The file and app endpoints beside it Behind the same switch. Release builds write only under /home, /app and /mnt/sd, and never serve keys or passwords. Development builds have no authentication and reach every path. Anyone let in can list, read, write and delete files, and start or stop apps BLE console and debug service Starts at boot by default on Retro and on Modern (Tab5, NARYA v4); turn it off with the BLE Auto Start setting (ble_auto_start). The headless AtomS3R and StickS3 run it only in setup mode. While it runs it uses no pairing, no bonding and no encryption (deliberately, because pairing breaks Web Bluetooth on Windows): anyone in radio range can connect, look at running apps and their variables, start or stop them, read the log, and read and write ordinary files. It cannot be stopped without a reboot Remote debugger over TCP Linux builds only. No authentication. The simulator listens on all interfaces; the Linux program's package has it off, and listens only on 127.0.0.1 when it is turned on Wi-Fi credentials Stored in plain text on the device, in /home/wifi.toml (what the Wi-Fi page writes) or /etc/wifi.toml. Release builds do not serve them over HTTP. Development builds do: the file endpoints reach every path, keys and passwords included, so that /home can be backed up and restored over Wi-Fi. Over BLE they are readable only while BLE Setup is open on the machine Service keys An API key for the speech service sits in plain text in /home/secrets.toml, kept like the Wi-Fi password: on development builds the file endpoints serve it over HTTP too, as they serve the rest of /home Apps An app you download runs with the same rights as any other. There is no sandbox between apps and the filesystem

Use these features only on a network you trust, and at your own risk. Do not forward a port to the device from the internet. Wi-Fi can be kept off at boot with wifi_auto_start in Config, and BLE likewise with ble_auto_start (BLE Auto Start); once BLE is running it cannot be stopped without a reboot.

docs.title: Differences from R2P2
docs.text: Family mruby is based only on the core part of PicoRuby, and some gems used in PicoRuby's official R2P2 have been independently rewritten. As a result, there may be differences in the available classes and method behavior.

docs.title: Differences Between PicoRuby and CRuby
docs.text: PicoRuby is based on mruby, so some methods that are standard in CRuby may not be available.

docs.title: Heap Size
docs.text:
Each Family mruby app runs as an independent Ruby VM, with its own heap and stack allocated on PSRAM.

Item Retro, StickS3, AtomS3R Modern Linux simulator, Linux program Studio Standard app heap 500 KB 1024 KB 1536 KB 1536 KB Heap with large_memory = 1 1024 KB 2048 KB 3072 KB 3072 KB User apps at a time 3 5 5 5 large_memory apps at a time 2 1 1 1

max_apps in system_conf.toml lowers the number of user apps. The pool does not grow: an app runs out when no single free block is large enough, which can happen well before the total is used up. The Linux builds are 64-bit and need about 1.5 times the room for the same script, so they are about as tight as Modern; Studio is looser than any board, so check a large app on a board too.

You can check heap usage in the Monitor app.

docs.title: Language support status
docs.text: Language Status Ruby (PicoRuby) The main language. Everything documented here MicroPython Usable, with real limits: one Python app at a time, files read and written only whole (FmrbFile), strings that are bytes, and a smaller standard library. Drawing, sprites and sound are there. See MicroPython BASIC Feature-complete as of 2.0. Every known difference from Family BASIC V3 is catalogued. See FMRuby BASIC Lua A concept implementation. Not suitable for building a substantial application C, TinyGo, Rust, Zig As WebAssembly apps, experimental, from 3.1.0. Not on the ESP32-S3 boards (Retro, StickS3, AtomS3R). The SDK's names and shapes may still change

docs.title: Waiting inside an app
docs.text:
Prefer Machine.delay_ms, which is FreeRTOS vTaskDelay underneath:

Machine.delay_ms(500)

Better still, do not block at all: return the number of milliseconds until you want to be called again from on_update, and let the message pump do the waiting. An app that blocks processes no events while it does.

This was worse before 2.0

In 1.0 the tick that drives PicoRuby's task switching had to be disabled: calling it from outside the VM corrupted the VM stack. That is fixed — ticks are now accumulated by a signal source and applied at one point in the scheduler — and the Task feature works. The Machine.delay_ms recommendation above is about not blocking, not about the old corruption.

docs.title: File System Limitations
docs.text: Item Details Maximum file size Within LittleFS limits (a few MB recommended) Maximum path length FmrbConst::MAX_PATH_LEN File names ASCII recommended. Avoid Japanese characters and special symbols Dir#seek / Dir#tell Not supported (ENOSYS). Use rewind and count from the beginning

docs.title: Inter-App Message Size Limit
docs.text: The payload for Pub/Sub publish / send_message is limited to 176 bytes after MessagePack encoding. If you exceed this limit, consider transferring data via files or splitting it across multiple messages.

docs.title: Machine-specific limitations
docs.text: Most limits apply to both machines. These do not.

docs.text: Wi-Fi and BLE One radio, one at a time. Running the BLE console means Wi-Fi will not start, and vice versa Touch No touch panel. A USB mouse is the pointer Remote desktop Not available Firmware Two chips to flash, and both must be on the same version or the system will not boot Resident services Not carried in the Retro firmware. The clock, network and speech services are Modern only WAV playback play_wav returns false. The audio is at the far end of a serial link, and shipping a clip across it before a note could sound is too slow to be worth it Mouse wheel The same per-device rule as Modern

docs.title: Headless boards (M5Stack StickS3, AtomS3R)
docs.text: Desktop None. The board runs the one app named in startup_app (Welcome, as shipped) on its small screen (StickS3 240 x 135, AtomS3R 128 x 128) Setting up Wi-Fi Over BLE from the Family mruby Console: power on with the button held to enter setup mode. With no Wi-Fi settings at all the board starts in setup mode by itself. BLE runs only in setup mode Apps at a time Three, as on Retro (see Heap Size)

docs.title: Studio (the browser build)
docs.text:
Network FmrbNet.request fetches through the browser, so a server that refuses cross-origin requests cannot be read. Sockets — Net::HTTP, WebSocket — are not there Files /home and /app/usr are kept in the browser and nowhere else, and so are the settings. Everything outside them is built fresh on every reload. Download the archive to keep anything Browsers Desktop Chrome and Firefox. Safari is untested; phones and tablets are not a target, because the machine wants a keyboard One tab Open the page twice and only the first tab saves

See Family mruby Studio.

docs.title: Release Notes
docs.text:
What each release changed, newest first. Firmware comes from the installer; the version a machine is running is in the system menu under About. Studio always runs the newest one.

Every release replaces the whole flash image, /home included. Copy anything you want to keep off the device before flashing — see Console.

docs.title: 3.1.1 — 2026-11-28
docs.text:
A fix release. The Tab5 no longer restarts when a button in the Wi-Fi window is pressed, some writes to the flash no longer risk stopping the machine, and the UART guide describes the serial MIDI output as it behaves since 3.1.0.

The display firmware stays 3.1.0, so a 3.1.0 board needs only the main chip written (NARYA v3's WROVER does not need rewriting).

docs.title: 3.1.0 — 2026-11-27
docs.text: Applies to Modern, Retro, the headless boards, the Linux program and Studio.

docs.title: Changed: writing an app
docs.text:
Apps written for 3.0.0 need small changes:

  • No start code at the end of the file. The runtime starts the FmrbApp subclass the file defines; delete the trailing MyApp.new.start (and its begin/rescue). A file with more than one subclass names the one to start with class = "MyApp" in its metadata. A file where none can be picked, or an exception while starting, shows the reason in an error window. → Hello World
  • @gfx draws from the top-left of the app's own area. Inside the frame of a framed window, the window's top-left without a frame, the screen's in fullscreen. @user_area_x0 and @user_area_y0 are gone: drop the @user_area_x0 + additions. Mouse ev[:x] / ev[:y], sprites and UI widgets use the same origin; ev[:wx] / ev[:wy] and window_gfx are there for the window's own coordinates. → Drawing
  • System methods moved to FmrbSystem. The 34 class methods that change the machine (reboot, set_wallclock, the Wi-Fi, BLE, power and volume settings ...) are FmrbSystem.<name> now; FmrbApp.<name> keeps the ones an app reads. → Application
  • clear_time is clear_timer.
  • Metadata in the .rb. The .app.toml keys can also go in a #---fmrb comment at the top of the file; with both, a key in the .app.toml wins. → App Config
  • Lua apps run on a shell the system provides: define on_create / on_update / on_event and draw with the global gfx. → Lua
  • Lua and MicroPython follow Ruby's argument order. Lua's gfx:draw_text is (x, y, text, color), and the sizes are functions: FmrbApp.user_area_width(), user_area_height(), window_width(), window_height(). In MicroPython, _fmrb.read_file and _fmrb.file_size gave way to FmrbFile, and gfx.clear() needs its colour. → Other languages

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• UART for apps. A UART class with PicoRuby's API (UART.new(unit:, txd_pin:, rxd_pin:, baudrate:), gets, puts, read, write ...), guarded so that an app cannot open the system's own ports or pins, and a Serial Terminal app to try a device by hand. On the Tab5 the Grove port is free for it. → Hardware Control
  • Remote shell. An Asterism console's Terminal can enter a machine (remote <node>) to look at and change its files and apps, once its owner turns it on in the Receiving app; a mark (RS) on the menu bar shows while someone is in.
  • Remote control is closed on release builds until the owner allows it (Config > Remote control) and pairs a PC. → Remote Desktop
  • The editor holds up to five documents in tabs, with File > New and Close.
  • Chat (rooms kept by a chat host) and the AI helper (asks a tutor host over Asterism and puts hints or whole apps into the editor), on Modern machines on an Asterism network.
  • The P4-Nano starts at 640x360; Config has a Resolution row (426x240 or 640x360), and holding Shift while it starts brings it back at 426x240.
  • Kanji conversion in kana input, with a dictionary on the SD card. → The Desktop
  • Wi-Fi from the screen. The Network dialog opens a Wi-Fi page: pick a network, type the password; up to five are remembered and the strongest in reach is joined. → Connecting to Wi-Fi
  • The window menu. Right-click a title bar for Send to, Reload and Close.
  • Frameless windows (window_frame = "none"), with the Avatar sample. → App Config
  • Asterism wire protocol 2 (the asterism gem 0.14.0): connections are objects, topics carry declared types, and a shared place holds data with no single owner. Not compatible with 3.0.0 on the wire. → Network
  • Sending files and apps between machines over Asterism, with the Receiving app deciding whether, and from whom, this machine takes them. In the Shell, move is now amove, beside asend, anodes and areceive. → Shell Commands
  • The Linux program: a CRT look for the whole screen, Log Out in the power menu, touchpad taps and touch screens, routers with TLS, and an arm64 package. → The Linux Program
  • WebAssembly apps. Apps written in C, TinyGo, Rust or Zig and compiled to WebAssembly run on WAMR on the ESP32-P4 boards, the Linux program, the simulator and Studio (not on the ESP32-S3 boards), with the same functions Ruby apps have. The SDK is family-mruby-sdk; the same tour app in each language ships under /app/tinygo, /app/rust, /app/zig and /app/c, and an app dropped on the Studio page runs there. → WebAssembly Apps
  • One definition for every language. The functions apps call are generated from the firmware's type definitions for Ruby, Lua, MicroPython and WebAssembly alike. Lua gained sound, the log, the clipboard, the clocks, the window's state and files; MicroPython gained the rest of FmrbGfx (arcs, get_pixel, masks, blend_rect ...), FmrbApp.uptime_ms() and 64-bit integers. → Other languages
  • FmrbFile: read, write, append, list and delete whole files by path, the same in every language. → Files & I/O
  • A new boot. The logo comes on like a CRT television, over a chord that rises a fifth, and the desktop is up in about 1.2 seconds instead of 2.7. → The Desktop
  • The error window closes with Return or Esc as well as a click. The Monitor has a page for the WebAssembly runtime, ps in the Shell has an ENGINE column, and the launcher has an icon per language.
  • Smaller storage. Sprites, tile sheets, wallpapers and icons are palette PNGs (SpriteImage#load_bmp and TileSheet read PNG as well as BMP), and the voices are IMA-ADPCM WAVs, which play_wav plays. On the ESP32-P4 boards the Japanese fonts moved to a partition of their own. → Image & Icon Files, Sound, Hardware
  • /home over Wi-Fi. The file endpoints reach every path, keys included, so /home can be backed up before flashing and put back after. → Remote Desktop, Security
  • /app/test and Walk Scroller are left out of every board's image and the public browser build; they can be sent to a board over Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Machine.delay_ms and the like waited about a tenth of the time asked on the ESP32 machines.
  • Files, JSON, MIDI and Kernel methods behave as documented: each app has its own current folder for Dir.chdir, and GPIO refuses the system's pins.
  • Large Asterism messages over TLS no longer drop the connection (file transfers to a machine were slow because of it).
  • ls and the file lists mark folders on the ESP32 machines.
  • The F1 help jumps to a nested class's method, and String's class page is back.
  • The transfer app (receiving and sending files, moving apps, the remote shell) is built into the firmware and needs far less memory and stack.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
• NARYA v3 (Retro): the flash layout changed (the firmware partition grew from 6 MB to 8 MB, storage from 5 MB to 7.94 MB). The installer writes everything, which erases /home: copy what you keep first.
  • The core and the graphics-audio firmware must be the same version: on Retro, flash both chips.
  • The kanji dictionary is attached to the GitHub release: put fmrb_kanji.dic in /dict/ on the SD card. → The Desktop
  • Checked on the device: the Tab5 (the release build) and the P4-Nano. NARYA v3, StickS3 and AtomS3R are built by CI and checked in the simulator.

docs.title: 3.0.0 — 2026-11-07
docs.text: Applies to Modern, Retro, the headless boards, the Linux program and Studio.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• The Linux program. Family mruby as one program on a Linux PC: an amd64 .deb on the GitHub release (Ubuntu 26.04 or newer), chosen at the login screen. → The Linux Program
  • Headless boards. M5Stack StickS3 and AtomS3R run a single app on an Asterism network, flashed from the Web Installer.
  • Moving a running app. An app that declares movable = true can be written to an image and carried on from it, on the same machine or another one. → Application
  • Asterism. Machines on one network call each other's Ruby objects, with a game host for shared tables: Hide Jong (mahjong), Othello and a drawing board. → Default Apps
  • A high-resolution fullscreen. An app with fullscreen_hires = true runs at 640x360 while it is fullscreen on Modern and in Studio.
  • Mute and volume. A speaker in the menu bar mutes the whole machine with one click, and Config has a volume from 0 to 10. Both are remembered, on every machine and in Studio. → The Desktop
  • Icons on the desktop. The Launcher, the Editor, the Shell, the File Manager and a few apps sit on the wallpaper; the launcher's right-click menu adds and removes them. → The Desktop
  • A power button at the right end of the menu bar. Reset moved there from the system menu.
  • BLE Setup. A few minutes, opened on the machine, in which the web console may read and write the Wi-Fi and Asterism settings and the keys; outside it they are never read remotely. The speech service's API key moved from the service list to /home/secrets.toml. → System Services
  • The editor's font. View → Font picks 8, 12 or 16 pixels, kept in /home/editor.toml.
  • One clipboard for every app, joined to the PC's in the Linux program and to the page's in Studio. FmrbApp.clipboard / FmrbApp.set_clipboard.
  • Small helpers for app screens. fit_text, wrap_text, draw_text_lines and draw_button on @gfx, and FmrbUI::HitAreas for a screen drawn whole. → Drawing, UI Widgets
  • Settings and state for apps. app_settings (in /home) and app_state (in /tmp); the File Manager reopens in the folder it was closed in. → Application
  • FmrbAudio#main_volume= sets the volume of the music alone. → Sound
  • Resizable windows show a triangle in the bottom-right corner to drag. The File Manager asks before it deletes.
  • The launcher's rescan is a Reload button in its title bar (or F5).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• App memory on the ESP32-S3 boards. Three pools in all — one ordinary and two large — so three user apps run at a time. → Limitations
  • The Wi-Fi settings are read from /home/wifi.toml first, then /etc/wifi.toml.
  • HTTPS on the boards trusts a trimmed set of root certificates instead of the full bundle.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: The core and the graphics-audio firmware must be the same version: on Retro, flash both chips. The kanji dictionary for kanji conversion (added after 3.0.0) is not part of 3.0.0.

docs.title: 2.1.0 — 2026-09-09
docs.text: Applies to Modern, Retro, the simulator and Studio.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• Family mruby Studio. The firmware is compiled to WebAssembly and published, so the desktop, the editor and the sound chip run in a browser tab with nothing installed. → Studio
  • The App Store. It heads the launcher, fetches a published list over Wi-Fi, shows what fits on this machine and installs into /app/usr. On both boards and in the browser.
  • System services (Modern). Small resident jobs: the clock sets itself from the network, the machine publishes its own address, and text can be read aloud. The list is a file you can edit. → System Services
  • Colours you can change. The window frame, the desktop, the editor and the shell take their colours from the system theme, and any of them can be overridden by name in /home/colors.toml. The shell has a color command that writes it for you. → Colours
  • One table decides which app opens a file. A .md opens as a presentation, a .nsf in the music player, a .rb runs. → File Associations
  • New apps. PicoRabbit presents a slide deck written in Markdown, Robo Explorer is a maze you solve by writing the robot's brain, and Modern gains a video player, a microphone spectrum and a readout of its motion sensor. → Default Apps
  • Japanese in the editor. Kana input with Ctrl + Space, kanji on screen, and an editor that takes the whole screen.
  • Help on every method. F1 in the editor answers for all 577 of them, in two layers.
  • UI widgets. Buttons, lists, checkboxes and the rest, for apps that want them. → UI Widgets
  • FmrbNet.request. Fetch something without stopping the app, with the same code on a board and in the browser. → Network
  • The mouse wheel. The editor, the shell, the log and the file dialogs scroll with it.
  • Files and apps over Wi-Fi on Retro too. /fs and /app answer on both machines now; only the screen is Modern's. → Remote Desktop
  • Each board names itself. fmruby-XXXXXX.local, after its own MAC, and fmruby.local still answers. → Connecting to Wi-Fi
  • boot_splash and startup_app. Skip the logo and the jingle, or open one app as soon as the desktop is up. → The Desktop
  • WAV playback (Modern). play_wav mixes a file on top of the sound chip.
  • /home is yours. The samples, sprites, sounds and decks moved to /usr/share, and /home ships empty. → Files & I/O

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• on_event no longer needs super(ev). The base class keeps its own state in @_-prefixed names, and @running / @name are read through running? / name. Apps written against 2.0 keep working: an old super(ev) reaches an empty method. → FmrbApp
  • The theme presets are light, dark and cyberpunk. classic is gone; what it named is light.
  • The falling-block sample is BlockGame. Only the name changed.
  • flappy.rb is flappy.app.rb, like every other app.
  • Studio no longer offers colours on the page. Pick a theme in Config, inside the machine.
  • Modern's app pool is 1024 KB, and 2048 KB with large_memory = 1. Retro is unchanged. → Limitations
  • app_spawn_margin_kb decides how much internal RAM a start has to leave for the rest of the machine. → System Configuration

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Retro has to be flashed on both chips

The protocol between the two chips went from 4 to 5, and the check is strict: a 2.0.x fmruby-graphics-audio against a 2.1.0 fmruby-core does not boot. Flash both from the installer. → Firmware Update

Modern is one chip and needs only the Tab5 firmware.

docs.title: 2.0.1 — 2026-08-08
docs.text:
A maintenance release. The flash image stopped carrying the caches a development machine leaves behind, [[launcher_exclude]] hides whole app categories from the launcher, and Retro's desktop wallpaper reaches the WROVER as it already did in the simulator.

Both chips are at protocol 4, as in 2.0.0, so a 2.0.0 board can take this on one chip.

docs.title: 2.0.0 — 2026-08-07
docs.text: The release that added the second machine.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• Modern (ESP32-P4). A stock M5Stack Tab5, flashed from the browser, with its own panel, speaker, touch screen and Wi-Fi. → Modern
  • Remote desktop. The Tab5 serves its screen over Wi-Fi, and a browser on the same network drives it with a PC keyboard and mouse. → Remote Desktop
  • FMRuby BASIC. A Family BASIC-compatible interpreter with its own text screen, sprites and sound. → FMRuby BASIC
  • MicroPython. A .py file runs as an ordinary app.
  • MIDI. Serial MIDI out on the Tab5's GROVE port, MML from Ruby, and a player for standard MIDI files. → MIDI
  • A debugger on the device. Breakpoints and variables from the editor, and the same session over BLE or TCP from a PC. → Debugging
  • Ctrl + Tab. Switch between the running apps, and park a fullscreen one where it stands. → The Desktop
  • Per-app stack size. task_stack_kb in .app.toml, for an app that needs more than the default. → App Config
  • The Spinel ahead-of-time compiler became the standard engine for the kernel and the desktop, and the boot scan went from 13 s to 7.8 s.
  • The filesystem took its current shape: /app, /usr/share, /etc, /var — /data is gone.
  • Two fingers on the Tab5's touch screen are a right click.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: Retro has to be flashed on both chips: the protocol between them went from 3 to 4.

docs.title: 1.0.0 — 2026-05-19
docs.text: The first release. Retro (the narya-board) with the desktop, the launcher, the editor, the shell, tile maps and rounded windows, plus the sprite and map editors that run in a browser on the PC side.

docs.title: API Reference Overview
docs.text:
Lists all public Ruby APIs provided by Family mruby. Click each API name to jump to its detail page.

How to read this reference

The API is the same on both machines. An app written for one runs on the other.

Where these pages say "the graphics side", they mean whichever part of the hardware turns your drawing commands into a picture: on Retro that is a second chip across a UART link, and on Modern it is the same ESP32-P4 your code is running on. The calls are identical; only the cost differs, and Modern is the cheaper of the two.

A handful of things exist on one machine only — NTSC output adjustment on Retro, touch on Modern. Those are marked where they appear. See Choose your hardware for the full list.

docs.title: Key Instance Variables (when inheriting FmrbApp)
docs.text:
Variable Description @gfx FmrbGfx instance name App display name (from .toml app_screen_name) platform :esp32 / :linux running? true while the app is running fullscreen? Whether the app is in fullscreen mode @window_width / @window_height Overall window size @user_area_width / @user_area_height Size of the app's area. @gfx and mouse events take its top-left as (0, 0) @pos_x / @pos_y Top-left coordinates of the window (screen coordinate system). Changes when the window is moved

In fullscreen, (@pos_x, @pos_y) is (0, 0), pointing at the top-left of the screen. The base class keeps its own state in @_-prefixed variables, so what an app assigns is its own — see FmrbApp.

docs.title: Coordinate System and Color Format
docs.text:
• Coordinate system: origin at the top-left (0, 0) of the app's area (inside the frame of a framed window, the window or screen otherwise), X increases rightward, Y increases downward
  • Color: RGB332 (8-bit, R:3 G:3 B:2). Use constants like FmrbGfx::WHITE or generate with FmrbGfx.rgb_to_332(r, g, b)

docs.title: Drawing Flow
docs.text:
Drawing commands (fill_rect, etc.)
  | Accumulated in buffer
@gfx.present
  | Applied to screen

Nothing appears until present is called

Drawing methods are not displayed on screen until @gfx.present is called. Sprite operations such as SpriteInstance#move are also composited at the present timing.

Class reference: every class

docs.title: Sound (FmrbAudio)
docs.text:
FmrbAudio is the audio playback API. Create an instance by calling FmrbAudio.new(self).

class MyApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    @audio = FmrbAudio.new(self)
  end
end

Internally, it sends MSG_TYPE_APP_AUDIO messages to the kernel, which are processed by the audio engine on the graphics side.

Supported file formats

For details on supported audio file formats, see Audio File Formats.

docs.title: File Playback
docs.text:
Method Purpose play(path, track: 0) Start playing a file stop Stop playback pause Pause playback resume Resume playback

path is a file path (e.g. /usr/share/sounds/nsf/song.nsf). track: specifies the track number (used for files like NSF that contain multiple tracks).

docs.title: Playing a recording (play_wav)
docs.text:
@audio.play_wav("/home/voice.wav")
Method Purpose play_wav(path) Play a WAV mixed on top of the sound chip. true if it started stop_wav Stop it

Mono, 8-48 kHz, up to 2 MB, either 16-bit PCM or 4-bit IMA-ADPCM (WAV format 0x11, about a quarter of the size; in the development version). An ADPCM file is decoded as it plays, so it takes no more memory than the file itself. ffmpeg -i in.wav -ac 1 -c:a adpcm_ima_wav out.wav makes one; the voices that ship with the system are stored this way. It rides over whatever the sound chip is playing, so a spoken line or a recorded chime does not interrupt the music. One clip at a time for the whole machine: starting another replaces it.

Modern only

play_wav returns false on Retro without sending anything, so an app can call it unconditionally and fall back on the answer — which is what the hourly chime does: a recording if it can, its note if it cannot. Retro's audio lives on the WROVER at the far end of a serial link, and shipping a clip across it before a note could sound is too slow to be worth it.

docs.title: The microphone (Modern only)
docs.text:
Method Purpose mic_available? Whether this machine has one mic_rate Samples per second. Fixed by the hardware, so a spectrum's bin width follows from it mic_enable(on = true) Start or stop sampling mic_read(count, timeout_ms = 200) count 16-bit samples as a byte String, or nil if they did not arrive

Nothing is recorded and nothing leaves the device; the samples are handed to the app and that is all. The bundled Mic Spectrum app is the worked example.

docs.title: FMSQ Sequences
docs.text:
A mechanism for pre-loading sequences into slots before playback. Suitable for short sound effects and looping BGM.

Method Purpose load_fmsq(slot_id, binary_data) Register binary data into a slot. Bounded by the message size, so a real score does not fit load_fmsq_file(slot_id, path) Load a slot from a file already on the audio side (put it there with @gfx.sync_file first). This is the route for anything bigger than a jingle play_slot(slot_id) Play a registered slot 
data = File.open("/sfx.fmsq", "r") { |f| f.read }
@audio.load_fmsq(0, data)
@audio.play_slot(0)

For detailed specifications, see Audio File Formats.

docs.title: Tone Synthesis (note_on / note_off)
docs.text:
Directly drives NES APU-compatible channels. Allows playing short sound effects and game BGM from scripts.

@audio.note_on(channel, freq, volume = 10, duty = 2, sweep = 0)
@audio.note_off(channel)
Argument Range and Meaning channel Channel number. NES APU configuration: 0 / 1 = pulse wave, 2 = triangle wave, 3 = noise freq Frequency (Hz). Integer. May have a different meaning on the noise channel volume Volume. Approximately 0 to 15. Default 10 duty Pulse wave duty cycle. 0 to 3 sweep Frequency sweep value (packed APU register value)

docs.title: Example: Piano-style
docs.text:
class MiniPiano < FmrbApp
  KEYS = {
    "a" => 261, "s" => 293, "d" => 329, "f" => 349,
    "g" => 392, "h" => 440, "j" => 493, "k" => 523
  }

  def on_create
    @audio = FmrbAudio.new(self)
    @ch = 0
  end

  def on_event(ev)
    return unless ev[:character]
    if ev[:type] == :key_down && (freq = KEYS[ev[:character]])
      @audio.note_on(@ch, freq, 10, 2, 0)
    elsif ev[:type] == :key_up
      @audio.note_off(@ch)
    end
  end
end

docs.title: Track Numbers and Playback Control
docs.text:
Use Case Recommended Track BGM 0 SE (Sound Effects) 1 and above

Calling play(path, track:) with different track numbers simultaneously enables parallel playback on separate tracks (implementation dependent).

docs.title: The music's own volume
docs.text:
@audio.main_volume = 30   # percent, 100 to start with

Only the music changes — what play and play_slot play on the MAIN sound chip. Sound effects (SUB), WAVs and the machine's volume stay where they are, and it goes back to 100 when the app closes. The mahjong table uses it for a BGM that sits under the effects.

docs.title: NSF File Playback
docs.text:
NES Sound Format is supported.

@audio.play("/usr/share/sounds/nsf/song.nsf", track: 1)

A playback GUI sample is available in tool/nsf_player.app.rb. For details, see Audio File Formats.

docs.title: When a song is over (nsf_status)
docs.text:
An NSF has no length, so the audio side decides when a song is over — silence, its loop heard twice, or a time limit — and stops it. Ask about once a second and move on when it is over (development branch, after 3.0.0):

st = @audio.nsf_status            # nil when there is no answer
next_song if st && st[:state] == FmrbAudio::NSF_ENDED

st[:state] is NSF_IDLE, NSF_PLAYING, NSF_FADING or NSF_ENDED; st[:reason] says why it ended: NSF_END_SILENCE, NSF_END_LOOP or NSF_END_LIMIT.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
To stop any playing audio when the app exits, it is safe to call stop in on_destroy.

def on_destroy
  @audio.stop if @audio
end

docs.text:
• Audio File Formats -- FMSQ / NSF specifications and how to create them
  • MIDI -- driving this same sound chip through a MIDI device, or sending MIDI to an external instrument
  • Default Apps -- piano, flappy, nsf_player, and more
