docs.title: Processing-style Drawing (P5)
docs.text: P5 is a Processing / p5.js-style drawing DSL. It wraps FmrbGfx internally and lets you draw shapes in a p5 style with stateful fill / stroke / translate / rotate and more. P5 is built into picoruby-fmrb-app, so no additional require is needed.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
class MyApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    @p5 = P5.new(@gfx)
  end

  def on_update
    @p5.background(P5::BLACK)
    @p5.fill(P5::RED)
    @p5.no_stroke
    @p5.rect(10, 10, 60, 40)
    @p5.present
    33
  end
end

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
P5.new(gfx)

Argument: FmrbApp#@gfx (a FmrbGfx instance). Store it in your subclass as @p5 = P5.new(@gfx).

docs.title: Screen
docs.text: Method Purpose width Width of the app's area (the user area) height Height of the app's area background(color) Fill the entire screen with color present (alias: commit) Apply the frame to the screen

docs.title: Color Constants
docs.text:
Mirrors of FmrbGfx::* (RGB332).

P5::BLACK / WHITE / RED / GREEN / BLUE / YELLOW / CYAN / MAGENTA / GRAY

Custom colors can be specified with P5#color(r, g, b) (which calls FmrbGfx.rgb_to_332 internally) or directly as an RGB332 integer.

docs.title: Drawing State
docs.text: Method Purpose fill(color) / no_fill Fill color / disable fill stroke(color) / no_stroke Stroke color / disable stroke stroke_weight(w) Stroke width (>1 is implemented with parallel lines) blend_mode(mode) Blend mode (see below)

docs.title: Blend Mode
docs.text:
Constants provided: P5::REPLACE / P5::ADD / P5::XOR / P5::SUBTRACT / P5::MULTIPLY / P5::SCREEN.

Blend mode limitations

The backend only supports REPLACE / ADD / XOR, and these only take effect on rectangle fills (rect(), background()). Other shapes and SUBTRACT / MULTIPLY / SCREEN fall back to REPLACE behavior.

docs.title: Basic Shapes
docs.text:
Method Signature point(x, y) Single pixel (uses stroke color) line(x0, y0, x1, y1) Line rect(x, y, w, h) Rectangle (fill + stroke) circle(cx, cy, r) Circle ellipse(cx, cy, rx, ry) Ellipse triangle(x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2) Triangle arc(cx, cy, r, start, stop) Arc (angles in radians) bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3, x4, y4) Cubic Bezier (subdivided into 20 line segments) curve(x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3, x4, y4) Catmull-Rom spline quad(x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3) Quadrilateral begin_shape / vertex(x, y) / end_shape(close = false) A free polygon: open the shape, add its points, close it. end_shape(true) joins the last point to the first

alpha does nothing

It is accepted so that code written against p5.js still runs, but this machine has no alpha channel — a colour is one of 256, opaque. For translucency use blend_rect or the blend_mode below.

Arc mode

The p5.js OPEN / CHORD / PIE modes are not supported. Arcs are always drawn as a combination of pie shape (fill_arc) and outer ring (draw_arc).

docs.title: Affine Transforms
docs.text:
Uses the same post-multiply composition as p5.js / Processing (M' = M * op). translate(tx, ty); rotate(theta); rect(-30,-20,60,40) produces the standard behavior of rotating around the local origin after translation.

Method Purpose translate(tx, ty) Translation rotate(angle) Rotation (radians) scale(sx, sy = sx) Scaling push_matrix / pop_matrix Save / restore the matrix reset_matrix Reset to the identity matrix

When the matrix contains only translations, a fast path is used. When rotation or scaling is involved, it switches to a slower path with triangle decomposition.

docs.title: Text
Image
docs.text: Method Purpose image(image_id, x, y, scale_x = 1.0, scale_y = 0.0) Draw an image obtained via FmrbGfx#create_image_from_file. When scale_y = 0.0, it uses the same value as scale_x image_masked(image_id, mask_data, x, y, w, h) Draw with a 1bpp mask

docs.title: Pixel Operations
docs.text:
Method Purpose set_pixel(x, y, color) Direct pixel write get_pixel(x, y) Read back a pixel (slow due to round-trip to graphics side)

get_pixel cost

get_pixel is a synchronous call: it flushes every unsent drawing command, reads on the graphics side, and waits for the answer. On Retro that answer crosses the UART link, so a single pixel costs several milliseconds; it is cheaper on Modern but still a round trip. Avoid calling it in loops. Maintaining a local 2D array of drawing state is much faster than per-pixel reads.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class P5Spinner < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    @p5 = P5.new(@gfx)
    @angle = 0.0
  end

  def on_update
    @p5.background(P5::BLACK)
    cx = @p5.width / 2
    cy = @p5.height / 2

    @p5.push_matrix
    @p5.translate(cx, cy)
    @p5.rotate(@angle)
    @p5.fill(P5::CYAN)
    @p5.no_stroke
    @p5.rect(-20, -20, 40, 40)
    @p5.pop_matrix

    @p5.present
    @angle += 0.1
    33
  end
end

The P5 pages of the PicoRuby demo (/app/demo/picoruby.app.rb) walk through the lot: basic shapes, affine transforms, Bezier, text, arcs, blend and get_pixel.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• FmrbGfx -- The internal wrapper. Accessible via P5#@gfx
  • Sprite -- Lower-level drawing and performance-oriented API

Class reference: P5

docs.title: Hardware Control (GPIO / I2C / UART / RMT / RTC)
docs.text:
APIs for operating hardware peripherals from Ruby.

Note

For pin layouts and electrical specifications, see Hardware. To check whether a pin is already in use by another function, use FmrbHw.pin_status.

Pin numbers differ between the machines

The GROVE pins are not the same on Retro and Modern, so an app that hardcodes a number runs on one machine only. Branch on the board instead:

ruby sda, scl = case FmrbConst::BOARD when "tab5", "naryav4" then [53, 54] # Tab5 GROVE else [47, 48] # narya-board GROVE 2 end

Some pins are held by the system and cannot be acquired at all — see Hardware for the reserved list on each machine.

docs.title: GPIO
docs.text: Digital input/output.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
GPIO.new(pin, flags, alt_function = 0)
Argument Purpose pin GPIO number flags Direction and pull configuration (can be OR-combined) alt_function Alternate function number (normally 0)

docs.title: flags Constants
docs.text:
Constant Meaning GPIO::IN Input GPIO::OUT Output GPIO::HIGH_Z High impedance GPIO::PULL_UP Pull-up resistor enabled GPIO::PULL_DOWN Pull-down resistor enabled GPIO::OPEN_DRAIN Open drain output GPIO::ALT Alternate function

Combine with OR:

btn = GPIO.new(10, GPIO::IN | GPIO::PULL_UP)
led = GPIO.new(11, GPIO::OUT)

docs.title: Instance Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose read Read the level (0 / 1) write(val) Output 0 or 1 high? Returns true if the level is High low? Returns true if the level is Low

docs.title: Class Methods (Direct Operation Without Creating an Instance)
docs.text: Method Purpose GPIO.read_at(pin) Read level GPIO.write_at(pin, val) Output level GPIO.high_at?(pin) / GPIO.low_at?(pin) Level check GPIO.set_dir_at(pin, dir) Change direction only GPIO.pull_up_at(pin) / GPIO.pull_down_at(pin) Enable pull resistor GPIO.open_drain_at(pin) Open drain GPIO.set_function_at(pin, alt) Alternate function

docs.title: Example: Toggle LED with a Button
docs.text:
class LedToggle < FmrbApp
  BTN_PIN = 10
  LED_PIN = 11

  def on_create
    @btn = GPIO.new(BTN_PIN, GPIO::IN | GPIO::PULL_UP)
    @led = GPIO.new(LED_PIN, GPIO::OUT)
    @led.write(0)
    @prev = 1
  end

  def on_update
    cur = @btn.read
    if @prev == 1 && cur == 0   # Falling edge
      @led.write(@led.read == 1 ? 0 : 1)
    end
    @prev = cur
    20
  end
end

docs.title: I2C
docs.text: Communicates with devices via the I2C bus.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
I2C.new(unit:, frequency: 100_000, sda_pin: -1, scl_pin: -1, timeout: 500)
Argument Purpose unit: Bus identifier. e.g. "ESP32_I2C0", "ESP32_I2C1" frequency: Clock frequency (Hz). Default 100kHz sda_pin: / scl_pin: -1 uses the default pins timeout: Timeout in ms

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose read(addr_7bit, length, timeout: @timeout, *write_data) Read (write_data triggers a write first, then read without STOP) write(addr_7bit, *data, timeout: @timeout) Write. Accepts Integer / Array<Integer> / String scan(timeout: @timeout) Scan addresses 0x08 to 0x77 and return a list of responding devices close Release the bus

docs.title: Example: Scanning I2C Devices
docs.text:
i2c = I2C.new(unit: "ESP32_I2C0", frequency: 400_000)
addrs = i2c.scan
Log.info("found: #{addrs.map { |a| a.to_s(16) }.join(', ')}")

docs.title: Example: Register Read/Write
docs.text:
i2c = I2C.new(unit: "ESP32_I2C0")
# Read 4 bytes starting from register 0x10
data = i2c.read(0x32, 4, 0x10)   # Arguments after the 2nd are write_data
i2c.write(0x32, 0x10, 0xAB)      # Write 0xAB to register 0x10

docs.title: RMT
docs.text: Drives WS2812B / WS2812 LEDs and infrared remotes via the ESP32 RMT peripheral.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
RMT.new(pin, t0h_ns:, t0l_ns:, t1h_ns:, t1l_ns:, reset_ns:)

Specifies NRZ encoding timing in nanoseconds. Standard values for WS2812B:

rmt = RMT.new(8,
              t0h_ns: 350,  t0l_ns: 900,
              t1h_ns: 700,  t1l_ns: 600,
              reset_ns: 50_000)

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose write(*params) Output byte sequence. Accepts Integer / Array / String arguments

docs.title: Example: Lighting WS2812B LEDs
docs.text:
class LedStrip < FmrbApp
  RMT_PIN = 8

  def on_create
    @rmt = RMT.new(RMT_PIN,
                    t0h_ns: 350,  t0l_ns: 900,
                    t1h_ns: 700,  t1l_ns: 600,
                    reset_ns: 50_000)
    set_color(0xFF, 0x00, 0x00)  # Red
  end

  def set_color(r, g, b)
    # WS2812B uses GRB order
    @rmt.write([g, r, b])
  end
end

A WS2812B matrix sample is available in /app/demo/led_matrix.app.rb.

The app draws the same pattern on screen as it sends to the panel, so you can see what it intends to do even with nothing wired up. Note the LED_PIN branch on FmrbConst::BOARD near the top of the source — the GROVE pins differ between the machines.

docs.title: Real-Time Clock (RX8900 / RX8130)
docs.text:
Both machines carry a battery-backed RTC on the I2C bus, at address 0x32. The part differs:

Machine Part Class Retro (narya-board) RX8900, on I2C1, shared with GROVE 1 RX8900 Modern (M5Stack Tab5) RX8130, on the internal bus RX8130

The two classes take the same arguments and answer to the same methods, so an app that picks the class by board runs on either:

i2c = I2C.new(unit: "ESP32_I2C0")
rtc = FmrbConst::BOARD == "tab5" ? RX8130.new(i2c) : RX8900.new(i2c)
rtc.sync_system_clock

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Return value / purpose init Initialise the RTC read_time {year:, month:, day:, hour:, minute:, second:, wday:} write_time(hash) Write a time sync_system_clock Set the system clock from the RTC. true on success vlf? Low-voltage flag. true means the stored time may be lost temperature Temperature in Celsius (Float). RX8900 only

docs.title: Example: sync the clock at startup
docs.text:
class ClockSyncApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    i2c = I2C.new(unit: "ESP32_I2C0")
    rtc = FmrbConst::BOARD == "tab5" ? RX8130.new(i2c) : RX8900.new(i2c)
    if rtc.vlf?
      Log.warn("RTC battery low; resetting")
      rtc.write_time(year: 2026, month: 1, day: 1,
                     hour: 0, minute: 0, second: 0, wday: 4)
    end
    rtc.sync_system_clock
    now = rtc.read_time
    Log.info("time: #{now[:year]}-#{now[:month]}-#{now[:day]} #{now[:hour]}:#{now[:minute]}")
  end
end

You usually do not need this

The system syncs from the RTC at boot, and FmrbApp.wallclock / FmrbSystem.set_wallclock go through the system clock (POSIX epoch), which also writes back to the RTC. Reach for the driver classes only when you want the chip's own features — the low-voltage flag, or the RX8900's temperature sensor.

docs.title: Six-Axis Sensor (BMI270, Modern only)
docs.text:
Modern carries a BMI270 accelerometer and gyroscope on its internal I2C bus, which the display driver serialises — so an ordinary I2C instance is all it takes.

i2c = I2C.new(unit: :ESP32_I2C1,
              sda_pin: FmrbHw::PIN_I2C1_SDA,
              scl_pin: FmrbHw::PIN_I2C1_SCL)
imu = BMI270.new(i2c)
if imu.probe && imu.init
  a = imu.read_accel     # {x:, y:, z:} in g
  g = imu.read_gyro      # {x:, y:, z:} in degrees per second
end
Method Return value / purpose BMI270.new(i2c, addr = nil) The address is found among 0x68 and 0x69 when not given probe Whether the part answered init(config_path = "/usr/share/imu/bmi270_config.bin") Upload the sensor's configuration blob. It has to be done once after power-on, and takes a moment ready? Whether the configuration took read_accel Acceleration, {x:, y:, z:} in g read_gyro Angular rate, {x:, y:, z:} in degrees per second read_raw Both, as raw 16-bit counts: {ax:, ay:, az:, gx:, gy:, gz:} read_temperature Degrees Celsius address / error The address it found, and why the last step failed

The bundled IMU app (/app/modern/imu.app.rb) is the worked example: it keeps drawing with a synthetic tilt on a board without the part, and says so on its status line.

docs.title: UART (serial)
docs.text: Apps can exchange text and bytes with a serial device wired to the board's pins (a LoRa radio, a GPS, another microcontroller ...). To just try it, open Serial Terminal from the menu, pick the unit, the pins and the speed, press Open, then type a line in the box at the bottom and press Enter to send it. What arrives is listed in the middle. (Family mruby 3.1.0 or later.)

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
• Cross TX and RX: our TX goes to the other side's RX, our RX to its TX.
  • Always connect GND, so both sides share the same reference.
  • The signals are 3.3 V. A device with 5 V signals can damage the board when wired directly: put a level shifter in between.
  • Use the same speed (baud rate) on both sides. 9600 and 115200 are common.

docs.title: Units and pins per board
docs.text:
A unit is the UART's number (1 for UART1). The pins in the table are examples; other free pins can be chosen too.

Board Units an app may open Example pins (TX, RX) Tab5 1, 2, 3, 4 the Grove port, G53 and G54 NARYA v4 (P4-Nano) 1, 2, 3, 4 free pins of the expansion header AtomS3R 1, 2 Grove, 2 and 1 StickS3 1, 2 Grove, 9 and 10 NARYA v3 2 GROVE 2, 47 and 48
  • UART0 (the console) and NARYA v3's UART1 (the link to the drawing side) are the system's and cannot be opened.
  • Pins used for the screen, the SD card, the radio, sound and the like cannot be chosen; you are told why.
  • On the Linux simulator only UART2 opens, and what you write comes straight back. The browser and the PC builds have no UART.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Hello < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    # unit and pins: the Tab5's Grove port
    @u = UART.new(unit: 1, txd_pin: 53, rxd_pin: 54, baudrate: 115200)
    @u.puts "hello"
  end

  def on_update
    line = @u.gets       # never waits
    Log.info(line) if line
    50
  end
end
  • Reading (gets, read, getbyte) never waits: it gives nil until something has arrived, so call it in every on_update. write and puts wait until the bytes are sent.
  • The API follows PicoRuby's UART class; close, closed? and dropped are added.
  • When the app ends, the system closes the UARTs it opened.
  • When it cannot be opened you get an IOError (in use, a system pin ...) or an ArgumentError (no such unit or pin ...), with the reason in the message.

docs.title: With the serial MIDI output
docs.text: The serial MIDI output uses UART2 and the first pin of the Grove port. While a MIDI app sends to "serial", that unit and pin cannot be opened as a UART ("used by the MIDI serial output"); they are free again once that app ends. The other way round, while a UART uses those pins, the serial MIDI output does not open.

docs.title: When it does not work
docs.text:
• Nothing arrives: check that TX and RX are crossed, GND is connected and the speed is the same on both sides.
  • Garbled characters: the speed or the format differs from the other side (8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit is the usual one).
  • "in use by another app": another app has the same unit open. Close it.
  • "used by the system": a unit or pin the system uses. Pick another one.
  • Dropped bytes (Serial Terminal's counter, dropped): reading does not keep up. Read more often, or give a larger rx_buffer_size: (up to 16384).

docs.title: Pin Assignment Check
docs.text:
Before using a pin, you can check whether the system is already using it.

unless FmrbHw.pin_available?(10)
  Log.error("Pin 10 already in use: #{FmrbHw.pin_status(10)}")
  return
end

For details, see FmrbHw.

Class reference: GPIO, I2C, UART, FmrbUart, FmrbHw

docs.title: Inter-App Messaging (Pub/Sub)
docs.text: A Publish / Subscribe mechanism for exchanging messages between applications. Provided as instance methods of FmrbApp.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Purpose subscribe(topic) Start subscribing to a topic unsubscribe(topic) Unsubscribe publish(topic, data = nil) Send a message to a topic. data can be Hash / Array / number / String / nil send_message(dest_pid, msg_type, data) Direct message to the kernel or a specific process (low-level)

data is automatically serialized to MessagePack internally (maximum 176 bytes).

docs.title: Receive Handler
docs.text:
Topic messages are received in on_control(msg), not on_event(ev).

def on_control(msg)
  if msg["cmd"] == "topic_data" && msg["topic"] == "demo"
    payload = msg["data"]   # The content passed by the sender to publish
    # ...
  end
end
msg Key Description "cmd" "topic_data" (when receiving a publish on a subscribed topic) "topic" Topic name "data" Payload passed by the publisher (Hash, etc.)

Note

subscribe, publish, unsubscribe, and send_message are syntactic sugar that send commands to the kernel via send_message(PROC_ID_KERNEL, MSG_TYPE_APP_CONTROL, ...). on_control is the entry point for all app control messages from the kernel, and Pub/Sub messages are routed through it.

docs.title: Publisher
docs.text:
class PubDemo < FmrbApp
  TOPIC = "demo"

  def on_create
    @count = 0
    redraw
  end

  def on_event(ev)
    if ev[:type] == :mouse_up && ev[:button] == 1
      @count += 1
      publish(TOPIC, {"msg" => "hello", "n" => @count})
      redraw
    end
  end

  def on_update; 100; end

  private

  def redraw
    clear_user_area(FmrbGfx::WHITE)
    @gfx.draw_text(4, 4,
                   "Sent: #{@count}", FmrbGfx::BLACK)
    @gfx.present
  end
end

docs.title: Subscriber
docs.text:
class SubDemo < FmrbApp
  TOPIC = "demo"

  def on_create
    @last = ""
    subscribe(TOPIC)
    redraw
  end

  def on_control(msg)
    if msg["cmd"] == "topic_data" && msg["topic"] == TOPIC
      data = msg["data"]
      @last = "n=#{data["n"]} msg=#{data["msg"]}"
      redraw
    end
  end

  def on_destroy
    unsubscribe(TOPIC)
  end

  def on_update; 100; end

  private

  def redraw
    clear_user_area(FmrbGfx::WHITE)
    @gfx.draw_text(4, 4, @last, FmrbGfx::BLACK)
    @gfx.present
  end
end

/app/demo/pub_demo.app.rb and sub_demo.app.rb are a matching pair of samples that demonstrate this behavior.

docs.title: Topic Design
docs.text:
Topic names are arbitrary strings. They work as long as the communicating apps agree on them. There are currently no widely-used reserved names in the project.

Recommended naming conventions:

  • Lowercase alphanumeric characters and underscores (e.g. "sensor_light")
  • Prefix app-specific messages with "<myapp>_<event>"
  • Document any public topics shared across multiple apps

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Item Value Maximum payload size 176 bytes (after MessagePack serialization) Types accepted for data Hash, Array, Integer, Float, String, Boolean, nil Send timeout 5 seconds (kernel internal)

To send data larger than 176 bytes, write it to a file and publish only the file path, or split the data into multiple messages.

docs.title: Difference from HID Events
docs.text:
Keyboard / mouse / gamepad input is delivered directly to on_event(ev) (routed by the kernel via MSG_TYPE_HID_EVENT). Do not confuse this with Pub/Sub.

Mechanism Receive Handler Use Case HID Input on_event(ev) Physical user input Pub/Sub on_control(msg) Arbitrary inter-app messages Direct send on_control(msg) General kernel control messages

docs.title: Direct Sending (send_message)
docs.text:
A low-level API for sending messages to the kernel or a specific app. subscribe and related methods are built on top of this.

send_message(FmrbConst::PROC_ID_KERNEL,
             FmrbConst::MSG_TYPE_APP_CONTROL,
             {"cmd" => "subscribe", "topic" => "foo"})
  • dest_pid: Destination process ID (FmrbConst::PROC_ID_*)
  • msg_type: Message type (MSG_TYPE_APP_CONTROL, etc.)
  • data: Any Ruby object (automatically serialized via MessagePack)

Class reference: FmrbApp

docs.title: Sprites (SpriteImage / SpriteInstance / GfxBlock)
docs.text:
This page covers the sprite and tile map APIs.

Class Role SpriteImage Sprite image buffer (reusable pixel data) SpriteInstance A sprite instance placed on screen (position, frame, visibility) GfxBlock A mechanism that caches drawing command sequences as bytecode on the graphics side and re-sends only the variable parameters

Call @gfx.present

After SpriteInstance#move, visible=, or frame=, you must call @gfx.present. Sprite compositing is performed at the present timing.

Sprites are composited on top of everything the canvas drew, so a windowed app starts with them confined to its user area — otherwise they would paint over its own title bar. To narrow that further, see keeping sprites inside a rectangle.

docs.title: SpriteImage
docs.text: A class that holds an image buffer. Referenced by SpriteInstance.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
SpriteImage.new(gfx,
                width:,
                height:,
                transparent_color: 0,
                use_transparent: false)
Argument Description gfx Parent FmrbGfx instance width: / height: In pixels transparent_color: Transparent color key (RGB332) use_transparent: When true, draws transparent_color as transparent

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose set_target Subsequent @gfx.fill_rect etc. draw into this image reset_target Restore the drawing target to the screen canvas draw { |gfx| ... } Syntactic sugar that makes this image the drawing target only within the block load_bmp(path) Load a picture into the image: a PNG or an RGB332 BMP, told apart by its first bytes (decoded on the graphics side, fast). PNG is in the development version destroy Release resources Attribute Description id Sprite image ID width / height Size

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
img = SpriteImage.new(@gfx, width: 32, height: 32,
                       transparent_color: 0, use_transparent: true)
img.draw do |g|
  g.fill_rect(0, 0, 32, 32, FmrbGfx::BLACK)  # Treated as transparent
  g.fill_circle(16, 16, 12, FmrbGfx::RED)
end

docs.title: Loading artwork
docs.text:
load_bmp is decoded on the graphics side, which reads its own filesystem — so the file has to be put there first. sync_file does that, and skips the copy when the bytes already match, so it is cheap to call on every start:

SRC   = "/usr/share/sprites/flappy"
CACHE = "/cache/app/flappy"

img = SpriteImage.new(@gfx, width: 16, height: 16,
                      transparent_color: 0, use_transparent: true)
@gfx.sync_file("#{SRC}/bird_body.png", dest: "#{CACHE}/bird_body.png")
img.load_bmp("#{CACHE}/bird_body.png")

The bundled artwork lives under /usr/share/sprites/<app>/, and an app with its own bundle directory (like rpg_demo) keeps it beside its code. Either way the copy goes under /cache, which the system rebuilds on its own.

The file is a PNG or an 8-bit BMP. A PNG's colours become RGB332 by keeping the top 3/3/2 bits of red, green and blue, and its alpha is not transparency — the image's transparent_color is. A BMP's bytes are RGB332 colour values, not palette indices. The bundled artwork is small palette PNGs (in the development version; 3.0.0 reads BMP only). A whole picture to draw once goes through the other door, FmrbGfx#create_image. See Image & Icon Files.

docs.title: How many there can be
docs.text:
Images and instances are the machine's, not the app's: every app draws from the same pool.

Modern Retro SpriteImage 160 64 SpriteInstance 320 128

An instance takes up to 8 frames.

docs.title: SpriteInstance
docs.text: Manages the on-screen position and animation of a sprite.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
SpriteInstance.new(gfx,
                   images,    # SpriteImage or Array
                   x:, y:,
                   z: 0)

Passing multiple SpriteImage objects in images creates animation frames.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose move(x, y) Change position visible = bool Show / hide frame = index Animation frame number destroy Release resources

docs.title: Example: Animated Sprite
docs.text:
class SpriteApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    frames = []
    3.times do |i|
      img = SpriteImage.new(@gfx, width: 16, height: 16,
                              transparent_color: 0, use_transparent: true)
      img.draw do |g|
        g.fill_rect(0, 0, 16, 16, FmrbGfx::BLACK)
        g.fill_circle(8, 8, 4 + i * 2, FmrbGfx::YELLOW)
      end
      frames << img
    end
    @sprite = SpriteInstance.new(@gfx, frames,
                                  x: 50,
                                  y: 30, z: 1)
    @frame = 0
  end

  def on_update
    @frame = (@frame + 1) % 3
    @sprite.frame = @frame
    @gfx.present  # Important
    150
  end
end

docs.title: GfxBlock
docs.text:
Block bytecode for speeding up repeatedly redrawn UI elements (window frames, scrollbar thumbs, HUDs, etc.).

How it works:

  1. The given block is evaluated twice to detect integer arguments that change, which become "registers"
  2. The drawing command sequence is compiled and cached on the graphics side
  3. On draw(kwargs) calls, only the changed register values are sent for re-execution

This is far more bandwidth-efficient than sending dozens of drawing commands every frame (FmrbApp itself uses this for drawing window frames).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Constraint Details The block must produce the same instruction sequence Varying the number of instructions with if is not allowed. A fixed number of iterations within a loop is OK String arguments are fixed The text string for draw_text is fixed at new time Only Integer / Float can be kwargs Boolean is not allowed Maximum 16 registers Total number of variable parameters Payload limit 220 bytes after compilation (UART single-frame limit)

docs.title: Available Drawing DSL
docs.text: Method Signature clear(color) -- draw_rect / fill_rect (x, y, w, h, color) draw_round_rect / fill_round_rect (x, y, w, h, r, color) draw_line (x0, y0, x1, y1, color) fill_circle (x, y, r, color) draw_text (x, y, str, color) (str is a fixed string)

docs.title: Example: Battery Gauge
docs.text:
class BatteryGauge < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    x = 5
    y = 5
    @gauge = GfxBlock.new(@gfx, fill: 50) do |r, fill:|
      r.draw_rect(x, y, 60, 12, FmrbGfx::WHITE)
      r.fill_rect(x + 1, y + 1, fill, 10, FmrbGfx::GREEN)
    end
    @level = 50
  end

  def on_update
    @level = (@level + 5) % 60
    @gauge.draw(fill: @level)
    @gfx.present
    300
  end

  def on_destroy
    @gauge.destroy if @gauge
  end
end

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Exception Trigger GfxBlock::StructureError The instruction sequence differs between the first and second evaluations GfxBlock::TooManyRegsError The number of variable parameters is 17 or more GfxBlock::UnsupportedKwargError A kwarg of a type other than Integer / Float / String was passed GfxBlock::PayloadTooLargeError The compiled payload exceeds 220 bytes

When to use GfxBlock

  • You draw shapes with the same structure every frame (HUDs, bars, frames, etc.)
  • Only coordinates or colors change, while the instruction sequence stays fixed
  • You want to send many drawing commands in a single present

For UI with changing shapes or many conditional branches, use regular FmrbGfx methods instead.

Class reference: SpriteImage, SpriteInstance, GfxBlock, FmrbHitMask

docs.title: Tasks & Timing (Task / Machine)
docs.text: Low-level APIs for task control and system control. Derived from picoruby-machine.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
A module for working with FreeRTOS tasks from Ruby.

Method Purpose Task.pass Yield control to the scheduler (gives other tasks an opportunity to run)

Within FmrbApp#main_loop, Task.pass is called after on_update, allowing other apps and the kernel to run.

loop do
  do_some_work
  Task.pass
end

docs.title: Machine
docs.text: Provides clock, delay, system reset, memory information, and more.

docs.title: Delay
docs.text:
Method Purpose Machine.delay_ms(ms) Wait for ms milliseconds using FreeRTOS vTaskDelay (returns: ms) Machine.busy_wait_ms(ms) Precise wait using a busy loop Machine.sleep(sec) Sleep for the specified number of seconds. Between 2 and 86400 seconds Machine.deep_sleep(sec) Deep sleep (not implemented)

sleep_ms pitfall

Kernel's sleep / sleep_ms may stall when used outside _spin (in an independent task) because tick does not advance. Use Machine.delay_ms for short waits. See Limitations for details.

docs.title: Clock
docs.text:
Method Purpose Machine.set_hwclock(unix_timestamp) Set a UNIX timestamp on the hardware clock Machine.get_hwclock Returns [tv_sec, tv_nsec]

Normally, FmrbSystem.set_wallclock(year, month, ...) is easier to use, and it calls Machine.set_hwclock internally.

docs.title: Uptime Information
docs.text: Method Return Value Machine.uptime_us Elapsed time since boot in microseconds Machine.board_millis Elapsed time since boot in milliseconds Machine.uptime_formatted String format ("hhh:mm:ss") Machine.unique_id Device unique ID string

docs.title: Memory and Diagnostics
docs.text: Method Purpose Machine.read_memory(addr, size) Read memory contents at the specified address Machine.stack_usage Stack usage (in bytes)

docs.title: System Control
docs.text: Method Purpose Machine.exit(status = 0) Exit the program Machine._reboot System reboot (not supported on POSIX)

docs.title: Displaying Uptime
docs.text:
class UptimeView < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    redraw
  end

  def on_update
    redraw
    1000   # Every 1 second
  end

  private

  def redraw
    clear_user_area(FmrbGfx::WHITE)
    @gfx.draw_text(4, 4,
                   "Uptime: #{Machine.uptime_formatted}",
                   FmrbGfx::BLACK)
    @gfx.present
  end
end

docs.title: Short Delay
docs.text:
# OK: Safe wait using FreeRTOS task
3.times do |i|
  Log.info("step #{i}")
  Machine.delay_ms(500)
end

# NG: Using sleep_ms outside _spin can cause it to stall
# sleep_ms(500)  <- This may hang in an independent task

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• For lifecycle control (controlling wait time via on_update return value), see FmrbApp
  • For sleep-related limitations, see Limitations

Class reference: Machine

docs.title: Tile Maps (TileSheet / TileMap)
docs.text:
A library for easily writing tile-based map rendering. Suitable for RPG-style grid worlds, tiled backgrounds, stage-based puzzles, and more.

Class Role TileSheet Wraps a tile image (a single PNG or BMP with tiles arranged in a grid). Can stamp individual tiles TileMap Loads an fmrb_map JSON file and draws tiles layer by layer using TileSheet#stamp

Both classes are built into picoruby-fmrb-app and require no additional require.

docs.title: TileSheet
docs.text: Handles tile sheet images (images with consecutive tiles arranged in a grid): a PNG or an 8-bit RGB332 BMP, as SpriteImage#load_bmp reads them.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
TileSheet.new(gfx, path, cols:, rows: nil, tile_size: 16, source: nil)
Argument Purpose gfx FmrbGfx instance path Path to the picture already transferred to the graphics side (use @gfx.sync_file or transfer_file to send it) cols: Number of columns in the sheet (in tiles) rows: Number of rows. If nil, read from the picture's header in source:, or, without it, estimated from the file size on the graphics side (an 8-bit BMP only) tile_size: Pixel width and height of a single tile (default: 16) source: This side's copy of the picture, the one sent with sync_file; its header gives the height. Pass it for a PNG when rows: is nil (development version)

Internally creates a SpriteImage with transparent color 0 and calls load_bmp.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose stamp(index, dst_x:, dst_y:) Stamp tile number index (row-major: row * cols + col) onto the canvas. nil or negative values are no-ops (for empty map cells) destroy Release the internal SpriteImage Attribute Description image Internal SpriteImage cols / rows Tile counts tile_size Pixel size

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
src = "/usr/share/sprites/test/tilesheet.png"
@gfx.sync_file(src, dest: "/cache/app/mymap/tilesheet.png")
sheet = TileSheet.new(@gfx, "/cache/app/mymap/tilesheet.png",
                      cols: 4, tile_size: 16, source: src)
sheet.stamp(0, dst_x: 0,  dst_y: 0)   # Stamp tile 0 at the top-left
sheet.stamp(5, dst_x: 16, dst_y: 0)   # Stamp tile 5 to the right

docs.title: TileMap
docs.text: Loads a map file and lays out tiles for each layer.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
TileMap.new(path)

path is a path on the core side (internal flash). Note that this is not on the graphics side. Two formats are accepted, and which one it is decided by the first four bytes:

Format .map.bin The packed form. One byte per tile, read straight out of the file .json The fmrb_map v1 JSON below

Prefer the packed form on the device. Loading a map used to mean parsing JSON, which for a large one took the best part of a minute; the packed form is read rather than parsed, and the same map arrives in milliseconds. The JSON stays readable and diffable, so it is the form to keep in a repository — export the packed one beside it.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose render(sheet, origin_x:, origin_y:, max_cols: nil, max_rows: nil) Draw all layers. origin_* is the drawing position for the top-left tile. max_cols/rows clips the display range (for viewporting when the map is larger than the screen) render_view(sheet, origin_x:, origin_y:, view_x:, view_y:, view_w:, view_h:) Draw only the tiles the viewport touches, with sub-tile offsets. origin_* is where the viewport's top-left corner lands on the canvas; view_x / view_y are that corner in full-map pixels. This is what a scrolling world uses tile_at(x, y, layer: 0) The tile id at those tile coordinates, or nil when it is out of range or empty walkable?(x, y) Whether the tile there is in walkable_tiles. Out of range is false event_at(x, y) Return the event Hash at tile coordinates (x, y). Returns nil if none Attribute Description width / height Map width and height (in tiles) tile_size Pixel size of a single tile tilesheet_path Path of the tile sheet to use tilesheet_cols Number of columns in the tile sheet layers Layer array events Event array

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
map = TileMap.new("/app/game/rpg_demo/world.map.json")
# Build the sheet using map.tilesheet_path / map.tilesheet_cols
sheet = TileSheet.new(@gfx, map.tilesheet_path, cols: map.tilesheet_cols)

# Render into an 11x11 tile viewport
map.render(sheet, origin_x: 16, origin_y: 16, max_cols: 11, max_rows: 11)
@gfx.present

docs.title: fmrb_map JSON Format (v1)
docs.text:
{
  "format": "fmrb_map",
  "version": 1,
  "width": 20,
  "height": 15,
  "tile_size": 16,
  "tilesheet": "/usr/share/sprites/test/tilesheet.png",
  "tilesheet_cols": 4,
  "layers": [
    { "name": "ground", "data": [[0, 0, 1, ...], [...], ...] },
    { "name": "objects", "data": [[null, null, 5, ...], [...], ...] }
  ],
  "events": [
    { "x": 4, "y": 6, "kind": "talk", "text": "こんにちは" }
  ]
}
Key Description format Fixed as "fmrb_map" version 1 width / height Map size (in tiles) tile_size Pixel size of a single tile tilesheet graphics-side path of the sheet to use tilesheet_cols Number of columns in the sheet layers[] Each layer. data is a 2D array ([row][col] -> tile number, null for empty) events[] Arbitrary events. Retrieved via event_at(x, y)

docs.title: Map Creation Tools
docs.text:
Tile sheets and maps can be created with web tools (bundled in fmruby-core/tools/web/):

  • Sprite Editor: Create a BMP with 16x16 RGB332 tiles arranged in a grid
  • Map Editor: Place tiles + edit events -> export as a packed .map.bin or as fmrb_map JSON. It reads both

Start with ruby web_server.rb and access http://localhost:8080 (same server as the Console).

docs.title: Example: Simple RPG
docs.text:
A complete RPG demo is available in /app/game/rpg_demo/. In fullscreen:

  • Left 176x176 (11x11 tiles): Field drawn with TileMap + TileSheet
  • Right 128x240: Panel displaying player coordinates / last event
  • Player is a separate picture (16x16) controlled via SpriteInstance with arrow keys / D-pad

This directory includes .app.rb / .app.toml along with world.png, world.map.json and the player's pictures (player_<direction>_<n>.png). The launcher performs a 3-level scan so it also picks up /app/<category>/<bundle>/*.app.toml, allowing you to keep assets alongside the app.

docs.title: UI Widgets (FmrbUI)
docs.text:
A small widget set for apps that draw their own window. Apps used to build their own button tables, hit tests and pressed-state drawing; this holds one copy of that.

def on_create
  @ui = FmrbUI.new(self)
  @ui.label(:title, 0, 0, 108, 10, "Motif")
  @ui.toggle(:round, 0, 12, 50, 16, "Round", group: :motif, on: true)
  @ui.toggle(:diamond, 58, 12, 50, 16, "Diamond", group: :motif)
  @ui.button(:save, 0, 34, 108, 14, "Save")
  @ui.flush
end

def on_event(ev)
  case @ui.handle(ev)
  when :round, :diamond then redraw
  when :save then save
  end
  @ui.flush
end
The Kamon demo's panel: labels, two groups of toggles, and steppers with a unit

docs.title: Two rules it is built around
docs.text:
Nothing is allocated in the steady state. Widgets are made in on_create; the event and redraw paths allocate nothing at all.

Nothing is drawn per frame. Each widget carries a dirty flag, and flush draws only those — calling present once, and not at all when nothing was dirty.

docs.title: The box
docs.text:
FmrbUI.new(app, bg: …, text_size: 1, bg_painter: nil)

Pass the app itself. The canvas is read from it, and widget coordinates are those of @gfx: (0, 0) is the top-left of the user area, and moves with it on a resize or fullscreen.

Argument bg: The colour a widget paints inside itself — a Label's box, a Stepper's value field, a Scrollbar's track. Defaults to the window background text_size: The default scale for the widgets made from here on. A widget can override it with its own text_size: bg_painter: Who repaints the ground where a widget used to be

Left out, the hole a hidden widget leaves is filled with bg:, which is right while the ground is one colour. Where the ground is a picture — a wallpaper, a border, a rounded corner — pass an object answering paint_bg_rect(gfx, x, y, w, h), usually self:

@ui = FmrbUI.new(self, bg_painter: self)

def paint_bg_rect(gfx, x, y, w, h)
  gfx.fill_rect(x, y, w, h, 0x01)
end

That method draws the rectangle and nothing else: no present, no allocation, and it puts back any text size or font it changed. The name is fixed.

docs.title: The widgets
docs.text:
Factory label(id, x, y, w, h, text, align: :left, text_size: nil) Text. align: is :left / :center / :right button(id, x, y, w, h, text, accent: nil) A push button. Inverted while held; handle reports the id when it is released on top of it toggle(id, x, y, w, h, text, group: nil, on: false, on_text: nil) On/off. Toggles sharing a group: behave as radio buttons stepper(id, x, y, w, h, value, min, max, step = 1) A < value > control. Stops at min / max enum(id, x, y, w, h, options, index: 0) A < choice > control over an array of strings. Builds no string when moved, so it is lighter than a Stepper scrollbar(id, x, y, w, h, total, visible, scroll = 0) A scrollbar text_field(id, x, y, w, h, text = "", max: 32) One line of text input

accent: paints a button in a given RGB332 colour instead of the theme's. Reserve it for the few controls whose colour carries meaning — a confirm dialog's Yes, a transport's Stop. On a Toggle it is the on colour.

A Stepper can be given a unit right after it is made: @size.suffix = "%" shows 70%.

A text field takes the focus on a click, and keys go to whichever field has it. Enter makes handle report the id, Escape drops the focus. The caret does not blink — blinking would mean drawing every frame — and there are no arrow keys: characters go on the end and backspace takes from the end.

docs.title: Driving it
docs.text:
Method handle(ev) Feed one event. Returns the id of the widget whose operation completed, or nil. A press only updates the pressed look; the id comes on release over the same widget flush Draw the changed widgets. true when anything was drawn (and present was called once), false when nothing changed

Call flush after drawing your own picture, so present happens once.

docs.title: Changing a widget from the app
docs.text: Method set_text(id, text) Change the text set_on(id, on) / on?(id) A toggle's state set_value(id, value) / value(id) A stepper's or enum's value set_range(id, min, max) A stepper's limits option_text(id) The chosen string of an enum field_text(id) / set_field_text(id, text) A text field's contents set_enabled(id, flag) Enable or grey out set_visible(id, flag) Show or hide. Hide before the flush that is meant to take it off screen move(id, x, y, w, h) Move and resize focus(id) Give a widget the focus invalidate_all Mark every widget for redraw

docs.title: What an author has to know
docs.text:
1. Do not draw every frame. Nothing is drawn from on_update
  2. No blocks. Dispatch on the id handle returns — a widget stores no callback
  3. Coordinates are relative to the user area. Getting this wrong is not silent: a widget placed outside the window is reported when it is created
  4. Hide a widget before the flush that is meant to take it off screen
  5. bg: is the colour a widget paints inside itself, not the colour of what is behind it
  6. Only if you pass a bg_painter: paint_bg_rect draws that rectangle and nothing else

Wiping the user area is not on this list: clear_user_area redraws the window frame and marks the widgets itself.

docs.title: Click targets for a screen drawn whole (FmrbUI::HitAreas)
docs.text:
A game table or any screen that redraws everything each time does not need widgets — only to know what was clicked. FmrbUI::HitAreas keeps that list and draws nothing; the button picture is FmrbGfx#draw_button. Do not mix it with the widgets above.

@hits = FmrbUI::HitAreas.new

# while drawing
@hits.clear
@gfx.draw_button(x, y, 60, 16, "OK", theme_accent, theme_fg_light)
@hits.add(:ok, x, y, 60, 16)

# in on_event
case @hits.id_at(ev[:x], ev[:y])
when :ok then close_dialog
end
Method clear Empty the list, before drawing add(id, x, y, w, h [, data]) Add a target. It lasts until the next clear at(x, y) [id, x, y, w, h, data] of the target at the point, or nil. Where targets overlap, the one added first wins id_at(x, y) Just the id, or nil

docs.title: Utilities (JSON / MessagePack / BMP332)
docs.text: A collection of general-purpose utility APIs.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text: JSON string parsing and generation. Used for configuration files, map data, communication with web tools, and more.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose JSON.parse(string) Convert a JSON string to a Hash / Array JSON.generate(obj) / JSON.dump(obj) Convert a Ruby object to a JSON string

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
text = File.open("/home/conf.json", "r") { |f| f.read }
conf = ::JSON.parse(text)
Log.info("user=#{conf["user"]}")

File.open("/home/conf.json", "w") do |f|
  f.write(::JSON.generate({"user" => "kishima", "score" => 100}))
end

Use ::JSON

Writing JSON.parse(...) inside a class may cause picoruby's constant lookup to interpret JSON as a class-level constant, which fails if not found. Prefix with :: to explicitly refer to the top level: ::JSON.parse(...).

TileMap uses JSON.parse internally to read map files.

docs.title: MessagePack
docs.text: Binary data serialization. Used internally by publish and send_message, but also available for user apps.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose MessagePack.pack(obj) Serialize to binary (returns a String) MessagePack.unpack(binary) Deserialize

docs.title: Supported Ruby Types
docs.text: Hash, Array, Integer, Float, String, Boolean, nil

docs.title: Example: Saving Settings to a File
docs.text:
config = {"score" => 100, "name" => "Player1", "options" => [1, 2, 3]}

# Save
File.open("/save.dat", "w") do |f|
  f.write(MessagePack.pack(config))
end

# Load
data = File.open("/save.dat", "r") { |f| f.read }
restored = MessagePack.unpack(data)
Log.info("score = #{restored["score"]}")

More efficient than JSON

For data with many numbers and booleans, MessagePack produces smaller output and parses faster. Since Family mruby does not bundle a JSON library with picoruby, MessagePack is the standard format for saving structured data.

docs.title: BMP332
docs.text: Parses RGB332 format BMP image data.

docs.title: Methods
Example
docs.text:
data = File.open("/img.bmp", "r") { |f| f.read }
bmp = BMP332.parse(data)
Log.info("size: #{bmp[:width]}x#{bmp[:height]}")

# For displaying images, SpriteImage#load_bmp is faster

Note

For normal image display, SpriteImage#load_bmp or FmrbGfx#create_image_from_file is faster because decoding is done entirely on the graphics side. Use BMP332.parse when you need to work with the pixel array on the Ruby side (editing, inspection).

For detailed specifications, see Image & Icon Files.

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft
docs.text:
A fast Fourier transform, with the engine chosen at run time. The microphone spectrum app is what it was built for; anything that has to turn samples into frequencies can use it.

fft = Fmrb::Fft.new(size: 512, backend: :c)
mag = fft.forward(samples)              # size/2 little-endian int16 magnitudes
peak = Fmrb::Fft.peak_bin(mag)          # index of the loudest bin
hz = peak * rate / 512.0
fft.close

size is a power of two between 64 and 1024. samples is size int16 samples as a byte String — the shape FmrbAudio#mic_read returns.

Method Fmrb::Fft.new(size: 512, backend: :ruby) Pick the engine forward(samples) One transform. Returns the magnitudes run(samples, iters) iters transforms of the same input, timed inside the engine: [microseconds, magnitudes] close Release it Fmrb::Fft.bin(mag, index) One magnitude out of the result Fmrb::Fft.peak_bin(mag) Index of the loudest Fmrb::Fft.sine(size:, cycles:, amp:) A synthetic input, so engines can be compared on the same waveform Fmrb::Fft.bench(size:, iters:, backend:, reps:) Time one engine Fmrb::Fft.available?(backend) / .q15?(backend) Whether this build has it, and whether it computes in fixed point

The backends are :ruby, :c, :c64, :dsp, :spinel and the fixed-point :ruby_q15, :c_q15, :spinel_q15. Which exist depends on the build, so ask available? rather than assuming. The fixed-point ones differ from the floating ones by a few counts by construction — comparing results across the two families needs that allowance.

docs.title: ArgumentError
docs.text:
Wrong number or value of arguments

Inherits from: StandardError

Generated from the API signatures (sig/) of fmruby-core main@579eba38.

docs.title: Array
docs.text:
An ordered list of elements

Includes Enumerable. Here a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i] does not work (swap through a temporary). A block call costs about 0.4ms, so in a per-frame loop write while instead. The methods listed are the ones apps use, such as push, each and include?.

docs.title: Array.new
docs.text:
new(?Integer size, ?untyped object) -> Array

Make an array

Reserving the size up front beats growing it item by item. The second argument fills it.

a = Array.new
b = Array.new(16, 0)

docs.title: Array#[]=
docs.text:
[]=(Integer index, untyped value) -> untyped
[]=(Integer start, Integer length, untyped value) -> untyped

Set element at specified position

a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i] does not work here -- a known picoruby gap. Swap through a temporary instead.

a[0] = 1
t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t

docs.title: Array#[]
docs.text:
[](Integer index) -> untyped

Get element at specified position

A negative index counts from the end. Out of range gives nil, not an error.

a[0]
a[-1]

docs.title: Array#&
docs.text:
&(Array other) -> self

Elements that are in both arrays

Keeps what is in both.

[1, 2, 3] & [2, 3, 4]  #=> [2, 3]

docs.title: Array#+
docs.text:
+(Array other) -> Array

Concatenate arrays

It makes a new array; to add on the end use push.

c = a + b

docs.title: Array#-
docs.text:
-(Array other) -> self

Return new array excluding specified elements

Drops everything the other one has.

[1, 2, 3] - [2]  #=> [1, 3]

docs.title: Array#push
docs.text:
push(untyped object) -> Array

Append element to end

The same as <<; it returns the array so calls can be chained.

a.push(1)
a << 1

docs.title: Array#all?
docs.text:
all?(*untyped patterns) -> bool
all?(*untyped patterns) { (untyped element) -> untyped } -> bool

Whether every element passes

ok = a.all? { |v| v > 0 }

docs.title: Array#at
docs.text:
at(Integer index) -> untyped

Get element at specified position

The same as [].

a.at(2)

docs.title: Array#clear
docs.text:
clear() -> Array

Remove all elements from array

Empties the array itself, so everyone holding it sees it empty.

a.clear

docs.title: Array#collect!
docs.text:
collect!() { (untyped element) -> untyped } -> Array[untyped]

Replace each element with the block's result, in place

Rewrites the array in place instead of making a new one.

a.collect! { |v| v * 2 }

docs.title: Array#count
docs.text:
count() -> Integer

Return the number of elements

The same as length.

n = a.count

docs.title: Array#delete_at
docs.text:
delete_at(Integer index) -> untyped

Delete element at specified position

docs.title: Asterism.connect
docs.text:
connect(
  ?String? locator,
  app: String,
  ?node: String?,
  ?mode: Symbol?,
  ?listen: String?,
  ?config: (Hash | String)?,
  ?connect_timeout: (Integer | Float)?,
  ?check_timeout: (Integer | Float)?,
  ?credentials: (String | Asterism::Credentials)?
) -> Asterism::Connection

Open a connection (what Link does for you)

Connects to the router (locator), puts this app (app of node) on Asterism and returns an Asterism::Connection. An app on a machine normally uses Link (Link waits for WiFi, connects again and reads the settings); this is the entry Link calls. The app waits while it connects (about 1.5 s of check_timeout: looking for another copy of the same name, and a few seconds when there is no router). node: (the credentials' name when left out), app: (required), mode: (a client of a router when left out; :peer for no router), listen:, config: (TLS keys and the like; a Hash or a JSON5 String), connect_timeout: (CRuby on a PC only; ArgumentError on a machine), check_timeout: (seconds), credentials: (a .tar path or an Asterism::Credentials; it gives the default locator and node). Raises Asterism::Disconnected when it cannot connect, Asterism::Error when the same node/app is already there, ArgumentError for a bad name.

conn = Asterism.connect(
  "tcp/192.0.2.2:7447",
  node: "fmruby-aaa001", app: "demo")

expose(
  String name,

  methods: Array[untyped] | Hash[untyped, untyped],
  ?caller: (Symbol | String)?,
  ?doc: String?
) -> String

Expose an object to other machines

Others call it as "//". Pass methods: as a keyword: a Hash of method name => number of arguments ({ post: 1 }, checked before the call; -1 for any) or an Array of names. Only those can be called; a missing one raises ArgumentError. Exposed methods run inside update; what they raise reaches the caller as a RemoteError. caller: (not given when left out), a keyword name such as :from: every call passes the calling node's ID to the method under that keyword. doc: (none when left out) describes the object (2048 bytes at most). Returns the path. Call it in link_up.

  link.conn.expose("board", self,
    methods: { post: 1 })
end

docs.title: Asterism::ROS
docs.text:
Act as a ROS 2 node

How to use it: Network.

A bridge to ROS 2 (Jazzy, rmw_zenoh): make a node that publishes and subscribes to topics and calls and serves services. It assumes the ROS 2 side shares the Zenoh router (zenohd) and uses rmw_zenoh. Build it on a Link's conn.session (Asterism::ROS::Node.new(conn.session, "name")). Like Asterism::Connection, nothing runs behind your back: call Node#poll in every update.

Message types are files made from ROS 2 .msg / .srv files (the output of tools/asterism_msggen.rb); /usr/share/asterism/msgs on the machine holds std_msgs, geometry_msgs, sensor_msgs, nav_msgs and more. Give Asterism::ROS.require_type("std_msgs/msg/String") or the type's name (a String) to the methods and it is loaded. Messages travel as CDR. A big message (an image, a point cloud) uses the machine's memory.

node = Asterism::ROS::Node.new(
  @link.conn.session, "fmrb_node")
pub = node.publisher("/chatter",
  "std_msgs/msg/String")
pub << { data: "hi" }

The name is package/msg|srv/Name: ArgumentError for another shape, Asterism::ROS::UnknownType when there is no file.

twist = Asterism::ROS.require_type(
  "geometry_msgs/msg/Twist")

The type is the type itself or its ROS name. Raises Asterism::ROS::UnknownType for a type without a field table (written by hand, or generated long ago).

t = Asterism::ROS.field_types(
  "std_msgs/msg/Header")

An absolute name stays; a relative one goes under the namespace. An empty name raises ArgumentError. "~" and substitutions are not supported.

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node
docs.text:
A ROS 2 node over a Zenoh session

How to use it: Network.

Topics, services and timers hang off this node; closing it ends all of them. Receiving and answering (the subscribe, every and service blocks) run inside Node#poll. Do not wait in a block (a service call or a call to another machine would stall the update): start a call_async and look at done? later.

node = Asterism::ROS::Node.new(
  @link.conn.session, "fmrb_node")

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node.new
docs.text:
new(
  untyped session,
  String | Symbol name,
  ?namespace: String,
  ?domain: Integer,
  ?enclave: String
) -> Asterism::ROS::Node

Make a node on a session (it shows in ros2 node list)

session is an open Zenoh session (conn.session). name is one name (not empty, no "/"; otherwise ArgumentError). namespace: ("/" when left out), domain: (0; ROS_DOMAIN_ID), enclave: ("/"). Declares the node's liveliness at once.

node = Asterism::ROS::Node.new(
  conn.session, "fmrb_node",
  namespace: "/fmrb")

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node#poll
docs.text:
poll(?Integer steps) -> bool

Poll: receive, answer, fire the timers

Polls the session, answers the service requests that came in, hands the messages to the subscribe blocks and fires the timers that are due. False once the session is closed, true otherwise. steps (8 when left out) is the most times it repeats the session's work (it stops early when nothing is left).

def on_update
  @node.poll
  100
end

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node#publisher
docs.text:
publisher(
  String topic,
  untyped type,
  ?qos: String
) -> Asterism::ROS::Publisher

Make a publisher for a topic

topic is the topic name ("/chatter"; a relative one goes under the node's namespace), type is the type itself or its ROS name ("std_msgs/msg/String"). qos: (DEFAULT_QOS when left out). Raises Asterism::ROS::UnknownType or ArgumentError for a type that cannot be loaded.

pub = node.publisher("/chatter",
  "std_msgs/msg/String")

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node#subscription
docs.text:
subscription(
  String topic,
  untyped type,
  ?qos: String,
  ?depth: Integer
) -> Asterism::ROS::Subscription

Make a subscription you take messages from

Messages that arrive wait in it and you take them with each_pending. depth: (16 when left out) is how many can wait, qos: (DEFAULT_QOS). Use subscribe to get them in a block.

sub = node.subscription("/cmd",
  "std_msgs/msg/String")

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node#subscribe
docs.text:
subscribe(
  String topic,
  untyped type,
  ?qos: String,
  ?depth: Integer
) { (Asterism::ROS::Message msg, Asterism::ROS::Attachment? info) -> untyped } -> Asterism::ROS::Subscription

subscribe(
  String topic,
  untyped type,
  ?qos: String,
  ?depth: Integer
) -> Asterism::ROS::Subscription

Receive a topic in a block (from Node#poll)

|msg, info| is called inside Node#poll for every message (info is an Asterism::ROS::Attachment, or nil). Do not wait in the block. close the returned Subscription to stop. Without a block it is the same as subscription.

node.subscribe("/cmd",
  "std_msgs/msg/String") do |m, i|
  got(m.data)
end

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node#service
docs.text:
service(
  String service,
  untyped type,
  ?qos: String,
  ?depth: Integer
) { (untyped request) -> untyped } -> Asterism::ROS::Service

Serve a service (the block answers requests)

For every request the block gets it (type::Request) inside Node#poll and returns the answer (a type::Response or a Hash of its fields). depth: (8 when left out), qos: (DEFAULT_QOS). ArgumentError without a block. When the block raises, that request goes unanswered and the exception comes out of poll.

add = Asterism::ROS.require_type(
  "example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts")
node.service("/add", add) do |r|
  { sum: r.a + r.b }
end

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node#client
docs.text:
client(
  String service,
  untyped type,
  ?qos: String
) -> Asterism::ROS::Client

Make a client for a service

Call it with Client#call (waits) or call_async (does not). qos: (DEFAULT_QOS when left out). For occasional calls Node#call makes and keeps a client.

cli = node.client("/add", add)

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node#call
docs.text:
call(
  String service,
  untyped type,
  ?untyped req,
  ?request: untyped,
  ?timeout: (Integer | Float)?,
  ?timeout_ms: Integer?,
  **untyped fields
) -> Asterism::ROS::Message

Call a service once and wait for the response

node.call("/add", add, a: 2, b: 3). Give the request as field keywords, or a Hash or message positionally or as request:. The time limit is timeout: (seconds) or timeout_ms: (2 s when left out). It makes one client per service name and keeps it. The app waits for the answer, still answering this node's services meanwhile (the subscribe and every blocks do not run). Raises Asterism::ROS::TimeoutError when nothing answers in time, Asterism::Zenoh::ClosedError when the session is closed. If a field of the request is named timeout or timeout_ms, give the request as request: { ... }.

r = node.call("/add", add,
  a: 2, b: 3)
puts r.sum

docs.title: Asterism::ROS::Node#every
docs.text:
every(
  ?(Integer | Float)? seconds,
  ?ms: (Integer | Float)?
) { () -> untyped } -> Asterism::ROS::Timer

Call a block every so often (from Node#poll)

every(1.0) { ... } (seconds) or every(ms: 500) { ... }. The first call is one period from now. Runs inside Node#poll. After a long stall it does not fire the missed times at once (it counts from now). Do not wait in the block. Returns a Timer (cancel stops it). ArgumentError without a block or a period, with both, or with one that is not positive.

t = node.every(1.0) do
  pub << { data: "tick" }
end

docs.title: BMP332
docs.text:
RGB332 pictures (8-bit BMP and palette PNG)

How to use it: Utilities.

Pixels are a String of one RGB332 byte per pixel, top row first (width x height bytes); a transparent pixel is 0x01. A PNG's transparency (alpha below 128, tRNS) reads as 0x01. Width and height up to 2048.

To only show a picture no pixels are needed: hand its path to FmrbGfx#draw_picture.

docs.title: BMP332.load
docs.text:
load(String path) -> Hash

Read a PNG or BMP file into RGB332 pixels

The kind is told from the first bytes. Raises when it cannot be read. The pixels live in the VM, so a large picture (64 KB at 256x256) takes the VM pool.

bmp = BMP332.load("/home/a.png")
w = bmp[:width]
px = bmp[:pixels]

docs.title: BMP332.parse
docs.text:
parse(String data) -> Hash

Turn PNG or BMP bytes into RGB332 pixels

load, from the bytes instead of a file. The result is {width:, height:, pixels:}.

bmp = BMP332.parse(data)

docs.title: BMP332.save
docs.text:
save(String path, Integer width, Integer height, String pixels) -> void

Write RGB332 pixels as a PNG or a BMP file

A path ending in .png gets the palette PNG (only the colours used); any other an 8-bit BMP.

BMP332.save("/home/a.png", 16, 16,
            px)

docs.title: BMP332.png_path?
docs.text:
png_path?(String path) -> bool

Whether a path names a PNG

true when the name ends in .png (any case); the contents are not looked at. It is how save tells PNG from BMP.

fmt = BMP332.png_path?(path) ? "png" : "bmp"

docs.title: BMP332.encode_png
docs.text:
encode_png(Integer width, Integer height, String pixels) -> String

Encode RGB332 pixels as palette PNG bytes

png = BMP332.encode_png(16, 16, px)

docs.title: BMP332.info
docs.text:
info(?String path, ?data: String) -> Hash?

A picture's size and kind, without decoding it

Only the head is read (a PNG's IHDR, a BMP's headers). The result is {width:, height:, format: :png or :bmp, bytes: the file's size}; nil when it is not there or cannot be read. A picture too large to decode still gives its size. data: takes the bytes instead of a path.

info = BMP332.info("/home/a.png")
if info && info[:width] <= 48
  ok = true
end
BMP332.info(data: bytes)

docs.title: BMP332.to_png
docs.text:
to_png(
  ?String path,
  ?data: String,
  ?max_width: Integer,
  ?max_height: Integer,
  ?max_bytes: Integer,
  ?max_file_bytes: Integer
) -> Hash

Rewrite a picture as a small palette PNG

Reads a PNG or a BMP and writes it again as the palette PNG of only the colours used. It is all done in C; the pixels never enter the VM. The bytes are those of encode_png over parse's pixels. Transparency becomes the colour 0x01.

The result is {png: bytes, width:, height:}. A refusal is not an exception but {error: reason, ...}:

  • :too_big (with width:, height:): past max_width or max_height, refused from the head before anything is decoded
  • :too_heavy (bytes:): the PNG written is past max_bytes
  • :file_too_large (bytes:): the file is past max_file_bytes (65536 unless given); it is not read
  • :unreadable: not there, not a picture, or broken
  • :no_memory: the VM pool ran short

data: takes the bytes instead of a path. max_width: and max_height: are 2048 when left out; max_bytes: has no limit when left out.

r = BMP332.to_png("/home/a.png",
  max_width: 48, max_height: 48,
  max_bytes: 8192)
if r[:error]
  show(r[:error])
else
  FmrbFile.write(out, r[:png])
end

docs.title: Dir
docs.text:
List and operate on directories

How to use it: Files & I/O.

Dir.children is the easy way to list (an array of names); to go one by one, Dir.open and loop on read.

Dir.children("/home").each { |n| p n }

docs.title: Dir.new
docs.text:
new(String path) -> Dir

Open a directory

RuntimeError (the message is the path) when it is missing or not a directory. An ESP32 can have 10 open at once, for all apps together. What was left open is closed when the app ends. Same as Dir.open.

d = Dir.new("/home")

docs.title: Dir.open
docs.text:
open(String path) { (Dir dir) -> untyped } -> untyped
open(String path) -> Dir

Open a directory (a block closes it)

With a block it closes the directory on the way out and returns the block's value. RuntimeError when it is missing. Apps also use it to test existence (open and close for true; a RuntimeError for false); Dir.exist? is simpler for that.

Dir.open("/home") do |d|
  while (n = d.read)
    p n
  end
end

docs.title: Dir.exist?
docs.text:
exist?(String path) -> bool

Whether it is a directory

true only for a directory (a regular file gives false; File.exist? is true for both). false when it is missing or cannot be checked, never an exception. On an ESP32 "/" and "/mnt" count too. exists? is the same method.

Dir.mkdir("/home/d") unless Dir.exist?("/home/d")

Returns 0 when made. Dir.mkdir("/home/notes") unless Dir.exist?("/home/notes")

docs.text:
delete(String path) -> Integer

Returns 0 when deleted. RuntimeError (the message is the path) when it is not empty or is missing. "/" and "/mnt" cannot be deleted (on a device). rmdir and unlink are the same method. For a file use File.delete.

docs.title: File
docs.text:
Reading and writing files (File)

How to use it: Files & I/O.

Inherits from: IO

A subclass of IO; write, puts, print, flush, close and closed? are IO's. Implemented in the Family mruby gems picoruby-fmrb-filesystem (lib/gems/picoruby-fmrb-filesystem/: mrblib/file.rb, ports/esp32/fmrb_filesystem.c) and picoruby-fmrb-io. What CRuby's File has and this one lacks: gets, each_line, readlines, seek, eof?, File.read, File.write, File.binread, File.foreach, File.stat, File.mtime and more. Read with read; to write or read a whole file at once use FmrbFile. A failure is a RuntimeError (no Errno::ENOENT and the like; a missing file, a file that cannot be written and too many open files are told apart by the message only). Writable places are /home and /tmp (/tmp is a small temporary space in RAM).

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is SEPARATOR String The path separator

docs.title: File.new
docs.text:
new(String path, ?String mode, ?Integer perm) -> File

Open a file (new)

mode: "r" (default; read), "w" (truncate and write; created when missing), "a" (append; created when missing), "r+" (read and write; fails when missing), "w+" (truncate, read and write) and "a+" (read, and every write goes to the end; created when missing). A b may be added ("rb+" is "r+"). A mode starting with any other letter opens read-only (no error). read on a "w" or "a" file, and write, puts or print on an "r" file, raise IOError. perm is accepted and ignored.

RuntimeError ("failed to open file: path") when it cannot open; the reason (missing, no room, too many open) is not told apart. Only 10 files can be open on an ESP32, for all apps together. Close a File when done (File.open with a block does it).

f = File.new("/home/a.txt", "w")
f.write("hi")
f.close

docs.title: File.join
docs.text:
join(*String | Array[untyped] names) -> String

Join path parts

Joins the parts with exactly one "/" between them. Parts are Strings or arrays of Strings (nesting allowed); anything else is a TypeError. "" with no arguments.

File.join("/home", "a.txt")   #=> "/home/a.txt"

docs.title: File.basename
docs.text:

docs.title: FmrbApp
docs.text:
The base of every app; inherit from it

How to use it: Application, Inter-App Messaging.

An app is written as class MyApp < FmrbApp, overriding the methods that get called (on_create, on_update, on_event and so on). The file only defines the class; once it has been read, the class is made and started.

Draw on gfx (@gfx). @gfx is an FmrbGfx that FmrbApp prepares, with its origin at the top-left of the area the app owns; call gfx.present to show what was drawn. The window's size is read with window_width and window_height, colours with theme_fg and the like.

Methods to read first: on_create, on_update, on_event, gfx, set_timer, publish.

docs.title: FmrbApp.last_error
docs.text:
last_error() -> Hash?

The error of the app that failed last

The name and the error text of the last app that failed, as a Hash {name:, error:}. It is filled when a Ruby app ends on an exception, does not compile, is refused at start or cannot be restored from an image, and when a second Python app is started. There is one for all apps: the next app that fails replaces it. It is never cleared, and is nil until some app has failed since boot. name is the app's name (up to 31 bytes); error is the exception's text followed by the backtrace, one line each, if there is one (1023 bytes in all at most). Tell whether it is your own by name.

Log.info("#{e[:name]}: #{e[:error]}") if e

wasm_stats() -> wasm_stats

How the wasm runtime is doing

The runtime wasm apps run on (WAMR). running is 1 while it is up (while any wasm app runs), apps the apps using it, modules the modules loaded, natives the boundary's functions the firmware gives. pool_* is the shared pool every wasm app takes from (bytes; high is the most since boot), traps the calls that trapped (or ran too long) since boot. Log.info("#{s[:pages]}/#{s[:max_pages]} pages") if s

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_create
docs.text:
on_create() -> void

Called once as it starts

The screen and the window are ready by the time this runs. Set up the first frame and whatever state the app will keep.

A file only defines the class; it needs no starting code at the end. Once the file has been read, the class is made and started.

class MyApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    @n = 0
    clear_user_area
    gfx.present
  end
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_update
docs.text:
on_update() -> void

called every frame; draw here

Called over and over while the app runs. Draw one frame's worth of graphics here; movement comes from changing the position a little on each call.

Blocking in here blocks the other apps too, so never wait long in this method. Use set_timer when something has to happen later.

class MyApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    @x = 0
  end

  def on_update
    @x = (@x + 1) % window_width
    gfx.clear(FmrbGfx::BLACK)
    gfx.fill_circle(@x, 60, 8,
                    FmrbGfx::YELLOW)
    gfx.present
  end
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_destroy
docs.text:
on_destroy() -> void

Called once as it ends

Called once, just before the app ends: close files, save what should be saved.

It runs only on an orderly exit. An app that dies on an exception never gets here, so anything that must not be lost should be written out before then.

def on_destroy
  Log.info("MyApp: bye")
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_suspend
docs.text:
on_suspend() -> void

Called when the screen goes to another app

Called when another app comes to the front. This app keeps running; only its screen goes away. Nobody is looking at what it draws, so this is where to stop an expensive animation or a sound.

def on_suspend
  @paused = true
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_resume
docs.text:
on_resume() -> void

Called when the screen comes back

Called when this app gets the screen back. What was on it is gone; redraw here.

def on_resume
  @paused = false
  draw_screen
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_checkpoint
docs.text:
on_checkpoint() -> void

Called once the app is written to an image

Called once the image is written, just before the app closes. The app moved rather than ended, so on_destroy does not come. What is done here is not in the image. Only an app on mruby whose .app.toml says movable = true can be written (doc/checkpoint/movable_apps.md).

def on_checkpoint
  Log.info("written to an image")
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_restore
docs.text:
on_restore() -> void

Called when started from an image

Called in an app started from an image, just before it goes on from where it was written. Its instance variables, Tasks and timers are back as they were. The base has made its window again (the same place, size and frame, its fonts and GfxBlocks) and subscribed to its topics again, and the keyboard comes to it. What was drawn does not come back: the window is an empty frame, so an app that draws only when something happens draws here (one that draws everything in on_update need not). Make again here what the app itself made outside the VM (sprites, images). An app holding a file open cannot be written to an image. Moved to a machine with another screen (Retro and Modern), the window may be made smaller to fit it, or a fullscreen app gets that screen's size: on_resize then comes before on_restore, as after a resize. The build it moved to may lack a method not common to every machine: check with respond_to? or rescue NoMethodError (gather the differences in a small object of the app's own and absorb them there with respond_to? or method_missing; adding method_missing to a built-in class such as Array is not recommended). The arriving side tells the names it lacks in its log and its answer, and does not refuse. A method the app cannot go on without goes in its .app.toml as requires = ["name"]: it is not moved to a build without it. See doc/checkpoint/movable_apps.md.

def on_restore
  draw_screen
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_checkpoint_refused
docs.text:
on_checkpoint_refused(String reason) -> void

Called when its own image is refused

Called with the reason when the image asked for with checkpoint could not be written. The app goes on.

def on_checkpoint_refused(reason)
  Log.info("refused: #{reason}")
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#on_event
docs.text:
on_event(event ev) -> void

called on key and mouse input

ev is a Hash describing the input. Four fields cover most uses:

  • ev[:type] -- what happened: :key_down, :mouse_up and so on
  • ev[:scancode] -- the key's number. Look at this, not the character (kana input delivers the same numbers)
  • ev[:x] ev[:y] -- where the mouse is (from the area's top-left, as gfx draws; from the window's: ev[:wx] ev[:wy])

Use ev_ctrl?(ev) and friends to see whether Ctrl or Shift was held.

class MyApp < FmrbApp
  def on_event(ev)
    return unless
      ev[:type] == :key_down
    case ev[:scancode]
    when 0x4F then @x += 4  # right
    when 0x50 then @x -= 4  # left
    end
  end
end

docs.text:
on_resize(Integer new_width, Integer new_height) -> void

Called when the window is resized

Called when the window changes size, and when it enters or leaves full screen.

FmrbUI widgets stay where they were built, so a resize means building them again. Redraw the frame too.

def on_resize(w, h)
  detach_ui(@ui) if @ui
  @ui = FmrbUI.new(self)
  build_widgets
  redraw
end

docs.text:
draw_window_frame() -> void

Redraw the frame and the title

Draws the title bar, the border and the close button. Does nothing in full screen.

Usually there is no need to call it. The base draws the frame when the app starts, and clear_user_area draws it again after painting the area. After a resize, redrawing from clear_user_area in on_resize brings the frame along. Call it only after drawing over the frame's edge (when the area was painted with fill_rect instead of clear_user_area, say).

The title bar uses the default font, but the font in force before the call is put back, so set_font(:ja) does not have to be re-applied every frame.

Calls the block once, interval milliseconds later. It does not repeat -- call set_timer again inside the block for that.

The moment it fires is rounded to the app loop's own tick, so it is not accurate to the millisecond. The return value is the id clear_timer takes.

Call it from inside on_control or on_event. It ends the wait so the loop reaches on_update at once; use it when a message shows the app has to act sooner than planned. From on_update it does nothing, because the next wait is worked out there anyway.

def on_control(msg)
  @due = Machine.board_millis + 200
  request_early_update
end

docs.title: FmrbApp#publish
docs.text:
publish(String topic, ?untyped data) -> void

Send a notice to everyone

Sends data to every app subscribed to that topic.

One message carries at most 176 bytes. For anything larger, write it to /tmp and publish the path instead (/tmp lives in memory and is gone on the next boot).

publish("my_topic", { "n" => 1 })

docs.title: FmrbApp#send_message
docs.text:
send_message(Integer dest_pid, Integer msg_type, untyped data) -> bool

Send a message to another app

Sends straight to one process (dest_pid). data is any value MessagePack can pack (usually a Hash), and the packed size may be 176 bytes at most, the same limit as publish. msg_type is FmrbConst::MSG_TYPE_APP_CONTROL.

It returns true when sent, and false when the target has no queue (wrong pid, already ended) or does not take it within one second (also logged). Over 176 bytes raises ArgumentError. The sender's pid is not put in the message; add it yourself when you want a reply ("re" => FmrbApp.pid).

The receiver reads only a Hash whose "cmd" is a String. The cmd names the base owns (resize, moved, suspend, resume, stop, quit_request, ...) are handled by the base, and any other cmd reaches on_control as the Hash (if defined). A Hash without "cmd", or anything that is not a Hash, is dropped silently.

send_message(pid,
  FmrbConst::MSG_TYPE_APP_CONTROL,
  { "cmd" => "hello",
    "re" => FmrbApp.pid })

Put a file on the graphics side

sync_file("/home/a.wav",
          dest: "/cache/a.wav")

docs.title: FmrbAssoc
docs.text:
Which app opens which file

The place everything that opens a file for the user asks: the file manager's double click, the shell's open, and any app that hands a file on. The table has two layers: /etc/associations.toml (ships with the firmware) and, on top of it per extension, /home/associations.toml (the user's). One line each, extension = "answer".

The answer is one of three. A path always starts with /, so compare it with FmrbAssoc::RUN and FmrbAssoc::EDIT to tell them apart. - "run" run the file itself as an app - "edit" open it in the editor - "/app/..." start that app and hand it the file

The table is read once per VM. After editing a table, open the app that reads it again (there is no reload).

docs.text: Name Type What it is RUN String Answer: run the file itself as an app EDIT String Answer: open it in the editor DEFAULT String Answer for an extension with no entry (same as EDIT) SYS_PATH String Path of the table that ships with the firmware USR_PATH String Path of the user's table MAX_EXT_LEN Integer Longest extension looked at (8)

docs.title: FmrbAsterism::TableClient
docs.text:
The device side of a game host's table

How to use it: Network.

Finds the tables a game host (app "games") has, joins one, asks the member's view and leaves. The Link inside connects again; a host that leaves the network and comes back is handled too.

Use: make it in on_create; in every on_update, while update is true, collect the answers of the game's own calls (proxy), then call update_view. close in on_destroy.

Methods the app owns (called by the part): it calls the app by name (no blocks are given). Required: - table_state(path, state) a put of a table's state (a Hash); return what the list keeps (tables[path]) - table_joined(reply) join answered with a token (token is set; the view is asked next) - table_refused(why) join refused (the host's word) or not answered (why nil); table is nil again - table_view(view) the member's view (a Hash) Optional (called when the app has them): - table_link_up(link) after every connect (the subscription and on_join / on_leave are set) - table_link_down(link) a connect failed or the connection went away - table_watch every update while connected, before the states are read - tables_changed(added) a table joined the list (true) or a host's tables left it (false) - table_host_gone the joined table's host left the network - table_host_back that host came back (the view is asked again) - table_view_failed a view got no answer - table_dropped the host does not know this member; without it the part leaves - table_ask_view(px, token) ask the view yourself (px is the table's async proxy); return the Future Leaving or forgetting a table while its join is not answered drops that answer (the next join goes out at once). Any answer of the view, an error too, says the host is there.

def on_create
  @tc = FmrbAsterism::TableClient.new(
    self, "othello", tag: "othello")
end
def on_update
  if @tc.update
    @tc.update_view
  end
  100
end
def on_destroy
  @tc.close
end

How to use it: Sound.

An app makes one with @audio = FmrbAudio.new(self).
