Plays an NSF. The tunes live in /usr/share/sounds/nsf. track: (0 when left out) is the song inside the NSF.

@audio.play("/usr/share/sounds/nsf/test.nsf")

docs.title: FmrbAudio#play_raw
docs.text:
play_raw(String path, Integer track) -> void

play with nothing left out

The simple form, with no argument left out. track is the song inside the NSF, from 0. The wrapper is play (track: left out is 0).

@audio.play_raw("/usr/share/sounds/nsf/test.nsf", 0)

docs.title: FmrbAudio#stop
docs.text:
stop() -> void

Stop the song

@audio.stop

docs.title: FmrbAudio#nsf_status
docs.text:
nsf_status() -> nsf_status?

Ask where the song is

An NSF has no length, so the audio side decides when a song is over (silence, its loop heard twice, or a time limit) and stops it. Ask about once a second and move on when it is over. nil when there is no answer.

st = @audio.nsf_status
next_song if st && st[:state] == FmrbAudio::NSF_ENDED

docs.title: FmrbAudio#mic_available?
docs.text:
mic_available?() -> bool

Whether this machine has a microphone

true only on an ESP32-P4 machine (a Tab5 and the like); false elsewhere, so there is no need to check the machine first.

return unless @audio.mic_available?

docs.title: FmrbAudio#mic_rate
docs.text:
mic_rate() -> Integer

The microphone's sampling rate in Hz

47160 on an ESP32-P4 (it shares the speaker's clock and cannot be chosen); 0 on a machine without a microphone. A spectrum's bin width in Hz is this over the number of samples.

hz = @audio.mic_rate

docs.title: FmrbAudio#mic_enable
docs.text:
mic_enable(?bool on) -> bool

Turn the microphone on or off

on (true when left out). Turn it on before reading and off with false when done. true on success; false on a machine without one or when it fails to start (no exception). true if it is already so.

@audio.mic_enable
@audio.mic_enable(false)

docs.title: FmrbAudio#mic_read
docs.text:
mic_read(Integer count, ?Integer timeout_ms) -> String?

Read microphone samples

Returns count (1 to 4096, else ArgumentError) signed 16-bit little-endian samples as a String of 2 * count bytes. It waits until they are there (it blocks); timeout_ms (200 when left out) is the wait of each hand-over from the driver, about 256 samples at a time. nil when they did not arrive, and when the microphone is off or absent (never a short String).

bytes = @audio.mic_read(512, 300)
return if bytes.nil?

docs.text:
load_fmsq(Integer slot_id, bin binary_data) -> void

Put song data into a slot

Loads a tune into a slot. play_slot is what sounds it.

data = File.open(path, "r") { |f| f.read }
@audio.load_fmsq(0, data)

  "/usr/share/music/round.mml")

docs.text:
play_slot(Integer slot_id, ?instance: Integer) -> void

Play the song in a slot

instance: (MAIN when left out) is the APU that plays it, FmrbAudio::MAIN or FmrbAudio::SUB.

@audio.play_slot(0)

docs.title: FmrbAudio#play_slot_raw
docs.text:
play_slot_raw(Integer slot_id, Integer instance) -> void

play_slot with nothing left out

The simple form, with no argument left out. instance is the APU that plays it, MAIN (0) or SUB (1): a long tune on MAIN and the short effects on SUB, so an effect never cuts the tune. The wrapper is play_slot (instance: left out is MAIN).

@audio.play_slot_raw(0, FmrbAudio::SUB)

docs.title: FmrbAudio#main_volume=
docs.text:
main_volume=(Integer percent) -> void

Set the volume of the music (MAIN) only

0 to 100 (%), 100 to start with. Only the music of play and of play_slot on MAIN changes; the effects (SUB), WAVs and the machine's volume stay. It goes back to 100 when the app closes.

@audio.main_volume = 30

docs.title: FmrbAudio#play_wav
docs.text:
play_wav(String path) -> bool

Play a recorded sound (WAV)

Mono, 8000 to 48000Hz, up to 2MB, 16-bit PCM or 4-bit IMA-ADPCM. It plays over the APU. Only one at a time: calling again while one sounds replaces it. Retro cannot play it and gets false back (true when it does play).

ok = @audio.play_wav("/home/a.wav")
# false on Retro

Stop the WAV that is playing

The frequency is in Hz. It sounds over a tune that is already playing. volume (10 when left out) is 0 to 15, duty (2) the pulse width 0 to 3, sweep (0).

@audio.note_on(0, 440)

@audio.note_on_raw(0, 440, 10, 2, 0)

docs.title: FmrbColors
docs.text:
The colour-name table, and /home/colors.toml

A colour is an RGB332 integer, 0..255. The names are the web's, mapped onto the 256 colours (a list of 101, plus aliases that land on the same colour). /home/colors.toml holds only what an app overrides: a missing file, section or key means "use the theme".

bg = FmrbColors.by_name("navy")   #=> 2

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is PATH String The overrides file

docs.title: FmrbColors.shade
docs.text:
shade(Integer color, ?Integer? avoid) -> Integer

A step darker than a theme colour

Down two of the seven red/green steps and one of the three blue ones. When the result would be 0x01 (the desktop's transparent key), the colour itself or avoid, it goes the other way. For a bar that must not merge with its neighbour.

bar = FmrbColors.shade(
  FmrbConst::THEME_MENU_BG, bg)

docs.title: FmrbColors.by_name
docs.text:
by_name(String name) -> Integer?

Look a colour up by name

The name must be lowercase and in the list or the aliases. Otherwise nil.

FmrbColors.by_name("black")   #=> 0

docs.title: FmrbColors.name_of
docs.text:
name_of(Integer value) -> String?

The name to show for a colour

nil for a colour without a name. An alias is never returned, only the list's name.

FmrbColors.name_of(0)   #=> "black"

docs.title: FmrbColors.name_at
docs.text:
name_at(Integer index) -> String?

The nth name in the list

From 0. nil out of range.

FmrbColors.name_at(0)   #=> "black"

docs.title: FmrbColors.palette_size
docs.text:
palette_size() -> Integer

How many names the list holds

FmrbColors.palette_size.times { |i| p FmrbColors.name_at(i) }

docs.title: FmrbColors.palette_value
docs.text:
palette_value(Integer index) -> Integer?

The nth colour of the list

From 0. nil out of range. Same order as name_at.

FmrbColors.palette_value(0)   #=> 0

docs.title: FmrbColors.to_color
docs.text:
to_color(String text) -> Integer?

Turn text into a colour

"0x24" (hex), "36" (decimal), "black" or "\"black\"" (a name) become 0..255. Anything else is nil, so a typo leaves the theme colour (it never paints black). A hex or decimal above 255 is cut to its low 8 bits.

FmrbColors.to_color("0x1C")   #=> 28

docs.title: FmrbColors.to_text
docs.text:
to_text(Integer value) -> String

The text to write back for a colour

Its name when it has one, otherwise the "0x1C" form.

FmrbColors.to_text(28)   #=> "0x1C" or a name

docs.title: FmrbColors.section
docs.text:
section(String name) -> Hash[String, Integer]

Read one section's overrides

Returns { "bg" => 36, ... }. A missing file or section, non-TOML text, a non-colour value give an empty Hash or are skipped; nothing raises. An integer is cut to 8 bits (a negative one is skipped), a string goes through to_color.

c = FmrbColors.section("editor")
bg = c["bg"] || FmrbConst::THEME_WINDOW_BG

docs.title: FmrbColors.set
docs.text:
set(String section, String key, Integer? value) -> bool

Write one override

Writes a colour to key key of section section. A nil value removes the key (back to the theme). It writes as FmrbToml.update does (other lines and comments stay). true when the file holds it now, false when it could not be written or the file is not TOML.

FmrbColors.set("shell", "bg", 0x24)

docs.title: FmrbColors.clear
docs.text:
clear(String section) -> bool

Remove a whole section

Drops the heading and everything up to the next section, then rewrites the file. true when there is no file, false when the write fails. Other sections are kept, but the file is rewritten whole.

FmrbColors.clear("shell")

docs.text:
Constants: machine, build, keys, theme

How to use it: Constants & System Info.

Values are fixed when the VM starts and do not change while an app runs. Constants that differ by machine or build (BOARD, PLATFORM, HW_FAMILY, CHIP_*, FLASH_SIZE_MB and others) say so in their notes.

KEY_* are USB HID Usage IDs. Compare them with ev[:scancode] to get the same answer on every machine. ev[:keycode] differs by machine for character keys (ASCII on SDL).

if ev[:scancode] == FmrbConst::KEY_ESC
  stop
end

docs.text:
Read and write whole files by path

How to use it: Files & I/O.

Functions called by path; nothing stays open. There are read, write, append, exist?, size, delete, mkdir and list. A call reads or writes the whole file, so a big file is held in memory entirely. To read a little at a time from a position, use File.

docs.title: FmrbGfx
docs.text:
A canvas: shapes, text, images, sprites

How to use it: Drawing.

An app does not make one; it uses the gfx (@gfx) that FmrbApp prepares. The origin (0, 0) is the top-left of the area the app owns, and colours are RGB332 numbers (FmrbGfx::RED and so on). The drawing methods return the canvas itself, so calls chain. Drawing alone shows nothing: call present once at the end of a frame.

Methods to read first: clear, fill_rect, draw_text, draw_image, present.

docs.title: FmrbGfx.rgb_to_332
docs.text:
rgb_to_332(Integer r, Integer g, Integer b) -> Integer

Make a colour from red, green and blue

Packs three 0-255 values into one byte: three bits of red, three of green, two of blue, so nearby colours collapse onto the same value and fine gradients do not survive.

Avoid combinations that come out as 0x01. The desktop uses 0x01 as its transparency key, so a window painted with it shows through.

FmrbGfx.rgb_to_332(255, 0, 0)  #=> 224

docs.title: FmrbGfx.video_control
docs.text:
video_control(:play | :pause | :stop | :rewind action) -> video_status?

Play, pause, stop or rewind the video

There is one player. Acts on the video video_open opened and returns its state afterwards (nil when there is no answer). :stop closes the file; the canvas keeps the last picture. The wrappers are FmrbVideo's play, pause, stop and rewind.

FmrbGfx.video_control(:play)

docs.title: FmrbGfx.video_status
docs.text:
video_status() -> video_status?

The video player's state

{state:, shown:, dropped:}, or nil when there is no answer. state is 0 idle, 1 playing, 2 paused, 3 finished; shown and dropped count frames. The wrapper is FmrbVideo#status.

st = FmrbGfx.video_status

hsv_to_rgb(Integer h, Integer s, Integer v) -> Array

Make a colour from hue, saturation and value

h is 0-360, s and v are 0-255. It returns [r, g, b], which is not a colour yet -- pass it through rgb_to_332.

r, g, b = FmrbGfx.hsv_to_rgb(hue, 255, 255)

canvas_width() -> Integer

Canvas width in pixels

The width of the whole canvas. A windowed app may only draw inside its area (area_width, the same as @user_area_width), which is not the same thing; for a fullscreen app the two agree.

origin_x() -> Integer

Where the origin is on the canvas (x)

Every coordinate drawn is added to it on its way to the canvas (the firmware adds it): 1 for a framed window's gfx, 0 for window_gfx and the rest. While drawing into a sprite image it is not added to what is drawn, but it still is to sprite coordinates (set_sprite_clip, SpriteInstance).

FmrbApp.set_text_cursor(

  @gfx.origin_y + y, 12)

clear(Integer color) -> FmrbGfx

Paint the whole canvas one colour

Fills the whole canvas. In a windowed app that erases the title bar and frame the app drew itself; to clear only the inside of the window use FmrbApp#clear_user_area, which redraws the frame and marks any attached FmrbUI widgets for redraw.

For a fullscreen app clear is the right call, and faster than a fill_rect over the same area.

@gfx.clear(FmrbGfx::BLACK)
@gfx.present

get_pixel(Integer x, Integer y) -> Integer

Read one pixel's colour

A synchronous round trip to the graphics side. Not something to do per pixel in a loop scanning the screen.

Outside the canvas it returns 0, which is also black -- the return value does not tell the two apart.

c = @gfx.get_pixel(60, 40)

) -> FmrbGfx

Draw a line with a thickness

The graphics side has no thick-line primitive, so this stacks thickness one-pixel lines side by side. The cost grows with the thickness, which shows if thick lines are drawn every frame.

@gfx.draw_thick_line(10, 10, 60, 40,
                    2, FmrbGfx::WHITE)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_rect
docs.text:
draw_rect(
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  Integer color
) -> FmrbGfx

Draw the outline of a rectangle

(x, y) is the top-left corner, w the width, h the height. It draws the outline only, so whatever is underneath stays visible inside. Use fill_rect to colour the inside too.

gfx.draw_rect(10, 10, 100, 50,
              FmrbGfx::WHITE)  # frame
gfx.fill_rect(12, 12, 96, 46,
              FmrbGfx::BLUE)   # inside
gfx.present

docs.title: FmrbGfx#fill_rect
docs.text:
fill_rect(
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  Integer color
) -> FmrbGfx

Fill a rectangle

(x, y) is the top-left corner, w the width, h the height, and the inside is filled. To wipe the whole canvas, clear is faster.

For something that moves, paint over where it was in the background colour first, then draw it at the new place, and it leaves no trail.

class MyApp < FmrbApp
  def on_update
    # erase the old place
    gfx.fill_rect(@x, 100, 16, 16,
                  FmrbGfx::BLACK)
    @x = @x + 2
    # draw at the new one
    gfx.fill_rect(@x, 100, 16, 16,
                  FmrbGfx::RED)
    gfx.present
  end
end

blend_rect(

Fill a rectangle blended with what is under it

The last argument is the blend mode -- FmrbGfx::BLEND_ADD or FmrbGfx::BLEND_XOR -- not an opacity. Additive reads as a glow; XOR inverts what is underneath.

gfx.fill_rect(0, 0, 64, 64, FmrbGfx::BLUE)
gfx.blend_rect(16, 16, 32, 32,
               FmrbGfx::RED, FmrbGfx::BLEND_ADD)

Draw an arc

Angles are integer degrees. r0 is the inner radius and r1 the outer one, so a non-zero r0 gives part of a ring; r0 of 0 gives the outline of a pie slice.

@gfx.draw_arc(80, 60, 35, 45, 0, 360,
              FmrbGfx::WHITE)

  Integer color
) -> FmrbGfx

Fill a wedge of a circle

Angles are integer degrees. r0 is the inner radius and r1 the outer one: r0 of 0 fills a pie slice, a non-zero r0 fills part of a ring -- which is how a gauge or a pie chart is drawn.

@gfx.fill_arc(80, 60, 0, 50, 0, 120,
             FmrbGfx::BLUE)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_text
docs.text:
draw_text(
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  String text,
  Integer color,
  ?Integer? bg_color,
  ?mixed: bool
) -> FmrbGfx

draw a string

(x, y) is the top-left corner of the string. The screen's top-left is (0, 0): x grows to the right and y grows downwards. color is an RGB332 value -- a named one such as FmrbGfx::WHITE, or any colour made with FmrbGfx.rgb_to_332(255, 0, 0).

Nothing appears on the screen until present is called. A fifth argument paints the background of the characters in that colour (none when left out). mixed: true draws ASCII with the 6x8 font and Japanese with the 8x8 one, whatever font is selected.

class MyApp < FmrbApp
  def on_update
    gfx.clear(FmrbGfx::BLACK)
    gfx.draw_text(10, 20, "hello", FmrbGfx::WHITE)
    gfx.present
  end
end

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_text_raw
docs.text:
draw_text_raw(
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  String text,
  Integer color,
  Integer bg_color,
  bool mixed
) -> FmrbGfx

draw_text with nothing left out

The simple form, with no argument left out, for where speed matters (drawing many times a frame). A negative bg_color leaves the background alone; mixed true draws ASCII in 6x8 and the rest in misaki 8 (draw_text's mixed: true). The wrapper is draw_text.

gfx.draw_text_raw(10, 20, "hi",
  FmrbGfx::WHITE, -1, false)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_font
docs.text:
set_font(Symbol family, ?Integer size) -> Array[untyped]

Choose the font and size

family is :default (6x8 ASCII), :ja (Japanese) or :ja_bold (:ja in bold). size is the height in pixels: 8, 12 and 16 for :ja, 12 for :ja_bold. Which faces exist differs by machine (Retro stops at 12), so asking for a size or a weight it has not got gets you the nearest one. What comes back is the [family, size] actually chosen -- which is also how you find out that bold was unavailable and you should thicken the text yourself.

got = gfx.set_font(:ja, 12)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_font_raw
docs.text:
set_font_raw(:default | :ja | :ja_bold family, Integer size) -> FmrbGfx

set_font with nothing left out

The simple form, with no argument left out. It does not pick the nearest face this machine has, so a size it lacks is an error (:ja takes 8, 12 and 16, :ja_bold 12; :default ignores size). current_font is left as it is. The wrapper is set_font.

gfx.set_font_raw(:ja, 12)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_text_size
docs.text:
set_text_size(Integer size) -> FmrbGfx

Set the text scale

Scales the selected font by an integer factor. It is the same glyphs enlarged, so the edges get blocky. text_width reports the width after the multiplier.

@gfx.set_text_size(2)
@gfx.draw_text(4, 4, "BIG", 0xFF)
@gfx.set_text_size(1)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_text_size_raw
docs.text:
set_text_size_raw(Integer size) -> FmrbGfx

set_text_size without the wrapper

Only sends the scale (1 to 4) to the graphics side; current_text_size and what text_width measures stay as they were. The wrapper is set_text_size.

gfx.set_text_size_raw(2)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#text_width
docs.text:
text_width(String text) -> Integer

Measure how wide text would be

Measured with the font set_font selected and the multiplier set_text_size set, so measure again after changing either. It walks the UTF-8, so a mixed Japanese and ASCII string gives a real pixel width rather than a character count.

w = gfx.text_width(text)
x = (gfx.area_width - w) / 2
gfx.draw_text(x, 20, text, FmrbGfx::WHITE)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#font_height
docs.text:
font_height() -> Integer

The height of one line

The height of the font currently selected -- the spacing to use when stacking lines. It changes with the font.

y += @gfx.font_height + 2

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_wallclock
docs.text:
draw_wallclock(
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer color,
  Integer bg_color
) -> bool

Draw the time now

The time is formatted inside the call, so calling it every second allocates nothing. A negative bg_color leaves the background as it is.

gfx.draw_wallclock(300, 2,
                   theme_fg, theme_bg)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_free_iram
docs.text:
draw_free_iram(
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer color,
  Integer bg_color
) -> bool

Draw how much memory is free

Fetching and formatting both happen inside. Where no figure can be read, it draws dashes. A negative bg_color leaves the background as it is.

gfx.draw_free_iram(360, 2,
                   theme_fg, theme_bg)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#load_image
docs.text:
load_image(String path) -> void

Load an image file and place it

Does sync_file, create_image, draw_image, present and delete_image in one call -- enough when a picture just has to appear.

coord: takes [x, y] or :center; left out, it draws at the top left. Not something to call every frame: it builds and throws away the image each time.

gfx.load_image("/home/pic.png", coord: :center)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#create_image
docs.text:
create_image(String path) -> image_info?

Make an image from a file

Takes a PNG. Sprite artwork (an RGB332 PNG or BMP) goes through SpriteImage#load_bmp instead. Handing a BMP to this does not raise: you get an empty screen-sized image and nothing appears.

The graphics side reads its own filesystem, so send the file with sync_file first. Returns {id:, width:, height:}, or nil when it could not be read.

path = "/home/pic.png"
gfx.sync_file(path)
img = gfx.create_image(path)
gfx.draw_image(img[:id], x: 0, y: 0) if img

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_image
docs.text:
draw_image(Integer image_id) -> FmrbGfx

Draw an image you made

Position and scale are keyword arguments (x:, y:, scale_x:, scale_y:). A scale_y of 0.0 means "the same as scale_x".

gfx.draw_image(id, x: 10, y: 20)
gfx.draw_image(id, x: 10, y: 20,
               scale_x: 2.0)   # both axes doubled

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_image_raw
docs.text:
draw_image_raw(
  Integer image_id,
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Float scale_x,
  Float scale_y
) -> FmrbGfx

draw_image with nothing left out

The simple form, with no argument left out. A scale_y of 0.0 means the same as scale_x. The wrapper is draw_image.

gfx.draw_image_raw(id, 10, 20,
                   1.0, 0.0)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#delete_image
docs.text:
delete_image(Integer image_id) -> FmrbGfx

Let go of an image you made

An image is a resource on the graphics side, and there is a limited number of them, so release one when it is done with. The system reclaims them when the app exits, so a missing cleanup at exit does not leak.

@gfx.delete_image(@image[:id])

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_tile
docs.text:
draw_tile(
  Integer image_id,
  Integer src_x,
  Integer src_y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h
) -> FmrbGfx

Draw one piece cut out of an image

Stamps part of a SpriteImage straight onto the canvas. No SpriteInstance is created, which suits the things that do not move -- terrain, a background. The destination is passed by keyword (dst_x:, dst_y:).

A SpriteImage made with use_transparent: true keeps its transparent colour transparent here. TileMap is the higher-level way to lay a whole map out.

scale: draws it at another size. 2 to 32 turns each pixel into a scale x scale block (scale: 2 is twice the size); -2 to -32 draws 1/|scale| of it (scale: -4 is a quarter, taking the top-left pixel of each block). It goes through draw_tile_scaled_raw.

sheet.load_bmp("/cache/app/x/tiles.png")
gfx.draw_tile(sheet.id, 0, 0, 16, 16,
              dst_x: 32, dst_y: 16)
gfx.draw_tile(sheet.id, 0, 0, 16, 16,
  dst_x: 0, dst_y: 40, scale: 3)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_tile_raw
docs.text:
draw_tile_raw(
  Integer image_id,
  Integer src_x,
  Integer src_y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  Integer dst_x,
  Integer dst_y
) -> FmrbGfx

draw_tile with nothing left out

The destination as plain arguments rather than keywords. The wrapper is draw_tile.

gfx.draw_tile_raw(sheet.id, 0, 0,
                  16, 16, 32, 16)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_tile_scaled_raw
docs.text:
draw_tile_scaled_raw(
  Integer image_id,
  Integer src_x,
  Integer src_y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  Integer dst_x,
  Integer dst_y,
  Integer scale,
  Integer clip_x,
  Integer clip_y,
  Integer clip_w,
  Integer clip_h
) -> FmrbGfx

draw_tile drawn larger or smaller

A scale of 1 to 32 turns each pixel into a scale x scale block; -2 to -32 draws 1/|scale| of the size (the top-left pixel of each block; 0 and -1 are 1). Out of range is ERR_ARG. The destination is cut to the clip rect (from the origin; none when clip_w or clip_h is 0) and to the canvas. The transparent colour is skipped as in draw_tile. The wrapper is draw_tile's scale:.

gfx.draw_tile_scaled_raw(id, 0, 0,
  16, 16, 40, 20, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#picture_info
docs.text:
picture_info(String path) -> picture_info?

Read a picture file's width and height

Reads only the head of a PNG or an 8-bit BMP; nothing is decoded (the same C as BMP332.info). The result is {width:, height:, format:, bytes:, mtime:}: format is 1 for PNG, 2 for BMP; bytes is the file's size and mtime when it was written (0 on a file system that keeps no time). nil when it is not there or cannot be read. The file is the app's own (it need not have been sent to the display side).

info = gfx.picture_info("/home/a.png")
w = info[:width] if info

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_picture
docs.text:
draw_picture(String path, Integer x, Integer y) -> bool

Draw a picture file, reading it in the first time

Just hand the path (or put_picture's name). A picture is read into a sprite image on the display side the first time; this FmrbGfx keeps up to picture_limit of them (8 unless set), letting the least recently drawn go first. A file written again (another size or time) is read again the next time it is drawn (looked at once a second at most). They all go when the app ends.

  • scale: 1 to 32 turns each pixel into scale x scale; -2 to -32 draws 1/|scale| of the size
  • checker: true lays the checkerboard under the transparent parts (draw_checker)
  • clip: [x, y, w, h] draws only inside that rect

false when it cannot be drawn (nothing raises); picture_error says why. A picture past 65,536 pixels is refused. A file past 65,536 bytes is read on the app side (BMP332.load: in the VM pool while it is read) and its pixels put. Transparent is the colour 0x01 (a PNG's alpha and tRNS).

gfx.draw_picture("/home/stamps/a.png",
  10, 20, scale: 2)
gfx.draw_picture(path, 0, 0,
  scale: -2, checker: true)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#picture_size
docs.text:
picture_size(String path) -> Array[Integer]?

A picture's width and height, as [w, h]

From the store when the picture is there, else from the file's head (picture_info); nothing goes to the display side. nil when it is not a picture.

w, h = gfx.picture_size("/home/a.png")

docs.title: FmrbGfx#put_picture
docs.text:
put_picture(
  String name,
  Integer width,
  Integer height,
  String pixels
) -> bool

Put RGB332 pixels in the picture store by name

pixels is width x height bytes, top row first; 0x01 is transparent. Draw it with draw_picture(name, ...). Putting the same name again writes the pixels again. No file is involved. false when there is no room.

gfx.put_picture("mine", 16, 16, px)
gfx.draw_picture("mine", 0, 0,
  scale: 4)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#release_picture
docs.text:
release_picture(String path) -> FmrbGfx

Let go of one picture in the picture store

gfx.release_picture("/home/a.png")

docs.title: FmrbGfx#release_pictures
docs.text:
release_pictures() -> FmrbGfx

Let go of every picture in the picture store

Not needed when the app ends (the pictures go with the canvas). For letting go of pictures no longer drawn, all at once.

gfx.release_pictures

docs.title: FmrbGfx#picture_limit=
docs.text:
picture_limit=(Integer n) -> Integer

How many pictures the picture store keeps

8 unless set; fewer lets the oldest go now. The display side's sprite images are limited for the whole machine (64 and 256 KB on the sim and Retro, 160 on P4).

gfx.picture_limit = 16

docs.title: FmrbGfx#picture_error
docs.text:
picture_error() -> Symbol?

Why the last picture could not be drawn

:unreadable (not there, not a picture), :too_big (past 65,536 pixels), :no_room (no room on the display side), :not_sent (could not be sent there). nil after one that worked.

unless gfx.draw_picture(path, 0, 0)
  Log.info(gfx.picture_error.to_s)
end

docs.title: FmrbGfx#draw_checker
docs.text:
draw_checker(Integer x, Integer y, Integer w, Integer h) -> FmrbGfx

Draw the checkerboard that stands for transparency

White and light grey cells (cell: px, 4 unless given) over (x, y, w, h); clip: [x, y, w, h] cuts it. One strip is made on the display side and stamped, height / (cell x 2) commands.

gfx.draw_checker(0, 0, 64, 64)
gfx.draw_checker(0, 0, 64, 64,
  cell: 2)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#create_mask
docs.text:
create_mask(Integer width, Integer height, bin data) -> Integer

Make a mask

data is one bit per pixel: ceil(width / 8) bytes per row, most significant bit leftmost. Only the pixels whose bit is set are drawn.

Returns a mask_id for draw_image_masked; release it with delete_mask.

mask = @gfx.create_mask(48, 48, bits)
# bits: 6 bytes x 48 rows

docs.title: FmrbGfx#delete_mask
docs.text:

docs.title: FmrbGfx#present
docs.text:
present() -> FmrbGfx

show what has been drawn

Drawing methods only queue commands; nothing reaches the screen until present sends them. Sprite compositing also happens at present, so it is needed after SpriteInstance#move or visible= as well.

Call it once at the end of a frame. Calling it after every shape costs a whole-screen transfer each time.

gfx.clear(FmrbGfx::BLACK)
gfx.draw_text(10, 10, "hi", FmrbGfx::WHITE)
gfx.present   # now it appears

docs.title: FmrbGfx#present_raw
docs.text:
present_raw(Integer x, Integer y, bool positioned) -> FmrbGfx

present with nothing left out

With positioned false the canvas goes where the window is (x and y are not used); with true it goes to (x, y) on the screen. The wrapper is present (present(x, y) gives a position).

gfx.present_raw(0, 0, false)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#destroy
docs.text:
destroy() -> FmrbGfx

Let go of this canvas

Throws away a canvas made by the app. They go on their own when the app ends, so this is for one that is finished with early.

g = create_canvas_gfx(width: 64,
                     height: 64)
g.destroy

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_viewport
docs.text:
set_viewport(
  Integer src_x,
  Integer src_y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h
) -> FmrbGfx

Shift what part of the canvas is shown

Moves a viewport smaller than the canvas across it. The canvas is treated as a torus, so the source rectangle wraps at the edges: with a canvas a little larger than the viewport, stamping only the newly exposed tiles as it moves scrolls an arbitrarily large world without redrawing it.

Modern (ESP32-P4) only; the Retro backend ignores the command. Gate it on FmrbConst::CHIP_MODEL == "ESP32-P4".

@map_gfx.set_viewport(vx % bw, vy % bh,
                      160, 120)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#clear_viewport
docs.text:
clear_viewport() -> FmrbGfx

Put the shown part back

Undo set_viewport: the whole canvas is composited again. Modern (ESP32-P4) only, as set_viewport is.

@map_gfx.set_viewport(8, 0, 160, 120)
@map_gfx.clear_viewport

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_composite_regions
docs.text:
set_composite_regions(Array[Hash] regions) -> FmrbGfx

Set the regions that are composited

Says which rectangles of the canvas are composited and how. It is the optimisation for a rounded window, where only the corners need transparency and the middle can take the fast path. Eight at most; nil or [] restores the default of the whole canvas.

For a windowed app the system sets this from rounded_corners in the .app.toml, so calling it directly is rarely needed.

@gfx.set_composite_regions([
  { dst_x: 0, dst_y: 0, w: 100,
    h: 20, transparent: false }
])

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_composite_regions_raw
docs.text:
set_composite_regions_raw(Array[composite_region] regions) -> FmrbGfx

set_composite_regions, every field given

Every field of each rectangle written out: src_x, src_y, dst_x, dst_y, w, h and transparent. An empty array restores the default (the whole canvas). The wrapper is set_composite_regions.

gfx.set_composite_regions_raw([
  { src_x: 0, src_y: 0, dst_x: 0,
    dst_y: 0, w: 8, h: 8,
    transparent: true }])

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_sprite_clip
docs.text:
set_sprite_clip(Integer x, Integer y, Integer w, Integer h) -> FmrbGfx

limit where sprites may appear

Sprites are composited on top of everything drawn into the canvas, so without a clip they paint over the window frame and title bar. This confines them to the given rect, in the same coordinates as SpriteInstance#move (from the origin, also while drawing into a sprite image).

Windowed apps start with their user area set, so calling this is only needed to narrow it further - e.g. to keep sprites out of a score bar.

# reserve the top 10px for the score; sprites stay below it
@gfx.set_sprite_clip(0, 10,
  @user_area_width,
  @user_area_height - 10)

docs.text:
write_sprite_image(
  Integer image_id,
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  bin pixels
) -> FmrbGfx

Write RGB332 pixels into a sprite image

pixels is w * h bytes, top row first, written from (x, y) of the image; what falls outside it is dropped. Up to 65,536 pixels a call (more is ERR_ARG). It travels with the drawing commands, so a draw_tile asked for earlier still draws the image as it was. The wrapper is SpriteImage#write_pixels.

  16, 16, pixels)

Play a motion-JPEG file into the canvas (Modern)

Sets the brightness of Retro's composite video signal. It does nothing on Modern. For when a CRT's own controls do not get there.

@gfx.set_output_level(200)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#set_chroma_level
docs.text:
set_chroma_level(Integer level) -> FmrbGfx

docs.title: FmrbGfx#sync_file
docs.text:
sync_file(String path, ?dest: String) -> bool

Send an image or sound file across

The graphics side reads its own filesystem, so an asset has to be put there first. This compares size and CRC32 and transfers only when they differ, so it is fine to call on every start.

Deciding with file_status[:exists] instead -- "it is there, skip it" -- leaves an edited asset stale for ever. Use this one for assets.

gfx.sync_file("/home/bird.png",
              dest: "/cache/app/x/bird.png")

docs.title: FmrbGfx#sync_file_raw
docs.text:
sync_file_raw(String path, String dest) -> bool

sync_file with nothing left out

The destination cannot be left out. The wrapper is sync_file (without dest: it uses the same path).

gfx.sync_file_raw(path, path)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#transfer_file
docs.text:
transfer_file(String path) -> bool

Send a file again whatever happens

Transfers unconditionally, without looking at what is already there. sync_file is the usual choice; this one is for when the destination is known to need rewriting.

@gfx.transfer_file("/data/a.bmp")

docs.title: FmrbGfx#transfer_file_raw
docs.text:
transfer_file_raw(String path, String dest) -> bool

transfer_file with nothing left out

The destination cannot be left out. The wrapper is transfer_file.

gfx.transfer_file_raw(path, path)

docs.title: FmrbGfx#file_status
docs.text:
file_status(String path) -> file_info

Whether the file arrived

Whether the graphics side has the file, and how big it is: {exists:, size:}.

Do not use it to decide whether to send an asset. exists stays true after the contents change, so an edited asset would stay stale; leave that decision to sync_file.

st = @gfx.file_status("/data/a.bmp")
st[:exists]
st[:size]

docs.title: FmrbHw
docs.text:
Read the table of how pins are used

How to use it: Hardware Control, Constants & System Info.

Which pins are system-only, and which an app's GPIO, I2C or RMT holds. Check with FmrbHw.pin_available? which pins an app may use on this board. Only a real board marks the table. The Linux sim, the native build and the browser build have no pins, so every entry stays PIN_UNUSED (49 pins).

if FmrbHw.pin_available?(5)
  io = GPIO.new(5, GPIO::OUT)
end

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is PIN_UNUSED Integer A pin nobody uses PIN_SYSTEM_EXCLUSIVE Integer System-only pin; apps cannot use it PIN_USER_GPIO Integer Held by an app as GPIO PIN_USER_I2C Integer Held by I2C PIN_USER_RMT Integer Held by RMT PIN_USER_SPI Integer Held by SPI (a reserved value) PIN_USER_PWM Integer Held by PWM (a reserved value) PIN_USER_UART Integer Held by UART (a reserved value) PIN_I2C1_SDA Integer Pin number of I2C1 SDA PIN_I2C1_SCL Integer Pin number of I2C1 SCL PIN_I2C2_SDA Integer Pin number of I2C2 SDA PIN_I2C2_SCL Integer Pin number of I2C2 SCL

docs.title: FmrbHw.pin_status
docs.text:
pin_status(Integer pin) -> Integer

How a pin is used (a PIN_* value)

A pin the system uses is PIN_SYSTEM_EXCLUSIVE even when the table does not hold it (the same pins GPIO refuses). A pin number out of range does not raise: it is PIN_UNUSED (0).

FmrbHw.pin_status(25) == FmrbHw::PIN_SYSTEM_EXCLUSIVE

docs.title: FmrbHw.pin_available?
docs.text:
pin_available?(Integer pin) -> bool

Whether an app can take the pin

true only for a PIN_UNUSED pin. A number out of range is false, and so is a system-only pin (one GPIO refuses) or one somebody already holds.

FmrbHw.pin_available?(5)   #=> true or false

docs.title: FmrbHw.pin_status_all
docs.text:
pin_status_all() -> Array[Integer]

How every pin is used

The index is the pin number and the value is a PIN_* (as pin_status gives it). The length is pin_count.

FmrbHw.pin_status_all[5]

docs.title: FmrbHw.pin_count
docs.text:
pin_count() -> Integer

How many pins the table has

55 on an ESP32-P4 board (GPIO 0..54); 49 elsewhere (S3, Linux sim, native, browser) (GPIO 0..48).

FmrbHw.pin_count   #=> 55 or 49

docs.text: Switch the display between Japanese and English

docs.title: FmrbI18n.add
docs.text:
add(Hash table) -> void

Add a table of words

Each app adds its own table. Keys it does not name are kept, so this table and the desktop's live side by side. A key named again for the same language is replaced by the later value.

FmrbI18n.add(
  "en" => { save: "Save" },
  "ja" => { save: "保存" })

docs.title: FmrbI18n.lang
docs.text:
lang() -> String

The language now, "ja" or "en"

An app moved to another machine speaks the language of that machine.

if FmrbI18n.lang == "ja"
  draw_ja
end

docs.title: FmrbI18n.t
docs.text:
t(Symbol key) -> String

Look a key up in the language now

docs.title: FmrbI18n.text_width
docs.text:
text_width(String str) -> Integer

Measure how wide text would be

A Japanese character is two cells wide, so length will not do. Use this to right-align or centre.

w = FmrbI18n.text_width(s)
gfx.draw_text(320 - w, y, s)

docs.title: FmrbI18n.truncate_to
docs.text:
truncate_to(String str, Integer max_px, ?String ellipsis) -> String

Cut it down to what fits the width

Never cuts a character in half. When it cuts it appends ellipsis (".." when left out, 12 pixels), and that counts inside max_px. "" appends nothing. Text that fits comes back as it is.

s = FmrbI18n.truncate_to(name, 120)

docs.title: FmrbI18n.strings
docs.text:
strings() -> Hash[String, Hash[untyped, String]]

The table of words itself

The table of words as a Hash of language to key to text, add writes into it. It starts as { "en" => {}, "ja" => {} }, made the first time it is asked for.

docs.title: FmrbI18n.forget
docs.text:
forget() -> nil

Forget the language resolved so far

The next lang reads the machine's setting again. For an app moved to another machine the base calls it itself, so an ordinary app does not. It always returns nil.

FmrbI18n.forget

docs.title: FmrbI18n.half_kana?
docs.text:
half_kana?(String str, Integer i, Integer n) -> bool

Whether it is a half-width katakana

True when the 3 bytes from byte i are a half-width katakana (U+FF61 to U+FF9F). i is a byte position, not a character one, and n is the string's byte size (bytesize). False when fewer than 3 bytes are left. text_width uses it to count half-width kana as 4 pixels.

s = "ｱ"
FmrbI18n.half_kana?(s, 0, s.bytesize)
#=> true

docs.title: FmrbMidi
docs.text:
MIDI entry point: devices, songs, MML

How to use it: MIDI.

FmrbMidi.device(self) gives a device (MIDI::Device) wired to the built-in sound chip (the APU); send notes to it with note_on and the like. A standard MIDI file is played by FmrbMidi::SmfPlayer, MML by FmrbMidi::MmlPlayer. For an outside instrument, sam2695_device and serial_device make the device and register adds a transport. Measure a song's time with now_us.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is GM_DRUM_CHANNEL Integer The channel General MIDI keeps for drums

docs.title: FmrbMidi.device
docs.text:
device(FmrbApp app) -> MIDI::Device

Make this app's way of sounding notes

Gives you a device wired to the built-in sound chip. To play an outside instrument, register that transport as well.

@midi = FmrbMidi.device(self)
@midi.note_on(60)

docs.title: FmrbMidi.now_us
docs.text:
now_us() -> Integer

The time now, in microseconds

The clock to schedule notes against. Measure a song with this, never by counting frames -- a heavy frame stretches the music.

t0 = FmrbMidi.now_us

docs.title: FmrbMidi.register
docs.text:
register(untyped transport) -> untyped

Register somewhere to send notes

Registering the same transport twice adds it once.

FmrbMidi.register(transport)

docs.title: FmrbMidi.unregister
docs.text:
unregister(untyped transport) -> void

Stop sending notes there

FmrbMidi.unregister(transport)

docs.text:
transports() -> Array

Everywhere notes are being sent

FmrbMidi.transports.length

docs.title: FmrbMidi.gm_name
docs.text:
gm_name(Integer program) -> String?

The instrument's name from its number

0 to 127; anything else is nil. The names are shortened to 16 characters (program 0 is "Ac Grand Piano").

FmrbMidi.gm_name(0)
#=> "Ac Grand Piano"

docs.title: FmrbMidi.sam2695_device
docs.text:
sam2695_device(
  ?path: String,
  ?uart: Integer,
  ?tx: Integer,
  ?rx: Integer,
  ?baud: Integer
) -> MIDI::Device?

Make a device for an outside SAM2695 unit

M5Stack Unit MIDI and the like; MIDI goes out over a serial port (31250 baud). nil when it will not connect (in the sim when the FIFO that receives it is missing; on a device when the board has no MIDI output or the pins are taken). Using the nil raises NoMethodError, so always check. Each call sends GM System On and silences every channel, so make it once and keep it. It is not the built-in sound (FmrbMidi.device); switch with SmfPlayer#device=. path: (sim only), uart: and tx: (device only), rx: (-1 when left out: send only), baud: (31250 when left out). What is left out is the board's default.

@serial = FmrbMidi.sam2695_device
@serial.program_change(0) if @serial

docs.title: FmrbMidi.serial_device
docs.text:
serial_device(
  ?path: String,
  ?uart: Integer,
  ?tx: Integer,
  ?rx: Integer,
  ?baud: Integer
) -> MIDI::Device?

Make a device on a plain serial MIDI port

The same as sam2695_device without the reset sent to the unit. nil when it will not connect. The same keywords (path: uart: tx: rx: baud:; the board's default when left out).

@out = FmrbMidi.serial_device
@out.note_on(60) if @out

docs.title: FmrbMidi.scheduler
docs.text:
scheduler() -> untyped

The scheduler that sends timed notes, or nil

A song's notes are stamped with a time and handed to a C queue, and a timer sends them at that time. This is that queue. An app only asks whether it exists; the methods starting with _ are not for apps. nil when there is none (the host tests).

puts FmrbMidi.scheduler ? "yes" : "no"

docs.title: FmrbMidi.tick
docs.text:
tick() -> void

Send the note-offs that have come due

This is what ends the notes of MIDI::Device#trigger. Call it once in every on_update. Without it a triggered note stays on until the next MIDI message. Every device made, built-in or serial, is looked at here.

def on_update
  FmrbMidi.tick
  FmrbMidi.tick_delay(100)
end

docs.title: FmrbMidi.tick_delay
docs.text:
tick_delay(Integer default_ms) -> Integer

How long the app may sleep, in ms

Returns the shorter of the wait you pass and the time to the next scheduled note-off, in ms and never below 0. Return it from on_update so a short note does not ring on until the next update.

def on_update
  FmrbMidi.tick
  FmrbMidi.tick_delay(200)
end

docs.title: FmrbMidi::ApuTransport
docs.text:
Sends MIDI to the built-in sound chip (APU)

How to use it: MIDI.

Made by FmrbMidi.device(self).

The APU has 4 voices (2 square, a triangle and noise), and one voice sounds only one note at a time. Channels 0, 1, 2 and 9 map to square 1, square 2, the triangle and the noise in that order, and other channels stay silent (change this with map_channel and auto_map). Program changes, pitch bends and SysEx are received and dropped. The voices use the APU on the SUB side, so they clash with the SUB sound effects of play_slot.

docs.text:
defer_voices(?Integer due_us, ?Integer owner) -> void

Begin a group of notes of one instant

Call it before sending several messages of one instant, such as a chord, and flush_voices after. Meanwhile only the voices' state changes, and flush_voices sends each voice's final state once (so the inner notes of a chord are not played in turn). due_us (now when left out) is a time on the FmrbMidi.now_us clock to send at. A group left open swallows every later note; FmrbMidi.tick closes it each time. Nothing happens when one is already open. owner (0 when left out) is stamped on what goes to the queue so that a player can drop only its own (the players pass it themselves).

How to use it: Network.

The machine owns the WiFi connection, so an app only looks at the state (connected?, ip_address, hostname, ssid). Fetching is FmrbNet.request, written the same way in the browser build too. The Linux sim, the native build and the browser build always answer "connected" (127.0.0.1, localhost).

Stops the calling app's task for up to timeout_ms (timeout_ms is 10000 when left out; a negative value is 0). true once an address is there, false on timeout. docs.title: FmrbNet.request
docs.text:
request(String url) -> FmrbNet::Request

Start fetching a URL

Returns a Request, not the answer (which is why it is not called get). Read the result later, once done? is true. There is no callback.

How it waits differs by build. The browser build fetches in the background, so done? stays false for a while and the screen keeps moving. A real board, the Linux sim and the native build finish inside request, so the app's task stops until the server answers (done? is true from the start). It is a Net::HTTP GET only, and a failure goes into error, not an exception.

Turn receiving on or off

docs.title: FmrbReceiveConf.allow
docs.text:
allow(String | Symbol kind, String node, ?bool all_kinds) -> bool

Let a sender in

kind is "file", "checkpoint" or "app" (a Symbol works; anything else is an ArgumentError; with all_kinds true "rshell" too). node is a node name or pattern (letters, digits and . _ - * only, up to ENTRY_MAX bytes; "*" is everyone on the network, and a pattern like "pc-*" works), else an ArgumentError. One list holds at most 64 entries (more is an ArgumentError). true when it wrote, false when the list by hand already had it.

FmrbReceiveConf.allow("file", "pc-desk")

docs.title: FmrbReceiveConf.deny
docs.text:
deny(String | Symbol kind, String node, ?bool all_kinds) -> bool

Take a sender out

Takes it out of the list by hand and returns true. A node that is not in the list is an ArgumentError; when it is only in the console's list the message says it is changed there (the console's list is not changed here).

FmrbReceiveConf.deny("file", "pc-desk")

docs.title: FmrbReceiveConf.tell_transfer
docs.text:
tell_transfer(FmrbApp app, bool on) -> Symbol

Tell the transfer app the settings changed

app is the calling app (self), on whether receiving, sending or the remote shell is on. When on and the transfer app is not running it is started (:started); when running it is asked to read the settings again (:running, or :stopping when on is false: it ends once what is coming in is in). :none when it is not running and on is false.

FmrbReceiveConf.tell_transfer(self, on)

docs.title: FmrbText
docs.text:
Fit and wrap a text in pixels

How to use it: Drawing.

Mixed into FmrbGfx, so call it on @gfx. Widths are measured with the font and text size selected at the time of the call (the same numbers as text_width). It remembers nothing. Implemented in lib/gems/picoruby-fmrb-app/mrblib/fmrb-text.rb.

s = @gfx.fit_text(name, 80)
@gfx.draw_text(x, y, s, theme_fg)

docs.title: FmrbText#fit_text
docs.text:
fit_text(
  String text,
  Integer width,
  ?String mark,
  ?Integer? mark_w,
  ?Symbol? family
) -> String

Cut a text to fit a width in pixels

A text that fits comes back unchanged. Only when it has to be cut is the third argument appended as a mark ("…", ".."), with room kept for it; without a mark the text is just cut. The fourth argument is the mark's width in pixels (nil measures it), the fifth the font to measure with (nil means the current one).

@gfx.fit_text(title, 100)
@gfx.fit_text(title, 100, "…")
@gfx.fit_text(name, w, "..", nil,
              :default)

wrap_text(String text, Integer width) -> Array[String]

Wrap a text into at most two lines

Answers an array of one or two strings. The break goes at the last space of the first line when the rest then fits on one line; otherwise at the width, and a second line still too long ends in "…". For three lines or more, cut one line at a time with fit_text.

docs.title: FmrbToml
docs.text:
Read TOML; rewrite it by line

load reads a file and parse a string into a Hash. A failure is nil, not an exception; FmrbToml.error says why. The only writer is update, which changes only the lines of the keys you name, so comments, order and keys nobody here knows stay as a person wrote them.

conf = FmrbToml.load("/home/app.toml")
n = conf ? conf["name"] : nil

docs.title: FmrbToml.parse
docs.text:
parse(String text) -> Hash[String, untyped]?

Parse a TOML string into a Hash

A table ([a]) is a Hash, an array an Array, [[name]] an Array of Hash. Strings, integers (0x.. too), floats and true/false come back as themselves. A date and an unquoted word (bg = black) come back as the text that was written.

Text that is not TOML (even one bad line) gives nil; FmrbToml.error says why. No exception.

FmrbToml.parse("a = 1
[s]
b = "x"
")
#=> {"a"=>1, "s"=>{"b"=>"x"}}

docs.title: FmrbToml.load
docs.text:
load(String path) -> Hash[String, untyped]?

Read a TOML file into a Hash

A missing file gives nil with no log line (the ordinary state of a setting nobody has changed). An unreadable file or one that is not TOML gives nil and one log line (toml: path: reason). Either way FmrbToml.error has the reason.

conf = FmrbToml.load("/home/app.toml")

docs.title: FmrbToml.error
docs.text:
error() -> String?

Why the last parse, load or update gave nil

nil after a success.

Log.warn(FmrbToml.error) if conf.nil?

docs.title: FmrbToml.update
docs.text:
update(
  String path,
  Hash[String, untyped] values
) -> Hash[String, untyped]?

Set keys in a file, leaving the other lines alone

values is a Hash of name => value. A name is a top-level key ("rise_mg") or "table.key" ("editor.bg"; the last . splits table from key). A missing key is added (a missing table goes at the end of the file), and a nil value removes the key. A value is a String, a Symbol (written as a string), an Integer, a Float, true/false, an Array, a Hash, or an unquoted word from FmrbToml.raw.

The file is read back afterwards, and the Hash it holds now is returned when it has the values. A file that exists but is not TOML is left untouched and gives nil (it is somebody's text). A failed write or a value that does not read back is nil too. All of them leave the reason in FmrbToml.error. A missing file is created.

FmrbToml.update("/home/app.toml",
                { "editor.bg" => 36 })

docs.title: FmrbToml.raw
docs.text:
raw(String text) -> FmrbToml::Raw

A value written as it is, unquoted

Passed to update, it is written without quotes even though it is text (a colour name, bg = black).

  { "shell.bg" => FmrbToml.raw("black") })

docs.text:
dump_value(untyped value) -> String

The TOML text of one value

A String is quoted and escaped, numbers and true/false as they are, an Array or a Hash in one-line inline form. A Symbol is a string. Anything else is an ArgumentError ("no TOML for ClassName").

FmrbToml.dump_value("a\"b")  #=> "\"a\\\"b\""

dump_key(String key) -> String

Returned as it is when it holds only letters, digits, _ and -; otherwise quoted.

docs.title: FmrbUI
docs.text:
Widget container

How to use it: UI Widgets.

docs.title: FmrbUI.new
docs.text:
new(
  FmrbApp app,
  ?bg: Integer,
  ?text_size: Integer,
  ?bg_painter: untyped
) -> FmrbUI

Create the widget box

Pass the app itself (FmrbApp). The canvas and the user-area origin are read from it.

bg: is the colour a widget paints inside itself - a Label's box, a Stepper's value field, a Scrollbar's track. It defaults to the window background; an app that clears its user area to something darker passes that colour instead. Left out, it becomes the window background of the machine an app is moved to (a colour passed is kept).

bg_painter: is who repaints the ground where a widget used to be. Left out, the hole is filled with bg:, which is right while the ground is one colour. Where it is a picture - wallpaper, a border, a rounded corner - pass an object answering paint_bg_rect(gfx, x, y, w, h), usually self. That method draws the rectangle and nothing else: no present, no allocation, and it puts back any text size or font it changed. The name is fixed.

text_size: is the default scale for the widgets made from here on (1 unless given). A single widget can override it with its own text_size:. The size is fixed when the widget is made and never follows the size the app happens to be in, and flush hands the app's size back afterwards.

docs.title: FmrbUI#label
docs.text:
label(
  Symbol id,
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  String text,
  ?align: Symbol,
  ?text_size: Integer
) -> FmrbUI::Label

Place a text label

align: chooses the alignment (:left / :center / :right, default :left). text_size: enlarges this one widget's text (1-4); useful for a heading.

@ui.label(:l_size, 4, 148, 60, 10,
          "Size")

docs.title: FmrbUI#button
docs.text:
button(
  Symbol id,
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  String text,
  ?text_size: Integer,
  ?accent: Integer
) -> FmrbUI::Button

Place a push button

Inverted while held; handle returns the id when the button is released on top of it. Releasing outside does nothing. text_size: enlarges the label (1-4), as on every widget.

accent: paints the button in that RGB332 colour instead of the theme's. Reserve it for the few controls whose colour carries meaning - a confirm dialog's Yes, a transport's Stop. On a Toggle it is the on colour.

@ui.button(:start, 4, 20, 60, 16,
           "Start")

docs.title: FmrbUI#toggle
docs.text:
toggle(
  Symbol id,
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  String text,
  ?group: Symbol,
  ?on: bool,
  ?on_text: String,
  ?text_size: Integer,
  ?accent: Integer
) -> FmrbUI::Toggle

Place an on/off toggle

Toggles sharing a group: name behave as radio buttons - only one is on. on: true starts it on; on_text: gives it a different label when on.

docs.title: FmrbUI#scrollbar
docs.text:
scrollbar(
  Symbol id,
  Integer x,
  Integer y,
  Integer w,
  Integer h,
  Integer total,
  Integer visible,
  ?Integer scroll
) -> FmrbUI::Scrollbar

Place a vertical scrollbar

x, y, w, h are the bar itself, not the list it scrolls (10 wide is the usual). total (how many there are), visible (how many fit) and scroll (the position; 0 when left out) are all it needs. The app owns the position. Push it in with set_value when keys move it, call set_range when the count changes, and read it back with value after the bar is pressed. The wheel is not answered here (use wheel_rows).

handle returns the id on the press (not the release), once for a held press. One press moves one step, and a press at an end returns nothing. direction says which way a held bar goes; the app does the repeating. While everything fits (total at most visible) it draws nothing and clicks pass through to the list behind. It is meant to be made in on_create (making allocates; an app whose window resizes builds it again in on_resize).

@ui.scrollbar(:sb, w - 10, y, 10, h,
              0, rows, 0)
# ...
@ui.set_range(:sb, @files.size, rows)
@ui.set_value(:sb, @scroll)

docs.title: FmrbUart
docs.text:
The app boundary's UART functions

How to use it: Hardware Control.

The layer under the UART class. Called by unit number; only the app that opened a unit may use it (another app's unit is a RuntimeError). A Ruby app normally uses UART; the other languages (C, Lua, MicroPython, wasm) see this shape as it is. The reading functions never wait. unit_mask tells beforehand which units this machine offers (0 in the browser and the native build).

r = FmrbUart.open(2, 47, 48, 115200,
                  8, 1, 0, 4096)
FmrbUart.write(2, "hi\n") if r == 0

docs.title: FmrbUart.open
docs.text:
open(
  Integer unit,
  Integer txd_pin,
  Integer rxd_pin,
  Integer baudrate,
  Integer data_bits,
  Integer stop_bits,
  Integer parity,
  Integer rx_buffer_size
) -> Integer

Open a UART: 0 when opened, else why not

Every argument is needed (parity 0 none, 1 even, 2 odd; rx_buffer_size a power of two from 16 to 16384); one pin may be -1. The answer (its low 8 bits): 1 no such unit, 2 no such pin, 3 both pins -1, 4 TX and RX on one pin, 5 the rate, 6 the format, 7 the buffer size (so far the caller's mistakes), 8 the system's unit, 9 another app has it, 10 MIDI has it, 11 a system pin, 12 a line a chip drives as TX, 13 a pin in use, 14 it did not open, 15 none in this environment. An answer about a pin has which one in the next byte (1 TX, 2 RX; r >> 8).

r = FmrbUart.open(2, 47, 48, 9600,
                  8, 1, 0, 4096)

docs.text:
finished?() -> bool

Whether it has played to the end

v.rewind if v.finished?

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft
docs.text:
Compute the spectrum of a sound

How to use it: Utilities.

Pass a byte String of 16-bit integers (little-endian) and get a byte String of magnitudes in the same form. The methods (backend:) are :ruby, :c, :dsp, :spinel, :c64, and the integer-only :ruby_q15, :c_q15, :spinel_q15. They all take and give the same thing; they differ in speed and in which builds have them.

fft = Fmrb::Fft.new(size: 512, backend: :c)
mag = fft.forward(pcm)
Fmrb::Fft.bin(mag, 8)

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is BACKENDS Array[Symbol] The names of the backends Q15_BACKENDS Array[Symbol] The fixed-point backends

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.new
docs.text:
new(?size: Integer, ?backend: Symbol) -> Fmrb::Fft

Make a transform

size: (512 when left out) is a power of two from 64 to 1024, backend: (:ruby when left out). An unknown backend or size is an ArgumentError ("unknown FFT backend: x", "FFT size must be a power of two in 64..1024: n"). Check a backend with Fmrb::Fft.available? first: not every build has every one.

:spinel and :spinel_q15 are one instance for the machine, held by the app that opened it first. A second app silently gets :ruby or :ruby_q15 (see backend). A build without it raises RuntimeError. Call close when done.

fft = Fmrb::Fft.new(size: 512, backend: :c)

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.available?
docs.text:
available?(Symbol backend) -> bool

Whether this build has a backend

:ruby, :c, :c64 and their Q15 forms are always true. :dsp only in a real-board build with esp-dsp, the :spinel ones only in a build that has the Spinel FFT. An unknown name is false.

Fmrb::Fft.available?(:dsp)

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.q15?
docs.text:
q15?(Symbol backend) -> bool

Whether a backend is fixed-point

Fmrb::Fft.q15?(:c_q15)   #=> true

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.micros
docs.text:
micros() -> Integer

The clock every backend is timed with (microseconds)

Use differences.

t = Fmrb::Fft.micros

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.spinel_total_us
docs.text:
spinel_total_us() -> Integer

Total cost of the last Spinel call

Microseconds of the last whole :spinel call (passing samples in, results out, and the first table build). Its gap to the transform-only time run returned is the cost of crossing the boundary.

Fmrb::Fft.spinel_total_us

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.sine
docs.text:
sine(?size: Integer, ?cycles: Integer, ?amp: Integer) -> String

Make a test sine wave

size: samples (512 when left out) holding cycles: periods (8 when left out) at amplitude amp: (12000 when left out), as 16-bit integer bytes. Its peak lands on bin cycles.

pcm = Fmrb::Fft.sine(size: 512, cycles: 8)

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.bin
docs.text:
bin(String mag, Integer index) -> Integer

Read one magnitude

The value at index (0..32767). Out of range is 0 (no exception).

h = Fmrb::Fft.bin(mag, 8)

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.peak_bin
docs.text:
peak_bin(String mag) -> Integer

The index of the loudest bin

Bin 0 (the DC part) counts. On a tie the lower index wins.

Fmrb::Fft.peak_bin(mag)   #=> 8

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft.bench
docs.text:
bench(
  ?size: Integer,
  ?iters: Integer,
  ?backend: Symbol,
  ?reps: Integer,
  ?samples: String?
) -> Hash[Symbol, untyped]

Time one backend

Defaults: size: 512, iters: 100, backend: :c, reps: 5, samples: a sine. It runs iters transforms reps times. The result is a Hash: :backend (asked for), :ran_on (ran), :size, :iters, :reps, :us_avg (per transform on average, a Float), :us_min (per transform in the best rep), :mag, :peak_bin. An unusable backend raises as new does.

r = Fmrb::Fft.bench(backend: :c)
r[:us_avg]

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft#size
docs.text:
size() -> Integer

The transform size

fft.size   #=> 512

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft#backend
docs.text:
backend() -> Symbol

The backend actually running

It can differ from the one asked for (when another app holds Spinel).

fft.backend   #=> :c

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft#forward
docs.text:
forward(String samples) -> String

One transform, returning the magnitudes

samples is size little-endian 16-bit integers as bytes (size * 2 bytes). The result is size/2 little-endian 16-bit integers: Hann-windowed, scaled by 2/size and clamped at 32767. Bin 0 is the DC part and tends to be the loudest. Read it with Fmrb::Fft.bin.

The :c family raises ArgumentError when too short ("need 512 int16 samples, got n bytes"). The :ruby family treats the missing part as 0 and goes on silently.

mag = fft.forward(pcm)

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft#run
docs.text:
run(String samples, Integer iters) -> [ Integer, String ]

Transform the same input iters times, timed

Returns [microseconds, magnitude bytes]. The time is the transforms only, measured inside the engine (not the call's cost). iters is 1 or more (the :c family raises ArgumentError below that). This is the form an app uses for each frame.

us, mag = fft.run(pcm, 1)

docs.title: Fmrb::Fft#close
docs.text:
close() -> nil

Be done with it

Gives up the Spinel instance (nothing for the other backends). Returns nil. Call it when the app ends if you used a :spinel backend.

fft.close

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast
docs.text:
Ray casting over a grid map

(Wolfenstein 3D style.) Every value is an integer: one cell is 256 in fixed point, angles are whole degrees, and one cast fires 40 rays across a 60-degree field of view. The result is a distance, a wall value and a face per ray. The backends are :ruby and :spinel (the same calculation as native code).

rc = Fmrb::Raycast.new
rc.set_map(MAP, 12, 12)
rc.cast(px, py, deg)
d = rc.dist(20)

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast.new
docs.text:
new(?backend: Symbol) -> Fmrb::Raycast

Make a caster

backend: (:ruby when left out) is :ruby or :spinel; anything else is an ArgumentError ("unknown raycast backend: x"). A build without :spinel raises RuntimeError, so check Fmrb::Raycast.available?(:spinel) first. :spinel is one per machine and held by the app that opened it first; a second app silently gets :ruby (see backend).

rc = Fmrb::Raycast.new(backend: :ruby)

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast.available?
docs.text:
available?(Symbol backend) -> bool

Whether this build has a backend

:ruby is always true, :spinel only in a build that has it, any other name false.

Fmrb::Raycast.available?(:spinel)

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast.micros
docs.text:
micros() -> Integer

The clock both backends are timed with (microseconds)

Use differences. The same clock as the time cast returns.

t = Fmrb::Raycast.micros

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast.unpack
docs.text:
unpack(String buf) -> Array[Hash[Symbol, Integer]]

Turn a packed result into an Array of Hashes

One { dist:, wall:, side: } per ray. It makes a Hash per ray, so it is heavy and not for each frame's drawing (read dist, wall and side). It takes the 6-bytes-per-ray form.

Fmrb::Raycast.unpack(buf)

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#backend
docs.text:
backend() -> Symbol

The backend actually casting

rc.backend   #=> :ruby

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#set_map
docs.text:
set_map(Array[Integer?] | String cells, Integer w, Integer h) -> nil

Hand over the map

cells is an Array of Integers, one per cell (row by row from the top left, w * h of them), or a String with one byte per cell. A value is 0..255 (cut to 8 bits, nil is 0). 0 is empty; anything else is a wall and its value comes back from wall. Outside the map counts as a wall (value 1). w and h are the width and height in cells. Returns nil. Call it once before cast.

A map :spinel cannot take (a size of 0 or less, a cell count that does not match) raises RuntimeError or ArgumentError ("map dimensions must be positive", "need n map cells, got n bytes").

rc.set_map([1,1,1, 1,0,1, 1,1,1], 3, 3)

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#cast
docs.text:
cast(Integer px, Integer py, Integer pa) -> Integer

Cast one frame of rays

px and py are the position (one cell is 256 in fixed point; cell * 256 + 128 is the middle of a cell), pa the heading (whole degrees; over 360 or negative is fine). Returns the time taken in microseconds. The result is read with dist, wall and side, not from the return value. Before set_map it raises RuntimeError ("set_map has not been called").

us = rc.cast(px, py, deg)

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#rays
docs.text:
rays() -> Integer

How many rays the last cast gave

0 before the first cast. Normally 40.

rc.rays   #=> 40

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#dist
docs.text:
dist(Integer i) -> Integer

Distance to the wall ray i hit

An integer in fixed point (256 = one cell). Already corrected to the distance perpendicular to the view (no fisheye). At least 1, never 0. 0 before cast. i runs from 0 up to under rays (outside it raises NoMethodError).

h = 6000 / rc.dist(i)

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#wall
docs.text:
wall(Integer i) -> Integer

The wall value ray i hit

The map's value. 0 means the ray ran out of its 24 steps without a hit. 0 before cast.

rc.wall(i)

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#side
docs.text:
side(Integer i) -> Integer

Which face ray i hit

0 is a vertical face, 1 a horizontal one. Use it to shade the two apart. 0 before cast.

dark = rc.side(i) == 1

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#fp_sin
docs.text:
fp_sin(Integer deg) -> Integer

Fixed-point sine of whole degrees

The result is -256..256 (256 = 1.0). Negative and over-360 degrees are fine. The same on either backend, so use it for movement and placement.

dy = rc.fp_sin(deg) * 8 / 256

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#fp_cos
docs.text:
fp_cos(Integer deg) -> Integer

Fixed-point cosine of whole degrees

The same form as fp_sin (-256..256).

dx = rc.fp_cos(deg) * 8 / 256

docs.title: Fmrb::Raycast#close
docs.text:
close() -> nil

Be done with it

Gives up the Spinel instance (nothing for :ruby) and drops the map. Returns nil. Call it when the app ends if you used :spinel.

rc.close

Changing a frozen object

Inherits from: RuntimeError

String literals may be frozen. Start from "".dup for a string you will change.

docs.title: GC
docs.text:
Control and statistics of the garbage collector

An ordinary app does not need it; an app that must keep a rhythm (playing, animating) uses it to avoid the pause of a collection. To switch it all at once use FmrbApp#idle_gc= (it sets scheduler_driven, debt_limit, step_limit and malloc_threshold together).

GC.start
n = GC.stat[:live]

docs.title: GC.start
docs.text:
start() -> nil

Run a full collection now

Returns nil. It runs to the end in one go, so the app stops meanwhile (longer with more live objects). Use it to level things before a measurement.

GC.start
before = GC.stat[:live]

docs.title: GC.disable
docs.text:
disable() -> bool

Disable collection

Returns true if it was already disabled, false if it was running. Memory only grows while it is off, so keep the span short and call GC.enable soon. generational_mode= raises RuntimeError while it is off.

was = GC.disable
work
GC.enable unless was

docs.title: GC.enable
docs.text:
enable() -> bool

Enable collection

Returns true if it was disabled, false if it was running (the pair of GC.disable).

GC.enable

docs.title: GC.stat
docs.text:
stat() -> Hash[Symbol, untyped]

Return GC statistics as a hash

The keys are Symbols. Keys in every build: :live (live objects), :debt (objects the collector is behind by), :state (phase: 0 idle, 1 mark, 2 sweep), :generational, :full, :step_limit, :malloc_increase and :malloc_threshold (both in bytes), :symbol_count, :dynamic_symbol_count.

Keys only in a measurement build: :total, :minor, :major (collection counts, MRB_GC_STATS) and the :prof_ pause statistics (a build made with FMRB_GC_PROFILE=1). An ordinary build does not have them, so allow for nil: GC.stat[:total] || 0.

live = GC.stat[:live] || 0

docs.title: GC.reset_stat
docs.text:
reset_stat() -> nil

Zero the pause statistics

Only in a measurement build (FMRB_GC_PROFILE=1). An ordinary build raises NoMethodError, so check GC.respond_to?(:reset_stat) first. Returns nil.

GC.reset_stat if GC.respond_to?(:reset_stat)

docs.title: GC.interval_ratio
docs.text:
interval_ratio() -> Integer

Interval ratio of the collector (percent)

The source comment gives 200 as the initial value.

r = GC.interval_ratio

docs.title: GC.interval_ratio=
docs.text:
interval_ratio=(Integer ratio) -> nil

Set the interval ratio (percent)

Returns nil. At 100 the next collection starts as soon as one ends (source comment).

GC.interval_ratio = 150

docs.title: GC.step_ratio
docs.text:
step_ratio() -> Integer

Step ratio of incremental collection (percent)

The source comment gives 200 as the initial value.

r = GC.step_ratio

docs.title: GC.step_ratio=
docs.text:
step_ratio=(Integer ratio) -> nil

Set the step ratio (percent)

Zero or less raises ArgumentError ("step_ratio must be positive"). Returns nil. A larger value makes one step longer.

GC.step_ratio = 200

docs.title: GC.step_limit
docs.text:
step_limit() -> Integer

Cap on the work of one step

0 means no cap.

n = GC.step_limit

docs.title: GC.step_limit=
docs.text:
step_limit=(Integer limit) -> Integer

Set the cap on the work of one step

0 means no cap. A negative value raises ArgumentError ("step_limit must be non-negative"). It returns the value you passed. It bounds the length of one step, which cannot be interrupted, so an app that keeps a rhythm lowers it (FmrbApp#idle_gc= sets 512).

GC.step_limit = 512

docs.title: GC.malloc_threshold
docs.text:
malloc_threshold() -> Integer

Malloc growth that triggers a collection

0 turns it off.

n = GC.malloc_threshold

docs.title: GC.malloc_threshold=
docs.text:
malloc_threshold=(Integer bytes) -> Integer

Set the malloc growth threshold

Advances a collection once malloc'd bytes have grown this much. It catches large allocations the object count does not show, such as the body of a String or an Array. 0 turns it off. A negative value raises ArgumentError ("malloc_threshold must be non-negative"). It returns the value you passed.

GC.malloc_threshold = 32 * 1024

docs.title: GC.generational_mode
docs.text:
generational_mode() -> bool

Whether generational mode is on

g = GC.generational_mode

docs.title: GC.generational_mode=
docs.text:
generational_mode=(bool enable) -> bool

Switch generational mode

Returns the true / false you passed. It raises RuntimeError while GC.disable is in effect ("generational mode changed when GC disabled"), and when you turn it on while scheduler_driven is true. scheduler_driven = true turns it off, and setting scheduler_driven back to false does not turn it on again.

GC.generational_mode = true

docs.title: GC.scheduler_driven
docs.text:
scheduler_driven() -> bool

Whether the scheduler drives the collector

d = GC.scheduler_driven

docs.title: GC.scheduler_driven=
docs.text:
scheduler_driven=(bool enable) -> bool

Hand collection to the scheduler's idle time

When true, allocation no longer drives collection; it advances in small steps while the app waits (_spin). Generational mode goes off, and it raises RuntimeError while GC.disable is in effect. false puts it back (generational mode does not return). An always-busy app never has idle time, so past debt_limit the allocation path forces a step. Usually use FmrbApp#idle_gc=. Returns the value you passed.

GC.scheduler_driven = true

docs.title: GC.debt_limit
docs.text:
debt_limit() -> Integer

Limit of how far collection may fall behind

0 turns it off. It only works while scheduler_driven is true.

n = GC.debt_limit

docs.title: GC.debt_limit=
docs.text:
debt_limit=(Integer limit) -> Integer

Set the limit of collection debt

While scheduler_driven is true and there is no idle time, once the debt (GC.stat[:debt]) passes this the allocation path forces one step (a pause of one step). It does nothing while scheduler_driven is false. 0 turns it off. A negative value raises ArgumentError. Returns the value you passed.

GC.debt_limit = 4096

docs.title: GC.step
docs.text:
step() -> nil

Run one bounded collection step

Returns nil. While scheduler_driven, a busy app calls it a few times per frame to spread collection into small slices (step_limit sets the length of one).

GC.step

docs.title: GPIO
docs.text:
Use one pin as input or output

How to use it: Hardware Control.

GPIO.new(pin, flags) makes it, then read and write. Join flags with |, as in GPIO::IN | GPIO::PULL_UP. A pin is an integer only. Check with FmrbHw.pin_available? which pins you may use (a system pin or one in use raises IOError).

led = GPIO.new(5, GPIO::OUT)
led.write(1)

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is IN Integer Input OUT Integer Output HIGH_Z Integer High impedance PULL_UP Integer Pull-up PULL_DOWN Integer Pull-down OPEN_DRAIN Integer Open drain (does nothing here) ALT Integer Alternate function (does nothing here)

docs.title: GPIO.new
docs.text:
new(Integer pin, Integer flags, ?Integer alt_function) -> GPIO

Open a pin

Pass in flags one of IN, OUT and HIGH_Z, plus PULL_UP or PULL_DOWN if needed, joined with |. alt_function (0 when left out) is for ALT and has no effect here.

The pin is claimed in the pin table. When it cannot be, IOError is raised and the pin's setup (direction, pull) is left alone: a system pin (one FmrbHw.pin_status gives as PIN_SYSTEM_EXCLUSIVE) is "GPIO n is used by the system", a pin another app (or another use such as I2C) holds is "GPIO n is in use by another app or driver". The board's buttons are not claimed and open with IN (pulls too) only; OUT and the like raise "GPIO n is input only (a system button or a chip's interrupt line)". A claimed pin goes back to the table when the app ends.

A String or Symbol pin is an ArgumentError ("Wrong GPIO pin name"), and so is a negative number; a number this board does not have is an ArgumentError ("GPIO n does not exist on this board"). No direction, or two or more, is an ArgumentError ("You must specify one of IN, OUT, HIGH_Z, and ALT", "IN, OUT and HIGH_Z are exclusive"), and so are both PULL_UP and PULL_DOWN.

sw = GPIO.new(7, GPIO::IN | GPIO::PULL_UP)

docs.title: GPIO.set_dir_at
docs.text:
set_dir_at(Integer pin, Integer dir) -> Integer

Set direction by pin number

Checked against the pin table as GPIO.new is: a free pin becomes this app's, a system pin or one in use raises IOError (nothing is changed). A board button takes IN only. Nothing else is remembered. dir is IN or OUT. Returns 0. Normally use GPIO.new.

GPIO.set_dir_at(5, GPIO::OUT)

docs.title: GPIO.pull_up_at
docs.text:
pull_up_at(Integer pin) -> Integer

Pull a pin up by number

Checked against the pin table like set_dir_at (a board button takes it too). Returns 0.

GPIO.pull_up_at(7)

docs.title: GPIO.pull_down_at
docs.text:
pull_down_at(Integer pin) -> Integer

Pull a pin down by number

Checked against the pin table like set_dir_at (a board button takes it too). Returns 0.

GPIO.pull_down_at(7)

docs.title: GPIO.open_drain_at
docs.text:
open_drain_at(Integer pin) -> Integer

Open drain by number (does nothing)

This machine's link does nothing. Returns 0. Checked against the pin table as an output (IOError when refused).

GPIO.open_drain_at(7)

docs.title: GPIO.set_function_at
docs.text:
set_function_at(Integer pin, Integer function) -> Integer

Alternate function by number (does nothing)

This machine's link does nothing. Returns 0. Checked against the pin table as an output (IOError when refused).

GPIO.set_function_at(7, 1)

docs.title: GPIO.read_at
docs.text:
read_at(Integer pin) -> Integer

Read by pin number

0 or 1. Reading changes nothing, so any pin can be read, a system pin or one in use too (it is not claimed). IOError when it cannot be read. A String, a Symbol, a negative number or a number this board does not have is an ArgumentError.

GPIO.read_at(7)

docs.title: GPIO.write_at
docs.text:
write_at(Integer pin, Integer value) -> Integer

Write by pin number

Same as GPIO#write (0 or 1 only; returns 0). Checked against the pin table like set_dir_at: a free pin becomes this app's; a system pin (a button too) or one in use raises IOError.

GPIO.write_at(5, 1)

docs.title: GPIO.high_at?
docs.text:
high_at?(Integer pin) -> bool

Whether a pin is high, by number

True when the value read is not 0. Any pin can be read, as with read_at; IOError when it cannot be.

GPIO.high_at?(7)

docs.title: GPIO.low_at?
docs.text:
low_at?(Integer pin) -> bool

Whether a pin is low, by number

True when the value read is 0. Any pin can be read, as with read_at; IOError when it cannot be.

GPIO.low_at?(7)

docs.title: GPIO#pin
docs.text:
pin() -> Integer

The pin number

led.pin   #=> 5

docs.title: GPIO#setmode
docs.text:
setmode(Integer flags, ?Integer alt_function) -> Integer

Set direction and pull again

Takes the same combinations as new. Without a direction flag the direction stays as it is, and so does the pull. Returns 0. Making a board button an output raises IOError.

sw.setmode(GPIO::IN | GPIO::PULL_DOWN)

docs.title: GPIO#read
docs.text:
read() -> Integer

Read the level (0 or 1)

IOError ("GPIO n could not be read") when the level cannot be read.

sw.read   #=> 0 or 1

docs.title: GPIO#write
docs.text:
write(Integer value) -> Integer

Write the level (0 or 1)

Anything but 0 and 1 is an ArgumentError ("Wrong value. 0 and 1 are only valid"). Returns 0. Use it on a pin set as an output. On a board button it raises IOError ("... input only").

led.write(1)

docs.title: GPIO#high?
docs.text:
high?() -> bool

Whether the level is high

true when the value read is not 0. IOError when the level cannot be read.

pressed = !sw.high?

docs.title: GPIO#low?
docs.text:
low?() -> bool

Whether the level is low

true when the value read is 0. IOError when the level cannot be read.

pressed = sw.low?

docs.title: GPIO::Error
docs.text:
Peripheral error codes and their exceptions

How to use it: Hardware Control.

The constants GPIO_ERROR_NONE (0), TIMEOUT (-1), GENERIC (-2), NO_DATA (-3), NOT_PERMITTED (-4), INVALID_ARG (-5) and IO (-6) are the codes.

GPIO::Error.peripheral_error(0)   #=> 0

docs.title: GPIO::Error.peripheral_error
docs.text:
peripheral_error(Integer code, ?String name) -> Integer

Turn a code into an exception

0 (GPIO_ERROR_NONE) returns 0. Any other code raises IOError (the message looks like "Timeout error in name"; an unknown code is "Unknown error in name. code: n"). name is "unknown peripheral" when left out. No bundled app calls it.

GPIO::Error.peripheral_error(-1, "uart")

docs.title: GfxBlock
docs.text:
A draft for drawing the same shape over and over

How to use it: Sprites.

Swap only the numbers and draw it as many times as you like.

docs.title: GfxBlock.new
docs.text:
new(FmrbGfx gfx) -> GfxBlock

Make a drawing to replay (the block says how)

Builds a drawing once and replays it with different numbers, which beats sending the commands from Ruby each time.

The block cannot capture an outer local (Spinel). Pass what it needs as an argument to draw.

@blk = GfxBlock.new(gfx) do |g, w, h|
  g.draw_rect(0, 0, w, h,
              FmrbGfx::WHITE)
end

docs.title: GfxBlock#draw
docs.text:
draw() -> void

Replay it with different numbers

@blk.draw(w: 100, h: 40)

docs.title: GfxBlock#destroy
docs.text:
destroy() -> void

Let go of the drawing

@blk.destroy

docs.title: GfxBlock#destroyed?

destroyed?() -> bool

Whether it has been let go of

return if @blk.destroyed?
