docs.title: Hash
docs.text:
A table that maps keys to values

Includes Enumerable. A missing key gives nil, not an exception, and a default value cannot be given. A String key and a Symbol key are different. each_key needs a block (this build has no Enumerator).

docs.title: Hash.new
docs.text:
new() -> Hash

Make an empty hash

No default can be given; a missing key is always nil.

h = Hash.new
h = {}

docs.title: Hash#==
docs.text:
==(untyped other) -> bool

Perform equality comparison

if h == other

docs.title: Hash#[]
docs.text:
[](untyped key) -> untyped

Get value for specified key

A missing key gives nil; it does not raise.

h[:name]
h["name"]

docs.title: Hash#[]=
docs.text:
[]=(untyped key, untyped value) -> self

Set value for specified key

A String key and a Symbol key are different. Mixing them loses the value.

h[:name] = "a"

docs.title: Hash#clear
docs.text:
clear() -> Hash

Remove all elements from hash

h.clear

docs.title: Hash#delete
docs.text:
delete(untyped key) -> (untyped | nil)

Delete specified key

Returns what was there, or nil.

v = h.delete(:name)

docs.title: Hash#each
docs.text:
each() { (untyped key, untyped value) -> untyped } -> self

Execute block for each key and value

The block takes two, the key and the value.

h.each do |k, v|

end

docs.title: I2C
docs.text:
Talk to I2C devices

How to use it: Hardware Control.

I2C.new opens the bus, and write and read send and receive bytes with a 7-bit address. The only units are :ESP32_I2C0 and :ESP32_I2C1. Use FmrbHw::PIN_I2C1_SDA and PIN_I2C1_SCL for the pins. Every failure is an IOError.

i2c = I2C.new(unit: :ESP32_I2C1,
  sda_pin: FmrbHw::PIN_I2C1_SDA,
  scl_pin: FmrbHw::PIN_I2C1_SCL)

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is DEFAULT_FREQUENCY Integer Default frequency (Hz) DEFAULT_TIMEOUT Integer Default timeout (ms)

docs.title: I2C.new
docs.text:
new(
  unit: Symbol | String,
  ?frequency: Integer,
  ?sda_pin: Integer,
  ?scl_pin: Integer,
  ?timeout: Integer
) -> I2C

Open an I2C bus

unit: is required (:ESP32_I2C0 or :ESP32_I2C1; a string also works). frequency: (100000 Hz when left out), sda_pin: and scl_pin: (-1 when left out), timeout: (500 when left out; the default wait of later read and write, in ms).

A bus that cannot be opened raises IOError, with a message for each cause (the unit is the name you passed): an unknown unit is "Invalid I2C unit: name", a bus another app already holds is "I2C unit name is in use by another app", a different pin for I2C1 on a board with a screen is "I2C unit name is fixed to other pins on this board (not SDA n / SCL n)", a screen not ready yet is "I2C unit name is not ready yet", and a bus that would not start on those pins is "I2C unit name did not start on SDA n / SCL n". On the boards with a screen (Tab5, NARYA v4, AtomS3R) I2C1 is fixed to the board's wiring, and anything but FmrbHw::PIN_I2C1_SDA and PIN_I2C1_SCL is refused. frequency: is not checked when opening, and neither is the pin table (FmrbHw.pin_status).

i2c = I2C.new(unit: :ESP32_I2C1,
  sda_pin: FmrbHw::PIN_I2C1_SDA,
  scl_pin: FmrbHw::PIN_I2C1_SCL)

docs.title: I2C#write
docs.text:
write(
  Integer addr,
  *Integer | Array[Integer] | String data,
  ?timeout: Integer
) -> Integer

Write to a device

addr is the 7-bit address. Pass any number of data arguments: an Integer (one byte), an Array of Integers, a String (bytes), mixed freely. All of it goes out in one transaction. A byte is cut to its low 8 bits. timeout: is in ms (the timeout: of new when left out). Returns the number of bytes sent.

A failure is IOError ("I2C write failed"). A wrong type is a TypeError ("argument must be Integer, Array or String", also for a non-Integer inside an Array).

i2c.write(0x41, 0x20, [1, 2])

docs.title: I2C#read
docs.text:
read(
  Integer addr,
  Integer len,
  *Integer | Array[Integer] | String write_data,
  ?timeout: Integer
) -> String

Read from a device

Reads len bytes from addr and returns them as a String of bytes. Data after len (a register number, say) is sent first, and the read follows without a STOP (passed as in write). timeout: is in ms (the timeout: of new when left out).

A failure is IOError ("I2C read failed"; a failed send before the read is "I2C write (for read) failed"). A len of 0 also raises "I2C read failed". One wait is rounded up to at least 10 ms.

v = i2c.read(0x41, 1, 0xFE)
v.getbyte(0)

docs.title: I2C#scan
docs.text:
scan(?timeout: Integer) -> nil

Probe the 7-bit addresses for devices

Reads and writes each address from 0x08 to 0x77 and prints the ones that answer with puts ("I2C device found at 7-bit address 0x41 ..."). It returns nil, not the list. It is for the shell and for development. timeout: is the value of new when left out.

i2c.scan

docs.title: I2C#close
docs.text:
close() -> nil

Release the bus

Gives up the ownership of the unit and its pins (the bus itself stays, so the same app or another one can open it again with I2C.new). Returns nil and raises nothing on failure.

i2c.close

docs.title: IO
docs.text:
An input/output stream

How to use it: Files & I/O.

The parent of File. $stdout and a file are the same kind of IO. read and write on a closed stream raise RuntimeError ("closed stream"), not IOError. Going the other way to how it was opened (read on a write-only "w" or "a", write, puts or print on a read-only "r") raises IOError. Every other failure is a RuntimeError; the reason (errno) is not told apart.

$stdout.puts "hello"

docs.title: IO#read
docs.text:
read(?Integer length) -> String

Read bytes (File overrides it as File#read)

Reads up to length bytes and returns them. length defaults to 1024 (for streams such as stdin; a file goes through File#read, which reads everything when it is left out). length of 0 or less returns "". A stream opened for writing only ("w", "a", stdout) raises IOError ("not opened for reading"). RuntimeError when the read fails ("failed to read from stream") or the stream is closed ("closed stream").

s = $stdin.read(16)

docs.title: IO#write
docs.text:
write(String str) -> Integer

Write a string

Writes str and returns the number of bytes written. Only a String is accepted (a number raises TypeError; puts and print call to_s first). A stream opened for reading only ("r", stdin) raises IOError ("not opened for writing"), through puts and print too. RuntimeError when the write fails ("write failed") or the stream is closed ("closed stream").

n = f.write("hello\n")   #=> 6

docs.title: IO#puts
docs.text:
puts(*untyped objects) -> nil

Write with a newline

Writes each argument after to_s and adds "\n" unless it already ends with one; with no arguments it writes just "\n". An Array is one line per element, nested ones too (puts [1, [2]] writes "1" and "2"; an empty Array is an empty line). An Array nested deeper than 16 (one that contains itself) prints "[...]" there. nil is an empty line. Always returns nil. As in mruby.

f.puts "line"
f.puts ["a", "b"]   # two lines

docs.title: IO#print
docs.text:
print(*untyped objects) -> nil

Write without a newline

Calls to_s on each argument and writes it. Always returns nil.

f.print "a", 1

docs.title: IO#flush
docs.text:
flush() -> self

Flush what was written to storage

Pushes a file's writes out to storage and returns self. Does nothing for stdout, stderr and a closed stream. RuntimeError when it cannot flush ("flush failed").

f.flush

docs.title: IO#close
docs.text:
close() -> nil

Close the stream

Calling it again is not an error (nothing happens once it is closed). Returns nil. Nothing happens for the standard streams. A file left open is not closed by the garbage collector; it is closed when the app ends. The number that can stay open is limited (10 for all apps together on an ESP32; see File.new).

f.close

docs.title: IO#closed?
docs.text:
closed?() -> bool

Whether it is closed

f.closed?

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
Reading and writing JSON

How to use it: Utilities.

JSON.parse reads, JSON.generate writes; to take a part out of a big JSON use JSON::Digger. All of it is a small implementation in Ruby, built for size rather than speed.

h = JSON.parse('{"a": [1, 2]}')
s = JSON.generate(h)   #=> "{\"a\":[1,2]}"

docs.title: JSON.parse
docs.text:
parse(String json) -> untyped

Parse a JSON string into Ruby values

{} becomes a Hash (keys are always Strings), [] an Array, numbers Integer or Float, and true, false, null as themselves (null is nil).

Failure raises. A text that does not start with a value, an empty string and an unclosed string raise JSON::ParserError; a broken structure (a missing : or ,) raises JSON::JSONError (the parent). Trailing junk after the JSON is dropped silently ("[1,2] xyz" is [1, 2]).

\uXXXX becomes the UTF-8 character (Japanese too, and a pair such as \ud83d\ude00). Floats are built by hand, so the last digits can differ from CRuby. It is all Ruby, so reading a big JSON whole is heavy.

h = JSON.parse('{"temp": 21.5}')
h["temp"]   #=> 21.5

docs.title: JSON.generate
docs.text:
generate(untyped obj) -> String

Turn a Ruby value into a JSON string

Writes Hash, Array, String, Integer, Float, true, false and nil. A Symbol becomes a string, and a Hash key is written as its to_s. Any other object is written as its to_s (no error).

The result is one line with no spaces. Japanese is left as it is (not escaped). A Float NaN or infinity has no JSON form and raises JSON::GeneratorError (nested ones too).

JSON.generate({ "a" => [1, nil] })
#=> "{\"a\":[1,null]}"

Generated from the API signatures (sig/) of fmruby-core main@579eba38.

docs.title: JSON::Digger
docs.text:
Take a part out of a big JSON

How to use it: Utilities.

Scans the string without reading the whole JSON and cuts out the part dig points at. It is for small memory: parse turns the cut part into a Ruby value.

j = '[{"d": {"name": "Remo"}}]'
JSON::Digger.new(j).dig(0, "d", "name").parse
#=> "Remo"

docs.title: JSON::Digger.new
docs.text:
new(String json) -> JSON::Digger

Make one on a JSON string

d = JSON::Digger.new(text)

docs.title: JSON::Digger#dig
docs.text:
dig(*String | Integer keys) -> JSON::Digger

Follow keys and positions to a part

A String is a Hash key, an Integer an Array position (from 0; a negative number is an ArgumentError). It returns itself, so dig and parse can follow. After digging, this Digger holds only the cut part. There is no way back: the next dig goes inside it. To take another place from the same source, make a new Digger.

A missing key raises JSON::DiggerError ("Key not found: name"). A shape that does not fit (a position on a Hash, a key on an Array) raises JSON::JSONError. Anything but a String or an Integer is an ArgumentError. An Array position past the end (an empty Array included) raises JSON::DiggerError ("Array index out of range").

d = JSON::Digger.new('{"a": [10, 20]}')
d.dig("a", 1).parse   #=> 20

docs.title: JSON::Digger#parse
docs.text:
parse() -> untyped

Turn the part it points at into a Ruby value

JSON::Digger.new('[1, 2]').dig(1).parse
#=> 2

docs.title: Kernel
docs.text:
Output, random numbers, Proc helpers

The line puts writes goes to the log, not the screen. print adds no newline. rand with max left out or 0 returns an integer from 0 to 4294967295 (not a Float as in CRuby). proc, lambda and -> turn a block into a Proc.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is MSG_TASK_KERNEL Integer The kernel's task id (0) MSG_TASK_HOST Integer The host task's id (1) MSG_TASK_SYSTEM Integer The system app's task id (2)

docs.title: Kernel.send_message
docs.text:
send_message(
  Integer task_id,
  Integer msg_type,
  String data,
  ?Integer timeout_ms
) -> bool

Put a raw string on a task's queue

task_id is from 0 to below the limit (9 on the devices) (outside it raises ArgumentError). data is at most 64 bytes (more raises ArgumentError). timeout_ms (100 when left out) is how long to wait while the queue is full.

It returns true when sent. It returns false when the task has no queue or the queue stays full for timeout_ms; no exception is raised.

Kernel.send_message(0, 1, "key_down:13")

docs.title: Kernel.receive_message
docs.text:
receive_message(Integer task_id, ?Integer timeout_ms) -> Array[untyped]?

Take one message off a task's queue

Returns a [type, string] array, or nil when nothing came within timeout_ms (1000 when left out). task_id outside 0 to below the limit (9 on the devices) raises ArgumentError, and a task with no queue raises RuntimeError, not nil. Passing the app's own number reads the very queue _spin reads.

msg = Kernel.receive_message(2, 5000)
type, data = msg if msg

docs.title: Kernel.broadcast_message
docs.text:
broadcast_message(
  Integer msg_type,
  String data,
  ?Integer timeout_ms
) -> Integer

Put a raw string on every queue

Puts the same message on every registered queue and returns how many took it. A full queue is waited for up to timeout_ms (10 when left out) each. data is at most 64 bytes (more raises ArgumentError).

n = Kernel.broadcast_message(99, "bye")

docs.text:
message_queue_exists?(Integer task_id) -> bool

Whether a task has a queue

task_id outside 0 to below the limit (9 on the devices) raises ArgumentError.

With max left out or 0 it returns an integer from 0 to 4294967295 (not a Float in 0...1 as in CRuby). With max it returns an integer from 0 up to, but not including, max (RNG.random_int % max). Integers only (no Range or Float). There is no way to seed it (no srand).

docs.title: Log
docs.text:
The log (goes to the serial port and the sim's terminal)

How to use it: Logging.

Log as a whole class is on the boundary to the system (%a{fmrb.boundary}, doc/app_boundary). info and the like are wrappers, each with a _raw form next to it that leaves nothing out (the mruby wrapper is in C and also reads the older form that takes the tag first, Log.info("TAG", msg)).

docs.title: MIDI::Device
docs.text:
A sender for sound; send notes and tones to it

How to use it: MIDI.

docs.title: MIDI::Device.new
docs.text:
new(untyped transport) -> MIDI::Device

Make a device on a transport

transport is whatever receives the MIDI. It needs send_packet(cable, cin, b1, b2, b3), read_available, bytes_available and connected? (device_info for info, transport_id for trigger). The built-in and outside devices are made by FmrbMidi.device and FmrbMidi.sam2695_device. To use trigger on a transport of your own, FmrbMidi.register it, give it @pending = [], note_on(channel, note, velocity) and note_off(channel, note), and include FmrbMidi::NoteScheduler.

dev = MIDI::Device.new(MyTransport.new)

docs.title: MIDI::Device#transport
docs.text:
transport() -> untyped

The transport behind the device

For the built-in sound it is a FmrbMidi::ApuTransport; call all_off, auto_map and map_channel on it.

@device.transport.all_off

docs.text:

docs.title: MIDI::Device#trigger
docs.text:
trigger(
  Integer note,
  ?Integer velocity,
  ?duration: Integer,
  ?channel: Integer
) -> void

Sound a note for a set length

Give it a length and a note-off is booked. It returns at once, so several notes can start together -- note_on plus a wait cannot. duration: is in ms (100 when left out). FmrbMidi.tick is what sends the stop, so keep calling it from on_update (without it the note rings until the next MIDI message).

Starts a chord within microseconds. Only :note_on entries are used, and duration_ms ends them.

  {type: :note_on, channel: 0,
   note: 60, velocity: 100,
   duration_ms: 200}])

docs.title: Machine
docs.text:
Time, waiting, and telling platforms apart

How to use it: Tasks & Timing.

Time is board_millis (ms) and uptime_us (microseconds), waiting is delay_ms and busy_wait_ms, and posix? tells the platform. Some methods behave differently on an ESP32 board and on Linux or the browser build (noted per method).

t0 = Machine.board_millis

docs.title: Machine.board_millis
docs.text:
board_millis() -> Integer

Milliseconds since boot

Use it to measure elapsed time: take the difference of two readings.

The unit is milliseconds. Integers are 64-bit in every build (MRB_INT64), so there is no wrap to worry about. Where it starts counting differs: an ESP32 counts from the board's boot, Linux and the native build from the host's boot (not the app's or the simulator's), the browser build from the start of the program. Do not give the value itself a meaning; use differences.

An app carried from another VM (checkpoint) goes on from the value it saw there (an offset between that VM and this one is added). uptime_us does not get the offset.

t0 = Machine.board_millis
elapsed = Machine.board_millis - t0

docs.title: Machine.uptime_us
docs.text:
uptime_us() -> Integer

Microseconds since boot

For finer measurements than board_millis. It starts counting where board_millis does (the board's boot on an ESP32, the host's boot on Linux and the native build, the start of the program in the browser). The offset of an app carried by checkpoint is not added. Integers are 64-bit.

t = Machine.uptime_us
work
dt = Machine.uptime_us - t

docs.title: Machine.uptime_formatted
docs.text:
uptime_formatted() -> String

Uptime as a string

Machine.uptime_formatted  #=> "0d 00:12:34.56"

docs.title: Machine.delay_ms
docs.text:
delay_ms(Integer ms) -> Integer

Block this app for ms milliseconds

Blocks the whole app task for ms milliseconds. While it waits, on_update and events are not handled and no other Task in the same VM runs. Unlike sleep_ms (which switches Tasks), it also stops outside _spin (startup, for instance).

A negative ms raises ArgumentError. It returns the ms you passed.

The resolution differs by platform. ESP32 waits in 1 ms steps (the FreeRTOS tick). Linux and the native build watch the real clock in 10 ms steps, so they wait up to about 10 ms longer. (ESP32 firmware from before 2026-11-25 waited only about a tenth of what was asked.)

Machine.delay_ms(100)

docs.title: Machine.busy_wait_ms
docs.text:
busy_wait_ms(Integer ms) -> Integer

Busy-wait for ms milliseconds

A negative ms raises ArgumentError. It returns the ms you passed.

On an ESP32 it spins the CPU and nothing else runs (ets_delay_us(1000 * ms)). Use delay_ms or sleep_ms for long waits. Linux and the native build call nanosleep once; they do not spin, and a signal can cut the wait short.

Machine.busy_wait_ms(2)

docs.title: Machine.sleep
docs.text:
sleep(Integer sec) -> Integer

Light-sleep for whole seconds

sec is in seconds, 2 to 86399. A negative value or 86400 or more raises ArgumentError. Under 2 it does not sleep: it prints a warning ("Cannot sleep less than 2 sec") and returns. It also warns before sleeping. It returns the sec you passed.

An ESP32 enters light sleep for the whole chip (esp_light_sleep_start). Linux and the native build do nothing and return at once. Do not use it to wait in an app; use delay_ms or sleep_ms.

Machine.sleep(5)

docs.title: Machine.deep_sleep
docs.text:
deep_sleep(Integer gpio_pin, bool edge, bool high) -> bot

Deep sleep (not implemented)

Always raises NotImplementedError in this build (it does not look at the arguments).

begin
  Machine.deep_sleep(5, true, false)
rescue NotImplementedError
end

docs.title: Machine.unique_id
docs.text:
unique_id() -> (String | nil)

Return the machine's unique ID

An ESP32 returns its MAC address as 12 hex digits (upper case). Linux and the native build return the 32 digits in /etc/machine-id (the host's ID). It is nil when it cannot be read (the browser build has no such file).

id = Machine.unique_id

docs.title: Machine.read_memory
docs.text:
read_memory(Integer address, Integer size) -> String

Read raw bytes from an address

Returns size bytes from address as a new binary string. The address is not checked: an unreadable one crashes the whole firmware. For debugging.

s = Machine.read_memory(addr, 16)

docs.title: Machine.stack_usage
docs.text:
stack_usage() -> (Integer | nil)

Stack usage (not supported)

Always nil in this build (both the ESP32 and the Linux code return 0, and 0 becomes nil).

Machine.stack_usage  #=> nil

docs.title: Machine.set_hwclock
docs.text:
set_hwclock(Integer tv_sec) -> true

Set the system clock

tv_sec is UNIX time (seconds since 1970, UTC). ESP32 only. It returns true. Linux, the native build and the browser build raise NotImplementedError (a ScriptError, not a StandardError, so rescue => e does not catch it; check Machine.posix? first). It does not write the RTC chip.

Machine.set_hwclock(epoch) unless Machine.posix?

docs.title: Machine.get_hwclock
docs.text:
get_hwclock() -> Array[Integer]

Read the system clock

An array of [seconds, nanoseconds] (UNIX time, UTC). ESP32 only. Linux, the native build and the browser build raise NotImplementedError (not caught by rescue => e).

sec, nsec = Machine.get_hwclock

docs.title: Machine.exit
docs.text:
exit(?Integer status) -> nil

Exit the program

Does nothing on an ESP32 (returns nil). On Linux and the native build the whole firmware process exits, so do not call it from an app. Close an app with FmrbApp#stop.

Machine.exit(0)
# on Linux the firmware ends

docs.title: Machine.reboot
docs.text:
reboot(?Integer wait_ms) -> nil

Reboot (not usable in this build)

Tries to reboot after wait_ms (0 when left out). It raises NotImplementedError on an ESP32 (the watchdog gem is not in the build). Linux and the native build end the process with exit code 120. To restart the machine use FmrbSystem.reboot.

Machine.reboot(1000)
# on Linux: exit code 120

docs.title: Machine.posix?
docs.text:
posix?() -> bool

Whether this is a POSIX build

True on Linux, the native build and the browser build; false on an ESP32 board (true unless RUBY_PLATFORM is "ESP32"). Use it to separate calls that only a board has (set_hwclock and so on).

if Machine.posix?
  # simulator
end

docs.text:
wifi_available?() -> bool

Whether Wi-Fi is available

True when Network::WiFi is defined. Family mruby has no such definition, so it is always false (ask FmrbApp and FmrbNet about Wi-Fi instead).

Machine.wifi_available?  #=> false

docs.title: Machine.check_signal
docs.text:
check_signal() -> nil

Raise a pending Ctrl-C as an exception

Raises Interrupt ("SIGINT") when Ctrl-C was received, SignalException ("SIGTSTP") for Ctrl-Z, and returns nil when nothing is pending. Only the standard input of Linux and the native build receives them (nothing sets it on an ESP32, so it is always nil there).

begin
  Machine.check_signal
rescue Interrupt
end

docs.title: Machine.poll_signal
docs.text:
poll_signal() -> (Symbol | nil)

Return a pending Ctrl-C as a Symbol

check_signal without the exception: :INT for Ctrl-C, :TSTP for Ctrl-Z, nil when nothing is pending.

case Machine.poll_signal
when :INT then stop
end

docs.title: Machine.signal_self_manage

Only raises a flag, which pop_signal_self_manage reads and clears.

docs.title: Machine.pop_signal_self_manage
docs.text:

Returns true when signal_self_manage raised the flag, and clears it.

docs.title: MessagePack
docs.text:
Turn values into bytes with MessagePack, and back

How to use it: Utilities.

pack makes a String of bytes from a Ruby value, unpack returns the value. dump and load are aliases.

bin = MessagePack.pack({ "a" => [1, 2] })
MessagePack.unpack(bin)   #=> {"a"=>[1, 2]}

docs.title: MessagePack.pack
docs.text:
pack(untyped obj) -> String

Pack a value into bytes

Writes nil, true, false, Integer (up to 64 bits), Float (always double), String, Symbol, Array and Hash. A Symbol is written as a string, so it comes back as a String (Hash keys too). A String with the binary flag (String#b and the like) is written as bin, a plain String as str.

A type that cannot be written (a Range, your own class) raises RuntimeError ("Failed to pack object to msgpack").

bin = MessagePack.pack({ cmd: "go" })

docs.title: MessagePack.unpack
docs.text:
unpack(String binary) -> untyped

Unpack bytes into a value

The String must hold exactly one value. Extra bytes, a cut-off value, an empty string, an ext type or an integer of 2^63 and over raise RuntimeError ("Failed to unpack msgpack data"). A bin value comes back as a String with the binary flag.

v = MessagePack.unpack(bin)

docs.text:
dump(untyped obj) -> String

docs.title: Module
docs.text:
Operations on classes and modules

Operations on classes and modules (Module), with a class as the receiver, as in Object.const_defined?(:X). Implemented in mruby's own src/class.c (const_defined?) and mruby-metaprog (remove_method).

docs.title: Module#const_defined?
docs.text:
const_defined?(Symbol | String name, ?bool inherit) -> bool

Whether a constant is defined

true when name is a constant. It returns false, not an exception, when the constant is not there (use it to see whether a gem is built in). NameError when name is not shaped like a constant name (it starts with a lowercase letter, ...).

inherit (true when left out): true also counts the constants of the parent classes and of Object; false counts only the ones the receiver holds itself.

if Object.const_defined?(:Digest)
  # Digest is there
end

docs.title: Module#remove_method
docs.text:
remove_method(*Symbol | String names) -> self

Remove methods defined in this class

Removes only methods defined directly in this receiver. One inherited from the parent cannot be removed: NameError ("method 'x' not defined in ..."). Once it is removed, a method of the same name in the parent is called instead.

Names are Symbols or Strings (anything else is a TypeError); several can be given at once. Returns the receiver (self). FrozenError on a frozen class.

self.class.remove_method(:draw_title)

docs.title: P5
docs.text:
Draw in the style of p5.js

How to use it: Processing-style Drawing.

Make it with @p5 = P5.new(@gfx). It only wraps an FmrbGfx, so you can draw on the same canvas with both. Pick colours with fill and stroke, draw shapes with rect, circle, line, text and so on, then show them with present. background fills the canvas; no_fill leaves outlines only.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is BLACK Integer black (RGB332) WHITE Integer white (RGB332) RED Integer red (RGB332) GREEN Integer green (RGB332) BLUE Integer blue (RGB332) YELLOW Integer yellow (RGB332) CYAN Integer cyan (RGB332) MAGENTA Integer magenta (RGB332) GRAY Integer gray (RGB332) REPLACE Integer plain overwrite (0) ADD Integer brighten where shapes overlap (1) XOR Integer invert where shapes overlap (2)

docs.title: P5.new
docs.text:
new(FmrbGfx gfx) -> P5

It only wraps an FmrbGfx, so you can draw on the same canvas with both.

docs.title: RNG
docs.text:
The source of random numbers

An ESP32 uses esp_random() (the hardware RNG); Linux and the native build read /dev/urandom (opening the file once per byte, so producing many numbers is slow).

r = RNG.random_int % 10

docs.title: RNG.random_int
docs.text:
random_int() -> Integer

A random 32-bit integer

An integer from 0 to 4294967295 (never negative). Narrow it with % n to get 0 to n-1 (what Kernel#rand(n) does). There is no way to seed it.

RNG.random_int % 10   #=> 0..9

A binary string of length bytes (bytes, not characters; count it with bytesize).

docs.text:
uuid() -> String

A version 4 UUID string

36 characters: lower-case hex in groups of 8-4-4-4-12 joined by -. It draws 32 random numbers, so it is not cheap.

How to use it: Sprites.

What is drawn here is put on the screen with a SpriteInstance.

docs.text:
new(FmrbGfx gfx) -> SpriteImage

Make an image (the size is in pixels)

Takes keyword arguments; the signature is positional because the type engine has none.

img = SpriteImage.new(gfx,
      width: 16, height: 16,
      transparent_color: 0x00,
      use_transparent: true)

docs.title: SpriteImage#id
docs.text:

What you hand to FmrbGfx directly.

w = img.width

h = img.height

docs.text:
set_target() -> void

Draw into this image from now on

Remember to send it back. draw does both ends for you.

docs.text:

docs.title: SpriteImage#draw
docs.text:
draw() -> void

Draw into this image (inside the block)

img.draw do |g|
  g.fill_rect(0, 0, 16, 16,
              FmrbGfx::RED)
end

docs.title: SpriteImage#load_bmp
docs.text:
load_bmp(String path) -> void

Read a PNG or BMP into this image

A PNG (its colours become RGB332 by their top 3/3/2 bits; a transparent pixel -- alpha below 128, tRNS -- becomes the transparent colour 0x01, so an image made with transparent_color: 0x01 leaves it out) or an 8-bit BMP whose pixel values are RGB332, told apart by the first bytes. The name is from when it read BMP only. It is decoded on the graphics side. A whole picture goes through FmrbGfx#create_image.

img.load_bmp(
  "/usr/share/sprites/flappy/bird_up.png")

docs.title: SpriteImage#write_pixels
docs.text:
write_pixels(String pixels) -> void

Write RGB332 pixels into this image

pixels is width x height bytes, top row first. x:, y:, width:, height: write a part only (the whole image by default). A picture made without a file.

img = SpriteImage.new(@gfx,
  width: 2, height: 2)
img.write_pixels("\xE0\x1C\x03\xFF")

Place an image on the screen

Give images one SpriteImage, or an array of them like the frames of a flip book. With several, frame= says which one is shown.

img = SpriteImage.new(gfx, width: 16, height: 16)
img.load_bmp("/app/img/player.png")
sp = SpriteInstance.new(gfx, img, x: 40, y: 80)
sp.move(48, 80)

docs.title: String#byteslice
docs.text:
byteslice(Integer start, ?Integer length) -> (String | nil)
byteslice(Range range) -> (String | nil)

Cut out a part by byte offset and byte length

Returns length bytes from byte start as a new string. Both count bytes. A Japanese character is 3 bytes (UTF-8), so a position from [], slice, length or index (which count characters) lands in the wrong place once the string holds Japanese. Pair it with bytesize and getbyte, which count bytes.

A negative start counts from the end; a length past the end stops at the end. A start right at the end (bytesize) gives ""; a start past it, or a negative length, gives nil (no exception), so put .to_s before another string method. Cutting inside a character does not stop it: you get the broken bytes.

Without length you get that one byte (nil from the end on). A range of bytes (2..4) works too.

s = "あいう"
s.byteslice(3, 3)   #=> "い"
s[1]                #=> "い"
s.byteslice(9, 1)   #=> ""
s.byteslice(10, 1)  #=> nil
rest = s.byteslice(3,
  s.bytesize - 3).to_s

docs.title: UART
docs.text:
Talk to a device over a serial line (UART)

How to use it: Hardware Control.

Written the way upstream PicoRuby's class is. Open with UART.new, send with puts and write, receive with gets and read. Reading never waits: it gives nil until something has arrived, so call it in every on_update. Only write waits until the bytes are on their way.

The units (unit:) and the pins depend on the board (a unit is the number of UART0 and so on):

Board Units an app may open Example pins Tab5 1, 2, 3, 4 the Grove port, G53 and G54 NARYA v4 (P4-Nano) 1, 2, 3, 4 the expansion header AtomS3R, StickS3 1, 2 Grove NARYA v3 2 GROVE 2, 47 and 48 Linux sim 2 (a stand-in) 47, 48 and others

UART0 (the console) and NARYA v3's UART1 (the link to the drawing side) are the system's: opening one is an IOError. The browser and the native build have no UART (IOError "not available in this environment"). Pins are guarded by the same table as GPIO: a system pin, or one another app or I2C holds, is an IOError. It cannot be used together with the serial MIDI output: while a MIDI app sends to serial, UART2 and its TX pin are MIDI's, free again once that app ends. The system closes a UART when the app ends.

The Linux sim's UART is a stand-in: what is written comes back to be read (a loopback). With uart2_in.fifo and uart2_out.fifo in the project directory, it reads from the first and writes to the second.

# unit and pins are an example
u = UART.new(unit: 1, txd_pin: 53,
  rxd_pin: 54, baudrate: 115200)
u.puts "hello"
line = u.gets   # nil if none yet

docs.title: Constants
docs.text: Name Type What it is PARITY_NONE Integer No parity PARITY_EVEN Integer Even parity PARITY_ODD Integer Odd parity FLOW_CONTROL_NONE Integer No flow control (the only one here) FLOW_CONTROL_RTS_CTS Integer RTS/CTS flow control (not here) WRITE_MAX Integer The most bytes one FmrbUart.write takes

docs.title: UART.new
docs.text:
new(
  unit: Integer | Symbol | String,
  ?txd_pin: Integer,
  ?rxd_pin: Integer,
  ?baudrate: Integer,
  ?data_bits: Integer,
  ?stop_bits: Integer,
  ?parity: Integer,
  ?flow_control: Integer,
  ?rts_pin: Integer,
  ?cts_pin: Integer,
  ?rx_buffer_size: Integer?
) -> UART

Open a UART

unit: is a number (2) or upstream's name (:ESP32_UART2). txd_pin: and rxd_pin: are GPIO numbers; -1 for one of them (receive only, send only). When left out: baudrate: 9600, data_bits: 8, stop_bits: 1, parity: PARITY_NONE, rx_buffer_size: 4096. rts_pin: and cts_pin: are not used.

Received bytes go into a receive buffer taken while it is open (rx_buffer_size bytes, a power of two from 16 to 16384, in PSRAM). A byte that arrives while it is full is dropped and counted by dropped.

Wrong arguments are an ArgumentError: an unknown name ("unknown unit"), a unit or pin this board does not have, both pins -1, TX and RX on one pin, a rate outside 300-5000000, a wrong format, the buffer size, anything but FLOW_CONTROL_NONE. When it cannot be opened it is an IOError with the reason: the system's unit ("UART0 is used by the system"), another app has it open, MIDI uses it, a system pin, a line a chip drives (an interrupt line) as TX, a pin in use, none in this environment. The same app opening the same unit again closes the one it had first (that object is closed: reading or writing it is an IOError ("closed")).

# unit and pins are an example
u = UART.new(unit: 2, txd_pin: 47,
  rxd_pin: 48, baudrate: 115200)

docs.title: App Config File (.app.toml)
docs.text:
Note

This page is about per-app settings. For the system's own settings — /etc/system_conf.toml and /etc/wifi.toml — see System Configuration.

A Family mruby app consists of an .app.rb main file paired with an .app.toml file of the same name. The .app.toml file specifies the app name, window settings, and other options. A Ruby app can instead carry the same keys in a #---fmrb comment at the top of the .rb (below), and can use both.

docs.title: File Naming Rules
docs.text:
<app_handle_name>.app.rb       # App main file
<app_handle_name>.app.toml     # Config file

Example:

my_clock.app.rb
my_clock.app.toml

Place the pair under /app/<category>/ (where category is any subdirectory such as demo, game, tool, etc.).

When the .toml is required

Launching a file directly — double-clicking it in the File Manager — needs the matching .app.toml; without it the spawn is refused and the desktop says why. Running from the editor with F5, or from the shell, works without one; the filename becomes the app name.

Language Extension mruby .app.rb Lua .app.lua BASIC .app.bas MicroPython .app.py WebAssembly (C, TinyGo, Rust, Zig) .app.wasm — see WebAssembly Apps (from 3.1.0)

docs.title: Key Reference
docs.text: Key Type Required Default Purpose app_handle_name string Optional (none) A handle name, conventionally the base name of the main file. The system does not read it app_screen_name string Optional the file name Display name shown on-screen and in the launcher class string Optional (none) The class to start ("MyApp"). Without it, the one FmrbApp subclass the file defines is started (a subclass that is the parent of another is not counted). Needed when a file defines more than one default_window_mode string Optional "window" "window" / "fullscreen" / "background" default_window_width integer Optional 100 Window width (px) default_window_height integer Optional 100 Window height (px) default_window_pos_x integer Optional 50 Window top-left X coordinate default_window_pos_y integer Optional 50 Window top-left Y coordinate resizable integer (0/1) Optional 0 Set to 1 to allow user resizing min_window_width integer Optional 0 Smallest width the user may resize to. 0 uses the system default (64) min_window_height integer Optional 0 Smallest height the user may resize to. 0 uses the system default (64) large_memory integer (0/1) Optional 0 Set to 1 to allocate a larger heap (for memory-intensive apps) launcher_visible bool / string Optional true Set to false or 0 to hide the app from the launcher rounded_corners bool / string Optional true Set to false to disable window corner transparency (optimization to gain fps) app_screen_name_<lang> string Optional (none) Localized display name, e.g. app_screen_name_ja. Used when the system language matches; otherwise app_screen_name task_stack_kb integer Optional 16 The app task's C stack, in KB. Raise it only if the app hits a stack protection fault. Clamped to 16-64 fullscreen_switchable integer (0/1) Optional 0 Set to 1 if a fullscreen app can be parked and restored on Ctrl + Tab (it must rebuild its canvas in on_resume) fullscreen_hires bool Optional false Let a fullscreen app run at 640x360 while it is fullscreen (Modern and the browser build). The size arrives in on_resize window_frame string Optional "normal" "none" for a window with no frame, title bar or close button (below) window_drag string Optional "title" (framed), "anywhere" (frameless) Where the window can be grabbed and moved: "title", "anywhere" or "none" single_instance bool Optional false Refuse a second copy of the same file exclusive_group string Optional (none) Refuse to start while another app with the same name (up to 15 bytes) runs, for apps that share a single resource movable bool Optional false The app may be written to an image and moved to another machine (Moving a running app) requires array Optional (none) Method names a movable app cannot go on without; it is not moved to a build that lacks them screens / needs_pointer array / bool Optional (none) For the keyboard-only desktop of the Linux program (320x170): the screen shapes the app can draw (["426x240", "320x170"]), and needs_pointer = false when it works without a mouse. Write them before the first [table] icon string Optional (default per extension) Icon file path (.icon format)

docs.title: Window Modes
docs.text:
Mode Behavior Size / Position window Window with title bar Uses default_window_* values fullscreen Occupies the entire screen (other apps are suspended) Size matches screen resolution; position is fixed at (0, 0) background Headless: no window, runs in the background (@gfx is nil) Not applicable

In fullscreen mode the app's area is the entire screen. In window mode it is the area inside the title bar (11px) and borders. Either way @gfx draws from its top-left as (0, 0), and its size is @user_area_width × @user_area_height.

A fullscreen app can also declare fullscreen_switchable = 1, which lets the user park it with Ctrl + Tab and come back to it later. See The Desktop > Switching between apps.

docs.title: Minimal Example
docs.text:
app_handle_name = "hello"
app_screen_name = "Hello"
default_window_mode = "window"
default_window_width = 160
default_window_height = 80
default_window_pos_x = 20
default_window_pos_y = 30

Corresponding Ruby file:

# /app/demo/hello.app.rb
class HelloApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    clear_user_area
    @gfx.draw_text(4, 4, "Hello!", theme_fg)
    @gfx.present
  end

  def on_update; 500; end
end

There is no start code at the end of the file: the runtime starts the FmrbApp subclass the file defines.

docs.title: Metadata in the .rb file
docs.text:
The same keys can go in a comment at the top of the .rb, so a one-file app needs no .app.toml. The block sits within the first 512 bytes, before the first line of code, and is TOML with # in front of each line:

#---fmrb
# app_screen_name = "Hello"
# default_window_width = 200
# default_window_height = 120
#---
class HelloApp < FmrbApp
  • When both are there they are merged key by key, and a key in the .app.toml wins: the comment can hold the defaults and the .app.toml override some of them.
  • Only .rb files are read this way (.lua, .bas and .py use other comment marks).
  • The launcher lists an .app.rb that has only the comment too.
  • An app distributed through the App Store needs an .app.toml: its app_id and the other installation keys are read from there.
  • From Ruby, FmrbApp.app_meta(path) returns an app file's merged metadata as a Hash of Strings.

docs.title: Frameless Windows
docs.text:
window_frame = "none"

A window with no frame, title bar or close button, for an avatar or a mascot. The app's area is the whole window and its ground is transparent, so only what the app draws shows. The window is moved by dragging it anywhere (window_drag = "anywhere", the default here); a press that does not move is a click, and holding still for a second is a long press. A right click or a long press calls on_frameless_right_click(ev), which by default opens the window menu (Send to, Reload, Close); Ctrl+Q also closes it.

By default the whole rectangle of the window takes clicks. To let clicks through where nothing is drawn, declare the shape: set_hit_shape([[x, y, w, h], ...]), set_hit_mask(hit_mask_from_art(rows, transparent: ".", scale: 3), x, y) or add_hit_sprite(sprite). A press outside it reaches the window behind. The sample is /app/demo/avatar.app.rb.

docs.title: Fullscreen App Example
docs.text:
app_handle_name = "shooter"
app_screen_name = "Shooter"
default_window_mode = "fullscreen"

In fullscreen mode, window size and position are ignored.

docs.title: When Large Memory Is Needed
docs.text: Setting large_memory = 1 selects a larger memory pool slot at startup. Currently only one slot is available.

docs.title: Specifying an Icon
docs.text:
icon = "usr/share/icon/blockgame.icon"
  • Place the file under /usr/share/icon/
  • The format is a text-based format. See Image and Icon Files for details
  • If icon is omitted, a default icon based on the main file extension is used (.rb -> ruby, .lua -> lua, .bas -> basic, .py -> python, .wasm -> wasm)

docs.title: Hiding from the Launcher
docs.text:
You can hide development or debug apps by setting launcher_visible = false.

launcher_visible = false

docs.title: Resizable Windows
docs.text:
resizable = 1

Set to 1 to enable resizing. The base class calls on_resize(w, h), so override it in your subclass to handle redrawing.

docs.title: App Placement
docs.text:
/app/
├── demo/                   # Samples and demos
├── game/                   # Games
│   └── rpg_demo/           # Assets can be placed alongside the app
│       ├── rpg_demo.app.rb
│       ├── rpg_demo.app.toml
│       ├── world.bmp
│       └── world.map.json
├── tool/                   # Tools
└── (any name)/
    ├── myapp.app.rb
    └── myapp.app.toml

The launcher scans subdirectories directly under /app to detect .app.toml files. It also scans one level deeper (/app/<category>/<bundle>/*.app.toml), so you can group images, maps, and other assets together with the app in the same directory.

Scanning happens only at startup

The app list is scanned once at system startup. After adding a new app via create_app or BLE, open the launcher and right-click to rescan, or restart the device (see Hello World - Reflecting changes in the launcher).

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• For how to create apps, see Hello World
  • For how to create icon files, see Image and Icon Files

docs.title: File Associations (associations.toml)
docs.text: One table decides which app opens which file. The file manager's double click, the shell's open, and any app that hands a file on all ask the same table, so they cannot drift apart.

docs.title: The file
docs.text:
rb  = "run"
lua = "run"
bas = "run"
py  = "run"

md  = "/app/tool/picorabbit.app.rb"
nsf = "/app/tool/nsf_player.app.rb"

txt  = "edit"
toml = "edit"
json = "edit"

One line per extension, written without the dot, and one of three answers:

Answer What happens run The file is a program. It is spawned as an app edit It opens in the editor /app/… That app is spawned and handed the file

An extension with no entry gets edit — showing a file is a better answer to "I do not know" than doing nothing. A directory is never opened this way.

docs.title: Two layers
docs.text:
File /etc/associations.toml Ships with the firmware /home/associations.toml Yours. It wins, per extension

So to send .md to the editor instead of the presentation tool, /home/associations.toml needs one line and nothing else:

md = "edit"

The table is read once, when the app that consults it starts. A change takes effect the next time that app is started.

docs.title: Receiving a file
docs.text: An app that is handed a file gets it exactly as it gets a file from the file selector, so an app that already handles that needs nothing new to be worth associating with an extension.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • App Config (.app.toml) — how an app gets into the launcher

docs.title: Audio File Formats
docs.text:
This page describes the audio file formats supported by Family mruby, along with how to create and convert them.

Format Purpose API FMSQ Sequence data for short BGM / sound effects. Loaded into a slot for playback FmrbAudio#load_fmsq, play_slot NSF NES music (NES Sound Format) FmrbAudio#play(path, track:) MID Standard MIDI files. Played through the MIDI layer, on the internal sound chip or an external instrument FmrbMidi::SmfPlayer

docs.title: FMSQ
docs.text:
FMSQ (Family mruby Sequence) is a proprietary format for writing NES APU-compatible music data. It is suited for short sound effects and BGM loops.

See https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/APU_registers

docs.title: File Structure
docs.text:
12-byte header + variable-length command stream. All values are little-endian.

+------+----------------+
| 0..3 | "FMSQ"         |  magic
| 4    | version (=1)   |
| 5    | flags (=0)     |  reserved
| 6..7 | frame_count    |  total frames
| 8..9 | data_size      |  command bytes
| 10..11 | loop_offset  |  0 = no loop
+------+----------------+
| 12.. | command stream |
+------+----------------+

docs.title: Opcode List
docs.text:
cc = channel number (00=Pulse1, 01=Pulse2, 10=Triangle, 11=Noise), aaaaa = register offset from $4000 (0x00-0x17).

Bit Pattern Instruction Following Bytes Total Size 0xxxxxxx WAIT (1-128 frames) 0 1 10cc0000 NOTE_ON 2-4 per channel 3-5 10cc0001 NOTE_OFF 0 1 10cc0010 PARAM MASK + variable 2 or more 110aaaaa REG_WRITE ($4000+aaaaa) 1 (DATA) 2 11100000 DPCM_PLAY 3 (RATE_FLAGS, ADDR, LENGTH) 4 11100001 DPCM_STOP 0 1 11100010 DPCM_RAW 1 (VALUE) 2 11111110 END 0 1 11111111 LOOP 2 (OFFSET) 3

APU emulator limitation: DPCM functionality is not currently supported by the APU emulator side.

docs.title: WAIT instruction
docs.text:
0xxxxxxx
  • Upper 1 bit = 0 -> WAIT
  • Lower 7 bits = number of frames to wait minus 1
Value Meaning 0x00 Wait 1 frame 0x01 Wait 2 frames ... ... 0x7F Wait 128 frames

docs.title: Channel instructions (NOTE_ON / NOTE_OFF / PARAM)
docs.text: High-level commands in the form 10ccxxxx. cc selects the channel (Pulse1=0, Pulse2=1, Triangle=2, Noise=3), and the lower 4 bits select the subcommand. NOTE_ON / NOTE_OFF also update the corresponding bit of $4015 (Status) internally.

docs.title: NOTE_ON
docs.text:
10cc0000. Following bytes depend on the channel:

Channel Following Bytes Write order Pulse1 / Pulse2 TIMER_LO, TIMER_HI, VOL_ENV, SWEEP (4 bytes) VOL -> SWEEP -> LO -> HI Triangle TIMER_LO, TIMER_HI, LINEAR (3 bytes) LINEAR -> LO -> HI Noise PERIOD_MODE, VOL_ENV (2 bytes) VOL -> LO

docs.title: NOTE_OFF
docs.text: 10cc0001. No following bytes. Only clears the corresponding channel bit in $4015 (the APU registers themselves are not modified).

docs.title: PARAM
docs.text:
10cc0010 [MASK] [DATA...]

Updates only the sub-parameters specified by the mask. The mask bits and their following data are as follows:

docs.title: Pulse PARAM (Pulse1 / Pulse2)
docs.text: mask bit Following data Write target 0x01 (TIMER) LO, HI (2 bytes) $4002/3 or $4006/7 0x02 (VOL) VOL_ENV (1 byte) $4000 or $4004 0x04 (SWEEP) SWEEP (1 byte) $4001 or $4005

docs.title: Triangle PARAM
docs.text: mask bit Following data Write target 0x01 (TIMER) LO, HI (2 bytes) $400A/B 0x02 (LINEAR) LINEAR (1 byte) $4008

docs.title: Noise PARAM
docs.text:
mask bit Following data Write target 0x01 (PERIOD) PERIOD_MODE (1 byte) $400E 0x02 (VOL) VOL_ENV (1 byte) $400C

Following bytes are read and written in mask bit order. No following byte is present for bits that are not set.

docs.title: REG_WRITE instruction
docs.text:
110aaaaa [DATA]

Direct write to an APU register. Preserves both the order and the values of APU register operations from NSF.

  • aaaaa: offset from $4000 (0-23)
  • DATA: value to write (1 byte)
  • Total: 2 bytes per write
offset (aaaaa) APU register Description 0x00 $4000 Pulse1 Volume/Envelope/Duty 0x01 $4001 Pulse1 Sweep 0x02 $4002 Pulse1 Timer Low 0x03 $4003 Pulse1 Timer High + Length 0x04 $4004 Pulse2 Volume/Envelope/Duty 0x05 $4005 Pulse2 Sweep 0x06 $4006 Pulse2 Timer Low 0x07 $4007 Pulse2 Timer High + Length 0x08 $4008 Triangle Linear Counter 0x0A $400A Triangle Timer Low 0x0B $400B Triangle Timer High + Length 0x0C $400C Noise Volume/Envelope 0x0E $400E Noise Period + Mode 0x0F $400F Noise Length 0x10 $4010 DMC Frequency/Flags 0x11 $4011 DMC DAC (7bit) 0x12 $4012 DMC Sample Address 0x13 $4013 DMC Sample Length 0x15 $4015 Status (Channel Enable)

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Ruby generators are available under fmruby-graphics-audio/tools/ (run on PC).

fmruby-graphics-audio/tools/gen_test_fmsq.rb     # Scale pattern
fmruby-graphics-audio/tools/gen_intro_fmsq.rb    # Jingle

Use these as a reference to write scales and chords, and generate .fmsq binary files.

docs.title: Playback
docs.text:
Load the data into a slot (by numeric ID), then play it.

data = File.open("/sfx.fmsq", "r") { |f| f.read }
@audio.load_fmsq(0, data)   # Register in slot 0
@audio.play_slot(0)         # Play

See FmrbAudio for details.

docs.title: NSF (NES Sound Format)
docs.text: NES Sound Format is a standard format for playing actual NES music. Family mruby supports playback of NSF files.

docs.title: Obtaining NSF Files
docs.text: • To create your own, export as NSF from a DAW like FamiStudio

docs.title: Playback
docs.text:
@audio.play("/usr/share/sounds/nsf/song.nsf", track: 1)

track: is the song number (1-based). Since an NSF file can contain multiple songs, you select the file first and then choose a specific song with the track parameter.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: • Some NSF files cannot be played

docs.title: Sample
docs.text: A sample NSF player GUI is available at /app/tool/nsf_player.app.rb (implements track forward/backward, track selection, and pause/resume).

docs.title: MID (Standard MIDI File)
docs.text:
New in 2.0. A .mid file is played by the MIDI layer rather than the audio slots, which means the same file can drive the internal sound chip or an external instrument on the GROVE port.

player = FmrbMidi::SmfPlayer.new(@device)
player.load("/usr/share/sounds/midi/song.mid")
player.play

Seven public-domain songs ship in /usr/share/sounds/midi, and the SMF Player app (/app/tool/smf_player.app.rb) plays them with a file list.

docs.title: On the internal sound chip
docs.text: The APU has four voices — two pulses, a triangle and noise — against MIDI's sixteen channels, so playing a general MIDI file through it is lossy by construction. Dense arrangements lose notes. An external General MIDI module has no such limit; see MIDI.

docs.title: Converting to FMSQ
docs.text:
For music you want as a fixed sequence rather than live playback, tools/midi/smf2fmsq.rb in the repository converts a .mid into an FMSQ stream:

ruby tools/midi/smf2fmsq.rb input.mid -o out.fmsq

It emits register writes carrying full APU state, so the result plays identically on both FMSQ players. The same four-voice reduction applies.

docs.title: WAV / MP3
docs.text: The sound chip does not play them: convert to FMSQ, or use MID or NSF. A recording is played on top of the sound chip with FmrbAudio#play_wav on Modern (and the Linux builds and Studio): a mono WAV, 16-bit PCM or 4-bit IMA-ADPCM (the latter in the development version). MP3 is not supported.

docs.title: Direct Synthesis (note_on / note_off)
docs.text:
You can drive the APU directly using FmrbAudio#note_on without any files. This is useful for rhythm, dialogue sound effects, button click sounds, and similar.

@audio.note_on(0, 440, 10, 2, 0)   # A4 on Pulse 1 channel
sleep_ms(200)
@audio.note_off(0)

See FmrbAudio - note_on / note_off for details.

docs.title: Colour Names
docs.text:
The machine shows 256 colours: three bits of red, three of green, two of blue, packed into one byte (RGB332). Anywhere a colour is asked for you can write that byte — 0x1F — but most of them have a name as well, and a name is what keeps a file a person edits a file a person can read.

The names are the web's, mapped onto the 256 this machine has. Mapping them collapses some (a 3-3-2 grid cannot tell ivory from snow), so the list comes in two parts: 78 names, one per distinct colour, and 23 further spellings that land on a colour already in the list. Both are understood; the 78 are what a picker offers back, and what a file is written with.

docs.title: The 78
docs.text:
The swatches are the colour as the machine expands it, so a name that looks approximate here looks the same on the screen.

black0x00 white0xFF red0xE0 lime0x1C blue0x03 yellow0xFC cyan0x1F magenta0xE3 silver0xB6 gray0x92 maroon0x80 olive0x90 green0x10 purple0x82 teal0x12 navy0x02 orange0xF4 gold0xF8 pink0xF6 hotpink0xEE deeppink0xE6 crimson0xC5 firebrick0xA4 tomato0xED salmon0xF1 orangered0xE8 darkorange0xF0 khaki0xFA tan0xD6 peru0xD1 chocolate0xCC saddlebrown0x88 sienna0x89 darkkhaki0xB5 yellowgreen0x99 olivedrab0x70 greenyellow0xBD chartreuse0x7C springgreen0x1D limegreen0x39 forestgreen0x30 darkgreen0x0C seagreen0x31 mediumseagreen0x55 lightgreen0x9E darkseagreen0x96 aquamarine0x7E turquoise0x5A darkturquoise0x1A lightseagreen0x36 lightcyan0xDF paleturquoise0xBF powderblue0xBB skyblue0x9B deepskyblue0x17 dodgerblue0x33 cornflowerblue0x73 steelblue0x52 royalblue0x4F midnightblue0x25 slateblue0x6A mediumpurple0x8F blueviolet0x87 darkorchid0x86 mediumorchid0xAA orchid0xCF violet0xF3 plum0xD3 thistle0xD7 lavender0xDB indigo0x42 mediumvioletred0xA6 palevioletred0xCE mistyrose0xFB lightgray0xDA dimgray0x6D lightslategray0x72 darkslategray0x29

docs.text:
Written in a file or typed at the shell, each of these is accepted and resolves to the colour beside it. Ask for the name back and you get that one.

Also understood Lands on darkred maroon 0x80 coral tomato 0xED lightyellow white 0xFF ivory white 0xFF beige white 0xFF wheat khaki 0xFA brown firebrick 0xA4 lawngreen chartreuse 0x7C palegreen lightgreen 0x9E darkcyan teal 0x12 mediumblue navy 0x02 darkblue navy 0x02 darkviolet purple 0x82 darkmagenta purple 0x82 lightpink pink 0xF6 darkgray silver 0xB6 slategray lightslategray 0x72 gainsboro lavender 0xDB whitesmoke white 0xFF snow white 0xFF azure white 0xFF honeydew white 0xFF linen white 0xFF

docs.title: Where a name works
docs.text: /home/colors.toml bg = "midnightblue" The shell's color command color bg skyblue, and color names lists the 78 The editor's Colors dialog It writes the same file An app, through FmrbColors Below

docs.title: From an app (FmrbColors)
docs.text:
Method FmrbColors.by_name("skyblue") The value, or nil when it is not one of ours FmrbColors.to_color(str) The same, but "0x1F" and "31" are accepted too FmrbColors.to_text(value) Its name, or "0x1F" when it has none. This is what gets written to a file FmrbColors.name_of(value) Its name, or nil FmrbColors.palette_size / name_at(i) / palette_value(i) Walking the 78, which is how a picker is built FmrbColors.shade(colour, avoid = nil) A step darker, or lighter when darker would land on avoid or on the colour itself. The editor's bars are made this way FmrbColors.section("editor") That section of the user's colours file, as a Hash

A name that is not one of ours gives nil rather than a colour. That is deliberate: a typo in a colours file leaves the theme colour in place instead of painting the app black.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Colours (colors.toml) — overriding an app's colours
  • System Config — the nine colours of the system theme
  • Drawing — FmrbGfx's own colour constants, and RGB332

docs.title: Colours (/home/colors.toml)
docs.text:
[theme] in /etc/system_conf.toml sets the look of the whole machine, and every app takes its defaults from there. This file is the one place to disagree with it for a single app — with no rebuild, and without the reboot a theme change needs.

[editor]
bg   = "midnightblue"
text = 0xFC

[shell]
bg = "black"

A missing file, a missing section and a missing key all mean "use the theme", so the file only ever holds what somebody deliberately changed. Deleting a line is how you go back.

A value is either a colour name or a number. The number is RGB332, written the same way as in system_conf.toml.

It lives in /home because it is yours: nothing the machine ships with is written there, and on Studio that is the directory which survives a reload and travels in the exported archive.

docs.title: From the shell
docs.text:
The shell changes its own two colours and writes them here for you:

color                    show the current two
color bg skyblue         the background
color text 0x1F          the text, as a number
color names              list every colour name
color reset              back to the theme

The change applies at once, with no restart.

Two lines in the shell, and it keeps them across boots

docs.title: From the editor
docs.text:
The editor has a Colors entry in its menu that walks its 31 colours, one at a time. It writes the same file, under [editor]. The editor holds its colours in constants, so it asks you to reopen it before the new ones are drawn.

The keys, in the order the dialog offers them:

Group Keys Text area bg, text, cursor, selection, gutter Menu bar menu_bg, menu_text, menu_key, menu_key_alt Status line status_bg, status_text, saved_bg, saved_text Dropdowns dropdown_bg, dropdown_text, dropdown_sel_bg, dropdown_sel_text Dialogs dialog_bg, dialog_text, dialog_border, dialog_key Problems problem_bg, problem_text Syntax syntax_keyword, syntax_string, syntax_comment, syntax_number, syntax_symbol, syntax_constant, syntax_variable, syntax_method

menu_key_alt is the same role as menu_key on a light panel — yellow on white is unreadable, so the key list uses its own.

docs.title: Colour names
docs.text:
The names are the web's, mapped onto the 256 colours this machine can show. Collapsing them that way means several web names land on the same colour, so the list comes in two parts: 78 names, one per distinct colour, and 23 further spellings that land on a colour already in the list. Both are understood; color names in the shell lists the 78.

All of them, with their colours, are on Colour Names.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Constants & System Info — reading the theme from an app

docs.title: HID Device Config (/etc/hid_devices.toml)
docs.text:
Not every USB device works. Some are never enumerated; others enumerate but report in a format the generic path reads wrongly. Verified Peripherals lists what has been tested.

This file fixes the second case: it spells out, per device, which bits of the HID report are buttons and which are axes. The symptoms it addresses are a cursor that jumps, moves on the wrong axis, or does not move while the buttons work. A device that never enumerates is a driver problem and this will not help.

docs.title: How a device gets its layout
docs.text:
The system tries these in order:

  1. This file. If a [[mouse]] or [[gamepad]] block matches the device's vendor and product ID, that layout wins outright
  2. Boot protocol. With no match, a boot-capable mouse is asked to send standard 3-byte boot reports
  3. Auto-detection. If the reports that arrive do not look like boot reports — longer than 3 bytes and starting with the mouse report ID — the system switches itself to a Report Protocol layout with 12-bit packed axes, which covers a common family of cheap mice

So a device only needs an entry here when all three fail.

docs.title: Writing an entry without a PC
docs.text:
The HID Inspector app does this interactively on the device itself. It is built into the firmware rather than installed under /app, so it is not in the launcher — press I on the desktop to start it:

  1. LIST — pick the misbehaving device from the connected list
  2. INSPECT — watch the raw report bytes as you move and click
  3. WIZARD — it walks you through moving one axis at a time and works out where each field sits
  4. RESULT — it shows the [[mouse]] block it generated; press S to append it to /etc/hid_devices.toml

The format below is for reading and hand-editing what it writes.

docs.title: [[mouse]]
docs.text:
[[mouse]]
vid = 0x046D
pid = 0xC534
name = "Logitech Unifying"
report_id = 0x02
report_len = 7
buttons = { offset = 0,  size = 8,  min = 0,     max = 1,    relative = false }
x       = { offset = 16, size = 12, min = -2048, max = 2047, relative = true }
y       = { offset = 28, size = 12, min = -2048, max = 2047, relative = true }
Key Meaning vid / pid USB vendor and product ID, as hex name Free text, used in the log so you can tell entries apart report_id The report ID byte. Omit it, or set -1, when the device sends none report_len Report length in bytes, not counting the report ID skip_control_transfer true to skip USB control transfers for this device. A few devices stall on them buttons Where the button bits are x / y Where the axes are wheel Where the wheel is. Optional, and the switch that turns it on protocol boot (the default) or report

Field tables take:

Key Meaning offset Bit offset from the start of the report data (after the report ID, if any) size Field width in bits min / max Value range. Negative min means the field is signed relative true for a mouse reporting movement, false for a touchpad or tablet reporting a position

Offsets are in bits, not bytes. A 12-bit axis starting halfway through byte 2 is offset = 20, and that is exactly the case the generic path gets wrong.

docs.title: The wheel
docs.text:
The wheel is opt-in, per device. Leave wheel out and the mouse behaves exactly as it always has, even if its descriptor has one; write it and the notches go to the focused window.

wheel = { offset = 24, size = 8, min = -127, max = 127, relative = true }

Plug the mouse in and the log says whether it reports a wheel, and where, in a line you can paste:

usb_task: Mouse VID=0x.... PID=0x.... reports a wheel (offset=24 size=8);
  add wheel = { offset = 24, size = 8, ... } to /etc/hid_devices.toml to use it

One notch is 1, and turning the wheel away from you is positive.

A Boot Interface mouse answers with three bytes — buttons, X, Y — and its wheel is simply not among them, so no offset can reach it. protocol = "report" asks that one device for its own format instead, which is where its wheel lives. Only a device named here is asked; every other mouse keeps the boot path it has always taken. Use the HID Inspector to read the report it then sends, because that layout is the device's own and not the standard three bytes. Over-declare report_len while measuring so the Inspector shows the whole report, then write the real length.

Do not expect the report descriptor to settle it: for a Boot Interface device the USB host stack returns garbage for the descriptor, so the bits have to be measured from live reports.

docs.title: [[gamepad]]
docs.text:
[[gamepad]]
vid = 0x0F0D
pid = 0x0009
name = "HORI PAD 3 TURBO"
report_len = 19
buttons = { offset = 0,  size = 16 }
hat     = { offset = 16, size = 4 }
left_x  = { offset = 24, size = 8, center = 128 }
left_y  = { offset = 32, size = 8, center = 128 }
right_x = { offset = 40, size = 8, center = 128 }
right_y = { offset = 48, size = 8, center = 128 }
Key Meaning vid / pid / name As above report_len Report length in bytes buttons Bitmask field: offset, size. Bit n becomes button n hat D-pad / hat switch: offset, size. Optional left_x, left_y, right_x, right_y, l2, r2 Axes: offset, size, center

center is the resting value of the axis — 128 for a stick that reports 0-255 — so the system knows which way is "pushed".

Button numbers reach your app as ev[:button] in a :gamepad_down / :gamepad_up event, and the GP_* constants name them. See Constants & System Info.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Blocks are matched by vid and pid only. A device that reports a different pid in a different mode needs an entry per mode
  • The shipped file contains working entries for a Logitech Unifying receiver, a Logickeyboard TITAN touchpad, a Sipeed NanoKVM-USB and a HORI PAD 3 TURBO. They are worth reading as examples even if you own none of them
  • Flashing firmware replaces this file along with the rest of /etc, so keep a copy of entries you worked out

  • Default Apps — the HID Inspector

docs.title: Image and Icon Files
docs.text:
This page describes the image and icon formats supported by Family mruby, along with how to create and convert them.

Format Purpose Related API PNG Pictures drawn whole; sprites, tile sheets, wallpapers and launcher icons FmrbGfx#create_image / SpriteImage BMP (RGB332) Sprites and tile sheets, and pixels to edit in Ruby BMP332 / SpriteImage .icon App icons (text format) --

docs.title: PNG
docs.text:
FmrbGfx#create_image and load_image take a PNG. In the development version SpriteImage#load_bmp (and so TileSheet) reads one too, telling it from a BMP by the first bytes: the colours become RGB332 by keeping the top 3/3/2 bits of red, green and blue, and transparency is the sprite's transparent_color, not the PNG's alpha.

The artwork that ships with the system — sprites, tile sheets, wallpapers and launcher icons — is PNG with a palette of only the colours it uses, at 1, 2, 4 or 8 bits per pixel. That is a tenth to a sixtieth of the size of the same picture as an 8-bit BMP, and a small one fits inside a single filesystem entry. A PNG whose palette entries are RGB332 colours spread to 8 bits per channel comes back as exactly those RGB332 values.

The sprite editor still opens and saves BMP only.

docs.title: BMP (RGB332)
docs.text:
The BMP that Family mruby reads is an 8-bit BMP using RGB332 color encoding.

Each pixel is 1 byte, and each pixel value is treated directly as an RGB332 color value.

  • R: 3 bits
  • G: 3 bits
  • B: 2 bits

A total of 256 colors can be represented.

docs.title: Format Specification
docs.text:
The BMP file format uses a standard 8-bit indexed BMP.

  • BMP header
  • BITMAPFILEHEADER
  • BITMAPINFOHEADER
  • 8-bit indexed BMP
  • 256-color palette
  • Palette contents are an RGB332 array
  • Each pixel value is treated as an RGB332 color value

The palette in the BMP is included for compatibility with PC image viewers. Family mruby does not reference the palette; it treats pixel values directly as RGB332 color values.

docs.title: RGB332 Color Composition
docs.text:
Component Bits Red 3 bits Green 3 bits Blue 2 bits

Total: 8 bits / 256 colors.

docs.title: Icon Files (.icon)
docs.text: A text-based file format that defines icons displayed in the app launcher.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
# <name> (<width>x<height>) color=0x<RGB332>
............
...111111...
..11111111..
.11111.1111.
111111..1111
.1111111111.
..11111111..
...111111...
....1111....
.....11.....
............
............
Character Meaning . Transparent (not drawn) 1 Pixel (filled with the specified color) # Comment line (color settings can be placed at the beginning)

docs.title: Comment Line Metadata
docs.text:
• color=0xNN specifies the color (RGB332) for all pixels
  • Defaults to white (0xFF) if omitted

docs.title: Recommended Size
docs.text: The standard launcher icon size is 12 x 12 pixels.

docs.title: File Location
docs.text:
/usr/share/icon/<name>.icon

When referencing from .toml:

icon = "/usr/share/icon/myapp.icon"

docs.title: Default Icons
docs.text:
If icon is omitted in the .toml, a default icon is used based on the main file extension:

Extension Default Icon .rb /usr/share/icon/ruby.icon .lua /usr/share/icon/lua.icon .bas /usr/share/icon/basic.icon .py /usr/share/icon/python.icon .wasm /usr/share/icon/wasm.icon

A WebAssembly app usually names its language's icon instead: c.icon, tinygo.icon, rust.icon or zig.icon.

docs.title: What the launcher loads
docs.text: The .icon text is the source. The launcher loads the picture beside it — <name>.png, or <name>.bmp where there is no PNG — which is the 12x12 grid drawn at twice the size. For an icon of your own, make the PNG from the .icon with fmruby-core's tools/gen_icon_png.rb (or rake icons there) and put both side by side (development version).

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• BMP332 API
  • Sprite
  • Sprite editor: /app/tool/sprite_editor.app.rb

docs.title: System Services (services.toml)
docs.text:
A service is a small job that stays resident: it wakes on a timer, or when something is published, and it has no window. The clock that sets itself from the network is one; so is the thing that reads a sentence out loud.

They all run inside a single app, the service host. A dozen small resident jobs therefore cost one task and one VM instead of a dozen — which is why they exist as services and not as apps you leave running.

Modern only

The service host is not carried in the Retro firmware. On Retro nothing here applies, and the Retro simulator behaves the same way.

docs.title: What ships
docs.text:
Service What it does clock Keeps the time of day hourly_chime Rings a note on the hour. Point it at a WAV and it rings that instead net Watches the network and publishes net/state. The address goes into the log the moment there is one timesync Sets the clock from an NTP server once the machine is on the network, so Set Clock stops being a chore after every power cut tts Says things out loud. Anything that publishes to tts/say is read aloud

Studio carries the first two; a browser tab has no clock to set and no speaker service to call.

docs.title: Two lists
docs.text:
File Bodies /etc/services.toml /usr/share/services/ Ships with the firmware /home/services.toml /home/services/ Yours. Read second, and wins field by field

Winning field by field is what makes the user list small. To switch off a service the firmware ships, that is the whole file:

[hourly_chime]
enable = false

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field file The source, under the list's own directory class The class inside it enable false keeps the entry but does not run it. Default true interval_ms How often on_tick is called. Omit it for a service that only reacts to topics oneshot true runs on_start once at boot, then drops the entry [<name>.config] Handed to the service as ctx.config

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
Copy the sample and list it:

cp /usr/share/samples/services/services.toml.example /home/services.toml
cp /usr/share/samples/services/heartbeat.rb /home/services/heartbeat.rb

The contract is five optional methods:

class HeartbeatService
  def on_start(ctx)          # ctx is the only way out to the rest of the machine
  def on_tick(now_ms)        # every interval_ms
  def on_wake(now_ms)        # after ctx.wake_in
  def on_event(topic, data)
  def on_stop
end

ctx offers publish, wake_in, audio, log, now_ms, config and stop_self.

Keep every method short. The services run one after another on one task, so time spent in one is time the others wait; the host logs a warning past 50 ms. A service that raises is switched off on its own after three errors, without taking the others with it.

docs.title: Starting an app at boot
docs.text:
An entry can name an app instead of a service:

[my_game]
app = "/app/game/robo_explorer/robo_explorer.app.rb"
fullscreen = true      # overrides the app's own window mode
delay_ms = 2000        # let the desktop settle first
restart = true         # start it again if it crashes (a kill stays killed)

docs.title: Switching one off
docs.text:
Two ways, and they are not the same:

svc stop <name> (or kill <name>) This session only. A reboot undoes it svc disable <name> Remembered, so it stays off after a reboot

svc start and svc enable are the other halves. What is remembered goes in /home/services_state.toml, which the host writes — your own services.toml is never rewritten. ps in the shell lists the services alongside the apps, and so does the Monitor.

docs.title: Speech
docs.text:
The tts service turns a published sentence into speech. A sentence said once is cached as a WAV under /tmp, which is in PSRAM rather than on the flash — speech is a couple of hundred kilobytes a go, and the flash is small and wears out. It plays from the cache afterwards with no network at all, until the next reboot empties it.

Two ways to synthesise:

[tts.config]
server = "http://192.0.2.5:50021"   # a VOICEVOX server on your PC
speaker = 1
timeout_ms = 3000

Or synthesise in the cloud, with no PC. The API key goes in a file of its own, /home/secrets.toml, not in the service list:

# /home/secrets.toml
[openai]
api_key = "sk-..."

[tts.config]
cloud_model = "gpt-4o-mini-tts"
cloud_voice = "alloy"
cloud_timeout_ms = 10000

The service list is an ordinary file that the remote file services hand to anyone who asks. secrets.toml is kept like the Wi-Fi password: never served over HTTP, and read over BLE only while BLE Setup is open on the machine. The key is still plain text on the flash, and only where it came from goes into the log, never the key itself.

To run with no network, leave the server line where it is and simply let it be unreachable: a miss then costs one refused connection and a log line, and everything already said still plays. Deleting the line changes the cache key, and the machine stops finding its own cache.

A phrase that has to sound with no network and after a power cut is not a job for the cache. Put a WAV in /home/voice/ and play it.

docs.text:
