docs.title: The Desktop
docs.text: The desktop is the same on both machines: a menu bar across the top, the wallpaper below it with a column of app icons, and windows on top of that.

docs.title: Family mruby
docs.text: Click it for the system menu. See the list below.

docs.title: Running apps (the taskbar)
docs.text:
Each running app gets a small square, in the order they started, immediately right of the title. This is the taskbar.

It is a list of windows, not of processes: a square is something you can click to bring to the front and type into. An app with no window — the service host, for one — has nothing to raise, so it is not listed. ps and the Monitor still show it.

  • The letter is the first character of the app's name

  • The colour is the language it runs on:

    Colour Language Red Ruby (mruby) Yellow MicroPython Green BASIC Blue Lua Gray Native C

  • A white border marks the app that currently has keyboard focus

  • Click a square to bring that app to the front and give it the keyboard
Three apps running. The white border is the one with the keyboard

An app parked by Ctrl + Tab (see below) stays in the taskbar while it is frozen, so you can always click your way back to it.

docs.title: Free internal RAM
docs.text:
The figure on the right — 137KB in the example — is free internal RAM, not total free memory. App heaps come from PSRAM, which is plentiful, but each running app also costs about 25 KB of internal RAM, and that is what runs out first. So this is the number that answers "can I open one more app?".

The Linux simulator has no such limit and shows ---KB.

The right-hand end, enlarged. Free RAM, kana, BLE, Wi-Fi, clock

docs.title: Kana input
docs.text:
A when you are typing ASCII, あ for hiragana, ア for katakana. Click it to step through the three. It is there from boot, in every language, because on a keyboard with no half-width/full-width key — or with no keyboard at all — that click is the way in. Ctrl + Space does the same thing from the keyboard.

Kanji conversion. On a board with the kanji dictionary on its SD card (/sd/dict/fmrb_kanji.dic), a reading typed in kana mode collects in a line at the bottom of the screen: Space (or the JIS Henkan key) shows candidates and steps through them, Enter or a digit commits, Esc goes back. Without the dictionary kana input works as before. Studio uses the browser's own Japanese input method and the Linux program the PC's. The guide on the device, /usr/share/doc/kanji.md, says where to get the dictionary and how to put it there.

docs.title: BLE
docs.text:
Appearance Meaning Nothing BLE is off Gray box, white B BLE is on, waiting for something to connect White box, inverted B A client is connected — the web console, typically

On Retro the system menu starts BLE and ble_auto_start in Config decides whether it comes up at boot; there is no way to stop it again short of a reboot. Modern has the same setting, and false there means nothing is advertised and nothing can connect — the link to the C6 still comes up, because Wi-Fi needs it.

docs.title: Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Signal bars, just left of the clock.

Appearance Meaning White bars Connected Gray bars with a red slash Not connected Nothing This build has no Wi-Fi

Click the bars to open the Network dialog, which shows the address the device was given. See Connecting to Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Sound
docs.text: A speaker just left of the clock. Click it to mute the whole machine, and again to bring the sound back; while muted the cell turns white and the waves become a cross. The apps keep playing underneath, so nothing is lost. The volume (0-10) is in Config, and both are remembered across a restart. An app reads them with FmrbApp.audio_muted? and FmrbApp.audio_volume.

docs.title: Clock
docs.text: Date and time. Set it from Set Clock; the timezone is a separate setting under Config.

docs.title: Power
docs.text: The button at the right end. On a board it holds Reset (reboot). In the Linux program it holds what the PC offers: Lock, Suspend, Log Out (or Exit), Restart and Power off, each asking before it acts. It is not shown where there is nothing to offer (the simulator and Studio).

docs.title: The system menu
docs.text:
Item What it does Launcher The grid of installed apps Editor The editor. It is built into the firmware, and heads the launcher grid with the Shell and the App Store File Manager Browse the flash filesystem Log Viewer The system log Monitor Running tasks, memory and services; a WASM page for WebAssembly apps Set Clock Date and time Config Language, keyboard layout, pointer speed, theme, wallpaper, timezone, volume, Wi-Fi and BLE autostart, display margins Mute / Unmute The same switch as the speaker in the menu bar Storage Clear cached files Network Wi-Fi state, address, hostname, and the Wi-Fi page BLE Start Retro only, and only when BLE did not start at boot BLE Setup Boards only. Opens a few minutes in which the web console may read and write the Wi-Fi and Asterism settings and the keys; it counts down, and choosing it again closes it Shortcuts Every key that works here, in one list About Version and chip information

Reboot is the power button at the right end of the menu bar.

Whatever Config changes is written back into /etc/system_conf.toml, keeping your comments and other settings intact. On hardware the dialog offers Save & Reboot for the settings that only take effect at startup.

docs.title: What happens before the desktop
docs.text:
Power-on shows the logo the way an old CRT television comes on — a thin line of light in the middle of the black that stretches sideways and opens up and down into the picture — over a short chord that rises a fifth and rings, and then the desktop comes up. The whole of it takes about 1.2 seconds (it took 2.7 in 3.0.0). That ceremony is boot_splash in /etc/system_conf.toml; setting it to false skips both and saves that time, which is worth having on a machine built to run one thing. Nothing else changes — the cursor, the status LED and the startup app all happen either way.

startup_app beside it names one app to open as soon as the desktop is ready, by the same path the launcher uses. Empty means the ordinary desktop. A fullscreen app named there takes the screen without the desktop showing first. Neither setting is in the Config dialog: edit the file in the Editor.

docs.title: Icons on the desktop
docs.text:
The wallpaper carries a column of icons on the left: the Launcher, the Editor, the Shell, the File Manager and a few apps (Flappy Demo, the BASIC demo, Breakout, the NSF player) as shipped. Double-click one to start it; windows sit on top of them. An app that is not on this machine is skipped.

To change the set, right-click an app in the launcher (or select it and press D) and pick Add to desktop or Remove from desktop. The choice is written to /home/desktop.toml; delete that file to go back to the default set. In the Linux program the PC's own applications (a terminal, a browser) can sit there too.

docs.title: The launcher
docs.text:
Double-click an icon to start an app. Arrow keys move the selection and Enter starts it.

The list is built once, at boot

The launcher scans the filesystem when the desktop starts. After you add an app, press the Reload button in its title bar (or F5) to rescan — otherwise your new app will not appear until the next reboot. Right-clicking empty space in the launcher offers Reload too.

Right-click an icon (on a Tab5, a two-finger tap), or press Tab on the selected one, for its menu: Add to desktop / Remove from desktop.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Action How Move Drag the title bar Focus Click anywhere in the window, or click its taskbar square Close The button in the title bar, or Ctrl + Q Window menu Right-click the title bar: Send to (move a movable app to another machine), Reload (start an app again from its edited file) and Close Resize Drag the triangle in the bottom-right corner — only windows that declare resizable have it

A click is decided on release, with a small movement tolerance, so a slightly shaky press does not turn into a drag.

Some apps have no frame at all (an avatar on the desktop, for instance). Drag them from anywhere; a right-click or a one-second press opens the same window menu.

docs.title: Scrolling
docs.text:
The mouse wheel scrolls the editor, the shell, the log viewer, the launcher and the file dialogs. It goes to the window that has the keyboard, not to the one under the pointer, so it behaves like a key rather than like a click.

In the simulator, in Studio and over the remote desktop it needs nothing. On a board a USB mouse has to be named in /etc/hid_devices.toml before its wheel does anything — plug the mouse in and the log prints the line to add.

docs.title: Always
docs.text:
Key Effect Ctrl + Q Close the app in the foreground, including a fullscreen one Ctrl + Tab Switch between the desktop and the running apps Ctrl + , The same thing. A browser keeps Ctrl + Tab for its own tabs, so Studio needs this one; it works on the boards too Ctrl + Space Turn kana input on and off

These are handled before the event reaches any app, so they work even when a fullscreen app has the whole screen.

docs.title: On the desktop
docs.text:
With no app focused and no dialog open, a single letter starts an app:

Key Starts L Launcher S Shell E Editor N NSF player I HID Inspector — see HID Device Config

That list is the [[shortcuts]] section of /etc/system_conf.toml. Add your own by naming the app's path. The Shortcuts entry in the system menu shows the list a machine actually has, read from its own configuration.

The menu bar answers to the keyboard too:

Key Effect F10 Open the system menu with the first entry picked ↑ ↓ Home End Move the selection. It wraps at both ends Enter Run the entry Esc or F10 Close the menu

The highlight is the same one the mouse moves, so the two ways of driving the menu cannot disagree about what is selected.

docs.title: Switching between apps
docs.text: Ctrl + Tab does one of two things, depending on what is in front.

docs.title: Windowed apps: cycle
docs.text:
It moves round-robin through the desktop and the running apps — the desktop first, then the apps in the order they started. Whatever it lands on comes to the front and takes the keyboard, so you can Ctrl + Tab from the editor to your app, type into it, and Ctrl + Tab back to keep editing.

The desktop is a stop on that ring because its menu bar and its letter shortcuts only answer while it holds the keyboard. Without it, starting one app meant the menu could only be reached with the mouse. While a fullscreen app is up the desktop is suspended and drops out of the ring.

docs.title: A fullscreen app: park it
docs.text:
Pressing Ctrl + Tab inside a fullscreen app parks it: the app freezes where it is, its canvas is hidden, and the desktop comes back. Its state and canvas are kept, so cycling round to it again — or clicking its taskbar square — restores the screen it had, without a redraw and without losing your place.

An app has to opt in

Only an app that declares fullscreen_switchable = 1 in its .app.toml can be parked. Others ignore Ctrl + Tab while fullscreen.

The declaration means "it is fine to freeze me mid-run". An app that leaves the sound chip playing should not declare it: frozen or not, the sound keeps going.

The bundled presentation tool, PicoRabbit, declares it — so you can leave a slide, go do something else, and come back to the same slide.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Modern (M5Stack Tab5) / Setup (Retro)
  • Default Apps — what is in the launcher
  • System Configuration — what Config writes, and everything it does not offer
  • App Config (.app.toml) — how your app declares its window
  • Connecting to Wi-Fi

docs.title: Firmware Update
docs.text:
Firmware is written from your browser. Nothing to install.

Installer: https://family-mruby.github.io/family-mruby-installer/

What a version changed, and whether it needs both chips, is in Release Notes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Item What works Browser Chrome, Edge or Opera (desktop). Firefox and Safari have no Web Serial and cannot flash USB cable Must carry data. Charge-only cables never appear in the port dialog

docs.title: How many chips you are flashing
docs.text:
This differs between the two machines, and it is the thing people get wrong.

Machine Chips to flash Buttons in the installer Modern (M5Stack Tab5) One — the ESP32-P4 Connect & Flash Tab5 firmware Retro (narya-board) Two — the ESP32-S3 and the ESP32-WROVER, separately Connect & Flash fmruby-core, Connect & Flash fmruby-graphics-audio

The installer checks the chip family before writing (ESP32-P4 / ESP32-S3 / ESP32), so pressing the wrong button gives you an error, not a broken device.

Flashing replaces the files on the device

The image includes the flash filesystem. Your own apps and any config files you edited on the device are replaced by the shipped contents. Copy anything you want to keep off the device first — see Console.

docs.title: Modern (M5Stack Tab5)
docs.text:
1. Open the installer
  2. Connect the Tab5 to your PC with a USB-C data cable
  3. Go to the Family mruby Modern (Tab5) section
  4. Choose a version (newest is preselected)
  5. Press Connect & Flash Tab5 firmware and pick the port
  6. Wait for it to finish, then let the device restart

The Tab5 connects over USB-Serial-JTAG, so no button has to be held to enter download mode. If the device sits in download mode after flashing — the serial log shows waiting for download — press reset once.

docs.title: Retro (narya-board)
docs.text:
The board has two MCUs and they are flashed independently, through different USB-C ports on the board:

  • The ESP32-S3 side port flashes fmruby-core

  • The ESP32-WROVER side port flashes fmruby-graphics-audio

  • Open the installer

  • Connect a USB-C data cable to the port for the chip you are flashing
  • Go to the Family mruby Retro section and choose a version
  • Press the matching button, then pick the port in the browser dialog
  • Repeat for the other chip, from the other port

Keep the two versions the same

Flash both chips with the same version. A new fmruby-core against an old fmruby-graphics-audio will not boot correctly — the link protocol between them has to match.

2.1.0 changes the link protocol

Coming from 2.0.x, fmruby-graphics-audio has to be flashed as well. Writing only fmruby-core leaves the two chips on different protocol versions, and the machine does not come up.

docs.title: The browser does not show a serial port
docs.text:
• The cable must carry data. Charge-only USB-C cables are never offered
  • Use a USB-certified cable, as short as is practical
  • Connect straight to the PC, not through a hub
  • Try another USB port
  • Check that your OS has the USB-serial driver for the chip (recent OSes ship it)

docs.title: Flashing stops part way
docs.text:
• Check the cable and the connection. Insufficient power or a loose contact is the usual cause
  • Press the button again and reselect the port
  • If it keeps failing, try another PC or another browser

docs.title: Nothing on screen after flashing
docs.text:
Modern: press reset once. If the log shows boot:0x204 (DOWNLOAD...) and waiting for download, the board stayed in download mode — reset is all it needs.

Retro: check that both chips are on the same version. An old fmruby-core with a new fmruby-graphics-audio (or the reverse) fails to boot. Flash both with the same release.

docs.title: Hello World
docs.text:
Run a minimal GUI app that displays "Hello, mruby!" on screen, and learn the workflow for writing your own apps.

This page covers a GUI app example

Family mruby apps fall into two main categories: GUI apps that draw to the screen, and headless apps that run in the background without a display. This page walks through a minimal GUI app. A headless app declares default_window_mode = "background" in its .app.toml; its @gfx is nil.

docs.title: Minimal app structure
docs.text:
A Family mruby app consists of a pair of 2 files.

hello.app.rb       # App body (Ruby)
hello.app.toml     # Configuration file

Place both files under /app/<directory-of-your-choice>/, then rescan from the launcher (described below) or restart the board, and the app icon will appear.

docs.title: Step 1: A minimal app that just displays text
docs.text:
Let's write an app that simply draws "Hello, Family mruby!" on the screen.

This sample does not allow closing the window

@gfx.clear fills the entire canvas including the title bar. The title bar and close button drawn by the FmrbApp base class at startup are overwritten and disappear, so the close button is no longer visible on screen. To exit, reset the board once. The next sample adds window frame drawing.

Create /app/usr/hello.app.rb and implement the code below.

You can write the code in the default app editor or via the web console. See Console for details on the console.

docs.title: /app/usr/hello.app.rb file
docs.text:
class HelloApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    @gfx.clear(FmrbGfx::BLACK)
    @gfx.draw_text(0, 0, "Hello, Family mruby!", FmrbGfx::WHITE)
    @gfx.present
  end
end

Code explanation

Code Role class HelloApp < FmrbApp App class that inherits from FmrbApp on_create Initialization called once at startup @gfx.clear(...) Fills the entire canvas with black @gfx.draw_text(0, 0, ...) Draws text at (0, 0), the top-left of the app's area (just inside the window frame) @gfx.present Flushes the buffer to the screen (required)

There is no HelloApp.new.start at the end: once the file has been read, the runtime makes the FmrbApp subclass it defines and starts it. If something goes wrong (no subclass, an exception while starting), an error window says why.

docs.title: hello.app.toml file
docs.text:
Create hello.app.toml in the same directory:

app_handle_name = "hello"
app_screen_name = "Hello"
default_window_mode = "window"
default_window_width = 160
default_window_height = 60
default_window_pos_x = 30
default_window_pos_y = 40
Key Purpose app_handle_name Internal handle name (should match the base name of the .rb file) app_screen_name Display name shown in the launcher and title bar default_window_mode "window" / "fullscreen" default_window_width/height Window size (px) default_window_pos_x/y Top-left coordinates of the window

The same keys can instead go in a #---fmrb comment at the top of the .rb, so a one-file app needs no .app.toml. See App configuration file (.app.toml) for a full list of keys.

docs.title: Launching and displaying on screen
docs.text:
1. Once the implementation is done, open the launcher and right-click to rescan (or restart the board)
  2. The title bar shows "Rescanning..." — wait 1-2 seconds and the new "Hello" app icon will appear
  3. Double-click the icon (or click with the mouse then press Enter)
  4. "Hello, Family mruby!" is displayed on screen

docs.title: Step 2: Displaying the window frame
docs.text:
In Step 1 we only drew text. To keep the title bar and close button, fill only the app's drawable area (the user area) instead of the entire canvas. clear_user_area does that, and puts the frame back as it goes.

Update the code as follows.

class HelloApp < FmrbApp
  def on_create
    redraw
  end

  def redraw
    clear_user_area                    # Fill the user area with the theme's page colour
    @gfx.draw_text(4, 4, "Hello, Family mruby!", theme_fg)
    @gfx.present                       # Flush to screen
  end
end
Point Description @gfx.clear(FmrbGfx::BLACK) to clear_user_area Clears the area inside the frame and redraws the frame. With no colour it uses the system theme's page colour theme_fg instead of a fixed colour The ink that goes with the theme, so the app follows the user's colours Drawing logic extracted into redraw Organized for easier redraws later

Where is (0, 0)?

@gfx and mouse events measure from the top-left of the area the app owns: inside the frame here, the screen's top-left in fullscreen. Its size is @user_area_width × @user_area_height. See FmrbApp > What the app can read for details.

Restart and run the app — the title bar and window frame will be drawn, and you should be able to close the app by clicking the button at the top right.

docs.title: Reloading a running app after edits
docs.text: After editing the code, right-click the title bar of the running app and choose Reload from the window menu. It saves you the trouble of closing and reopening the app.

docs.title: Shortcut: Generate a template with create_app
docs.text: Writing .rb and .toml files from scratch every time is tedious. The Family mruby shell has a create_app command that generates a complete set of template files based on Step 2 in one shot.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Launch Shell from the launcher and run:

> create_app my_clock
Created: /app/usr/my_clock.app.rb
Created: /app/usr/my_clock.app.toml
Tip: edit it with `edit /app/usr/my_clock.app.rb`

This automatically creates the following files, which you can use as a template.

  • /app/usr/my_clock.app.rb — Based on Step 2 (includes clear_user_area, with templates for all on_* lifecycle methods)
  • /app/usr/my_clock.app.toml — Standard-sized window configuration

docs.title: Reflecting changes in the launcher
docs.text: The launcher scans and fixes the app list at startup, so newly added files do not appear automatically. To trigger a rescan, right-click inside the launcher window. A restart also updates the list.

docs.title: App file naming conventions
docs.text:
The argument to the create_app command must contain only lowercase alphanumeric characters and underscores, starting with a letter. Examples:

Input Generated class name Display name hello HelloApp Hello my_clock MyClockApp My Clock snake01 Snake01App Snake01

The class name is generated by converting snake_case to CamelCase with an App suffix, and the display name (app_screen_name) is generated in Title Case.

docs.title: Destination directory
docs.text: Templates are placed in /app/usr/ (created automatically).

docs.title: Customizing the template
docs.text:
The template files themselves are located in /usr/share/template/:

/usr/share/template/app.rb.template
/usr/share/template/app.toml.template

Editing these files directly lets you customize the output of subsequent create_app calls to your preference.

Placeholder Meaning {{name}} Name in snake_case {{class}} Class name in CamelCase (with App suffix) {{title}} Display name in Title Case

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Try drawing shapes: FmrbGfx
  • Add event handling: FmrbApp > Event handling
  • Read existing samples: Default Apps

docs.title: Icon does not appear in the launcher
docs.text:
• Did you right-click in the launcher to rescan? (see Reflecting changes in the launcher)
  • Is the .toml file in the same directory as the .rb file?
  • Is app_screen_name specified in the .toml?
  • Have you set launcher_visible = false?
  • Is the file located under /app/<dir>/?

docs.title: App starts but closes immediately
docs.text:
• It may be crashing due to an exception. Check the logs:
    • Add Log.info in on_create to verify progress

docs.title: Nothing appears on screen
docs.text:
• Check that @gfx.present is being called
  • Check that drawing coordinates are within 0..@user_area_width and 0..@user_area_height

docs.title: An error window says the app could not start
docs.text:
• The file must define a subclass of FmrbApp. With more than one, name the one to start with class = "..." in the .app.toml
  • The error window closes with a click, or with Return or Esc; while it is up it holds the keyboard, so the keys do not reach the app behind it (development version)

docs.title: The Linux Program
docs.text:
Family mruby also runs as one ordinary program on a Linux PC. It is the same system as on the boards — the desktop, the editor, the shell, the bundled apps, the Ruby API — with Modern's screen scaled up to fill the display. Picked at the login screen, it is the desktop: the PC's own applications (a terminal, a browser) open as Family mruby windows beside your apps.

Items marked (development version) are on the development branch and in neither 3.0.0 nor its packages yet; they come with the next release.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
The package is a .deb attached to each release on GitHub.

Package For Status amd64 A PC with Ubuntu 26.04 or newer (or a distribution with the same wlroots 0.19) Attached to 3.0.0 arm64 Small arm64 Linux machines that use M5Stack's APPLaunch launcher (the Cardputer Zero), with an entry for the built-in screen and one for HDMI (development version). Built, not yet checked on that hardware

Install it with apt, which pulls in the libraries it needs:

sudo apt install ./family-mruby_<version>_amd64.deb

apt also offers a few recommended packages. They are optional; without one, only its feature is missing:

Package What it adds xwayland X11 applications (Wayland ones run without it) swaylock Lock in the power menu, and locking on suspend or lid close xdg-desktop-portal-wlr Sharing or recording the screen from a browser's video call fcitx5, fcitx5-mozc (suggested) Japanese kana–kanji input for Linux applications and Family mruby apps alike. Without them Family mruby's own kana input is used

docs.title: What it installs and how it runs
docs.text:
Path What it is /usr/bin/family-mruby The program /usr/bin/family-mruby-session The login-screen session: starts the program and watches it /usr/share/wayland-sessions/family-mruby.desktop The Family mruby entry at the login screen /usr/share/family-mruby/root/ The system's files (/app, /usr, /etc as shipped, the machine definitions), read-only

In the login-screen session the program is its own Wayland compositor: it takes the screen, keyboard, touchpad and mouse itself, draws the Family mruby screen at a whole-number scale, and lays the Linux applications' windows over it at the display's full resolution. Each Linux window gets a Family mruby title bar, frame and close button, and stacks, moves and resizes with the other windows. Family mruby's sound goes through PipeWire or PulseAudio.

If the program crashes, the session starts it again and says so in a notice; after the fourth crash within a minute it gives up and the login screen comes back. The session's own log is ~/.local/state/family-mruby/session.log.

docs.title: First start
docs.text:
1. Log out. At the login screen, choose the Family mruby session (in the session menu of the display manager) and log in.
  2. The Family mruby desktop comes up, in English. Change the language, the timezone and the rest under Config in the system menu, as on a board.
  3. The keyboard layout follows Linux's (keyboard_layout = "auto").

To try it without leaving your usual desktop, run it in a terminal instead:

family-mruby                         # in a window (the sdl machine definition)
family-mruby --machine linux_pc_wl   # as a compositor nested in the current desktop

docs.title: Machine definitions
docs.text:
How the program runs — which screen, input and sound to use, the screen size, the kind of desktop — is chosen by a machine definition, a small TOML file. The packaged ones are in /usr/share/family-mruby/root/machines/:

Name What it is sdl A window on an existing desktop. The default when no --machine is given linux_pc_wl The program as the Wayland compositor. What the login-screen session uses linux_pc An older way of being the session: one fullscreen window inside the cage compositor linux_pc_drm Straight on the display hardware (DRM/KMS) from a text console, no compositor cardputer_zero, cardputer_zero_hdmi The arm64 package's two launchers (the 320x170 built-in screen with a keyboard-only desktop, and HDMI)

--machine takes a name or a path to your own file, and --set key=value changes one field (--set display.rotate=90). A definition whose screen, input or sound cannot be opened is refused with the reason (exit code 3) rather than quietly falling back to something else.

docs.title: The login-screen session
docs.text:
The session reads /etc/default/family-mruby-session (a shell fragment; create it as root if it is not there):

ROTATE=90                     # 0, 90, 180 or 270: turn a display mounted sideways
FMRB_ARGS="--set display.look=crt"   # more arguments for the program

In a virtual machine the session draws without the GPU (WLR_RENDERER=pixman) and draws the pointer itself, because a virtual display adapter rarely gives the compositor a GPU it can use. Setting WLR_RENDERER=gles2 in the file tries the GPU anyway.

docs.title: The CRT look (development version)
docs.text: The whole screen — Linux windows included — can be drawn as a CRT, with scanlines, a shadow mask, glow, curvature and a vignette, plus NTSC colour bleed, flicker and noise. It needs the GPU. Open Display... from the system menu: switch between Sharp and CRT, set each effect from 0 to 100, or press Standard or Strong for a ready-made set. The choice applies at once and is kept in /etc/system_conf.toml ([crt]), where it wins over FMRB_ARGS.

docs.title: The power menu
docs.text:
The button at the right end of the menu bar holds what the PC offers, each asking before it acts:

Entry What it does Lock Locks the screen (needs swaylock; it asks for your Linux password) Suspend Suspends the PC Log Out Ends the session and returns to the login screen. Linux applications started inside are asked to close first, and ended if they are still there after a few seconds. The name is (development version): 3.0.0 calls the same entry Exit Restart Restarts the PC Power off Shuts the PC down

In the sdl window the menu has only Exit, which ends the program.

docs.title: Linux applications in the launcher
docs.text:
The launcher has a Linux section (the penguin) listing the applications installed on the PC — what their .desktop files in /usr/share/applications and ~/.local/share/applications describe. Open the section, double-click an application, and .. goes back. Its right-click menu puts an application on the desktop, like a Family mruby app. X11 applications start Xwayland the first time one is opened.

Window keys on the PC:

Key or action Effect Double-click a title bar Maximize, or restore Super + arrows Lay the window out: left or right half, maximize, restore Ctrl + Tab, Ctrl + , Always go to Family mruby, even when a Linux window has the keyboard

docs.title: Opening files with Linux applications
docs.text: The File Manager opens what Family mruby can open as it always does; any other kind of file goes to Linux's default application for it. Right-click a file for Open in Linux app, which lists the applications that take that type. The file associations table can name a Linux application as the target, too.

docs.title: Linux commands in the Shell
docs.text:
A line starting with ! runs as a Linux command, in the Linux directory that matches the Shell's current one (/mnt/host/src is ~/src):

> !git status
> !ls -l
> !

! alone opens the Linux shell (bash, or sh) inside the Shell; exit or Ctrl + D comes back. Ctrl + C stops the running command and Ctrl + Shift + V pastes into it. Output colours are shown; full-screen programs such as vim or top are not supported. See Shell Commands.

docs.title: Where your files are
docs.text:
Family mruby sees one filesystem, as on a board, but each top-level place is kept somewhere on the PC:

Inside Family mruby On the PC /home, /etc, /app/usr ~/.local/share/family-mruby/ (home/, etc/, app/usr/) — yours, kept across updates /tmp, /var, /cache, /data ~/.cache/family-mruby/ — can be deleted; it is rebuilt /app, /usr, /lib, /help … /usr/share/family-mruby/root/ — read-only; replaced by a package update /mnt/host Your Linux home directory, read and write /mnt/root Linux's /, read-only

/etc is copied from the system's on the first start. After an update, settings that are new in the package are added to it, and nothing you set is changed. Unlike a board, flashing a new release does not wipe /home: installing a newer .deb leaves it as it is.

docs.title: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, sound and notifications
docs.text:
Where NetworkManager and BlueZ are running (as on a usual Ubuntu desktop), Family mruby's settings window drives them:

  • Wi-Fi — the Network dialog's Wi-Fi... opens it: the networks in reach, Connect and Disconnect. A password goes to NetworkManager, which keeps it as its own tools do.
  • Bluetooth — from the system menu: turn the adapter on or off, connect and disconnect devices paired before. Pairing a new device is done in Linux's own tool.
  • Volume — the menu bar's speaker and Config's volume move the PC's output volume (PipeWire or PulseAudio), and so do the volume keys.
  • Notifications from Linux applications show at the top right.

Without NetworkManager or BlueZ the network status still shows, and those pages are not there.

docs.title: Asterism
docs.text: The package has no router set. Put the router in /home/asterism/config.toml as on a board (see Network). A router with TLS (tls/...) and the credentials .tar from the console work from the PC too (development version).

docs.title: Touchpad and touch screen (development version)
docs.text: In the compositor session a tap on the touchpad clicks (one finger left, two right; tap and drag to drag), two-finger scrolling scrolls by wheel steps, and a touch screen clicks and drags where it is touched, rotated with ROTATE. In 3.0.0 the touchpad clicks only when pressed down, and touch screens are not taken.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Screen. Family mruby's own screen is the display's resolution divided by two (1280x800 gives 640x400); a portrait or small display gets 426x240. Scaling is by whole numbers only, with black around. A fullscreen app shows Modern's 426x240 (or 640x360 for a high-resolution app) at the largest whole scale. One display only.
  • Linux windows cannot go fullscreen on their own; maximize is the largest they get.
  • Shell's ! handles lines and colours only (TERM=dumb).
  • No SD card. /mnt/sd and /sd do not exist; use /mnt/host.
  • No hardware pins. GPIO, I2C, the GROVE port and the boards' sensors are not there.
  • Retro (the two-chip machine) is not available as a Linux program; the simulator covers it.
  • Security. Every Family mruby app may start Linux programs, run Linux commands and read and write your home directory through /mnt/host — with your Linux user's rights. Any Wayland application in the session can capture the screen and type into the focused window, as under X11. The remote debugger is off in the package; when turned on (debugd = true in /etc/system_conf.toml) it listens on 127.0.0.1 only. See also Limitations.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Choose your hardware
  • Shell Commands
  • The Desktop
  • Release Notes

docs.title: Modern (M5Stack Tab5)
docs.text: From an unmodified M5Stack Tab5 to the Family mruby desktop. Nothing to solder, nothing to build — flashing happens from your browser and takes a couple of minutes.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• An M5Stack Tab5
  • A USB Type-C cable that carries data (a charge-only cable will not be seen by the browser)
  • A PC with Chrome, Edge or Opera — flashing uses Web Serial, which Firefox and Safari do not implement

That is the whole list. The Tab5 has the screen, the speaker and the battery built in.

docs.title: To actually type
docs.text:
You need a keyboard, and there are two ways to get one:

  • A USB keyboard in the Tab5's USB-A port, plus a USB hub if you want a mouse as well. Not every keyboard or hub is recognised — check Verified Peripherals, and expect to try a couple.
  • The M5Stack Tab5 Keyboard accessory, which clips onto the body and needs no USB port.

You do not need a mouse: the touch screen works as a trackpad (see Using touch below). A real mouse is still more comfortable for dragging windows.

A wireless keyboard-and-mouse combo works too: one receiver in the USB-A port, no hub

docs.title: Nice to have
docs.text:
• A Wi-Fi network. With Wi-Fi configured you get the remote desktop — your PC's browser shows the Tab5's screen and drives it with your PC's keyboard and mouse — and apps can reach the internet.
  • A GROVE cable if you want to talk to sensors, or send MIDI to an external sound module.

docs.title: Flashing the firmware
docs.text:
Modern is a single chip, so there is a single firmware to write.

  1. Open the Family mruby Web Installer in Chrome, Edge or Opera
  2. Connect the Tab5 to your PC with a USB-C cable
  3. Scroll to the Family mruby Modern (Tab5) section
  4. Pick the version you want (the newest is selected by default)
  5. Press Connect & Flash Tab5 firmware
  6. Choose the Tab5's serial port in the dialog the browser opens
  7. Wait. The installer checks the chip is an ESP32-P4 and refuses if it is not, so you cannot flash the wrong image by mistake

The Tab5 talks to your PC over USB-Serial-JTAG, which means you do not have to hold any button to put it into download mode — unlike many ESP32 boards. If flashing ever leaves it stuck, press the reset button once and try again.

This erases the flash filesystem

Flashing writes the whole image, including the file area. Anything you wrote on the device — your own apps, edited config files — is replaced by the shipped contents. Copy anything you care about off the device first (see Console).

More detail, including the Retro procedure and troubleshooting, is in Firmware Update.

docs.title: First boot
docs.text:
Press the power button. You will see, in order:

  1. A text boot screen listing what the system is bringing up — memory, filesystem, drivers. It is there so a failed boot tells you where it stopped
  2. The logo, opening from the centre, with the startup sound
  3. The desktop: a menu bar along the top, the wallpaper below it, and a mouse cursor
The boot screen. If a boot fails, this is where it stops

If you reach the desktop and the cursor follows your finger, everything works.

docs.title: Finding your way around
docs.text:
Click Family mruby at the top left for the system menu — Launcher, File Manager, Log Viewer, Monitor, Set Clock, Config, Storage, Network, About and Reset. The right end of the bar carries free internal memory, the BLE and Wi-Fi indicators, and the clock, and the squares next to the title are the apps you have running.

Ctrl + Q closes the app in front, Ctrl + Tab switches between them, and on the desktop a single letter starts one (L launcher, S shell, E editor).

The desktop is identical on both machines and is described in full in The Desktop — what every element of the menu bar means, how the launcher behaves, and what Ctrl + Tab does to a fullscreen app.

docs.title: Using touch
docs.text:
The touch panel behaves like a laptop trackpad, not like a phone. Your finger moves the cursor; it does not teleport the cursor to where you touched. This keeps dragging window title bars and scrollbars predictable.

Gesture Result Slide a finger Move the cursor. No click, so nothing under the cursor gets grabbed Quick tap Left click at the cursor position Hold still, then move Press and hold the left button, then drag. Lift to release Two-finger tap Right click at the cursor position

The hold that starts a drag is 150 ms, so an ordinary tap (about 100 ms) still reads as a click.

Pointer speed is adjustable: Config → mouse_scale_x / mouse_scale_y.

docs.title: Connecting to Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Wi-Fi gets you the remote desktop and the networking API. Credentials go in /etc/wifi.toml, which you create once on the device with the editor:

[wifi]
enable = true
ssid = "your-ssid"
password = "your-password"
hostname = "fmruby"

Save it, reboot from Reset, then check the system menu → Network.

Full instructions, and what to do when it will not connect, are in Connecting to Wi-Fi.

Both radios at once

On Modern the ESP32-C6 handles Wi-Fi and BLE together, so the web console over BLE keeps working while Wi-Fi is up. (On Retro the ESP32-S3 has one radio and runs one or the other.)

docs.title: Seeing the screen on your PC
docs.text:
With Wi-Fi up, the Tab5 serves its own desktop. Open

http://fmruby.local/

in a browser on the same network — or the address shown in the Network dialog, if mDNS does not resolve on your machine. You get the live screen, and your PC's keyboard and mouse drive the device, global shortcuts included.

This is the fastest way to work: type on your PC's keyboard, watch the real hardware run. See Remote Desktop for the details and the settings.

docs.title: Where your files go
docs.text:
The flash filesystem follows the usual Unix shape:

Path Contents /home Your files. Put your own .rb scripts here /app Installed apps, grouped into demo, game, tool, basic and so on /etc Configuration: system_conf.toml, wifi.toml /usr/share Bundled assets: fonts, wallpapers, sounds, MIDI and NSF songs /lib Ruby libraries reachable with require /var/cache Caches the system rebuilds on its own

docs.title: The browser does not offer a serial port
docs.text:
• Use a data-capable USB-C cable. Charge-only cables never appear
  • Connect straight to the PC, not through a hub
  • Chrome, Edge or Opera on the desktop. Firefox and Safari have no Web Serial

docs.title: Flashing finished but the screen stays dark
docs.text:
• Press the reset button once
  • If the serial log shows boot:0x204 (DOWNLOAD) and waiting for download, the board stayed in download mode. Press reset and it will boot normally

docs.title: The keyboard does nothing
docs.text:
• Check the keyboard is in the USB-A port, not the USB-C one
  • Some keyboards and hubs are not recognised; see Verified Devices
  • If the layout is wrong (symbols land in the wrong places), set Config → keyboard_layout to jp or us

docs.title: The clock is wrong
docs.text: Set the date and time from Set Clock in the system menu. The timezone is a separate setting, under Config.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Hello World — write and run your first app
  • Default Apps — what is already installed
  • Remote Desktop — work from your PC's browser
  • API Reference — what your app can call
  • Hardware — pin assignments and the GROVE port

docs.title: Setup (Retro)
docs.text: Getting the first screen out of the narya-board. If you have an M5Stack Tab5 instead, go to Modern (M5Stack Tab5); if you are not sure which machine this is, see Choose your hardware.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• USB Type-C cable (for power supply)
    • A standard cable used for smartphones, etc. will work fine
  • 5V USB power source
    • A PC USB port or a USB-AC adapter (5V 1A or higher)
  • NTSC-compatible display device
    • CRT monitor, video capture device, LCD with composite input, etc.
    • If you want to display on an HDMI-compatible monitor, you can use a converter device such as the following:
    • Amazon
  • RCA composite video cable (cable with yellow connector)
    • Shorter cables tend to produce more stable video
  • 3.5mm stereo mini-jack cable (for audio output)
    • For connecting to earphones or speakers
    • If you use a cable that converts to red/white RCA plugs and connect it to the HDMI converter device, you can route audio over HDMI as well.
  • USB keyboard
    • For confirmed working devices, see Verified Devices. Some keyboards may not be recognized due to compatibility issues.
  • USB mouse
    • For confirmed working devices, see Verified Devices. Some mice may not be recognized due to compatibility issues.

docs.title: Nice to Have
docs.text:
• USB Hub
    • Required if the keyboard and mouse are not an integrated unit.
    • For confirmed working devices, see Verified Devices. Some hubs may not be recognized due to compatibility issues.
  • SD card
    • For when you need to handle large data
  • USB gamepad
    • Plugs into the USB-A port like any other HID device. Apps receive :gamepad_down / :gamepad_up / :gamepad_axis events with a button or axis number; the numbers are the GP_* constants in Constants & System Info.
    • The bundled Raycaster game reads one, so it is the quickest way to check yours works.

docs.title: If You Want to Retain the Clock
docs.text:
• CR2032 button cell battery case & CR2032 button cell battery
    • By soldering a battery case and supplying power to the RTC, the device can retain the time even when the main power is turned off.

docs.title: If You Want to Supply Power from GROVE2
docs.text:
• Jumper pin
    • By soldering a pin header to the GROVE2 power selection area and attaching a jumper pin, you can output either 5V or 3.3V power.
    • Example product at Akizuki Denshi

docs.title: Connecting the Ports
docs.text: Referring to the diagram, connect cables to the Video and Audio ports, then connect the USB cable to the USB power source.

docs.title: Powering On
docs.text:
The device starts automatically when the USB Type-C cable is connected. There is no power switch.

To turn off the power, unplug the USB Type-C cable.

docs.title: Screen Displayed After Startup
docs.text:
After the logo is displayed, the following desktop screen will appear. If you can operate the mouse cursor, everything is working correctly.

A startup sound also plays while the logo is being displayed.

docs.title: Check the LED Status
docs.text:
LED State Meaning STATUS (green) Fast blinking Booting STATUS (green) Slow blinking every few seconds Running normally STATUS (green) Off or stays lit Possible hang-up ERROR (red) Lit System state error POWER Lit Power is connected USB-POWER Lit USB host power is supplied

If the POWER LED does not light up, the power supply is not connected. Please check the power source.

docs.title: Keyboard or Mouse Not Responding
docs.text: • If possible, try a different keyboard, try connecting without going through a USB hub, etc. Please restart the device after swapping peripherals.

docs.title: Keys that always work
docs.text:
Key Effect Ctrl + Q Close the app in the foreground, even a fullscreen one Ctrl + Tab Switch between running apps

On the desktop itself a single letter starts an app: L launcher, S shell, E editor.

The menu bar, the launcher and the rest of the desktop work the same on both machines and are described in The Desktop.

docs.title: Connecting to Wi-Fi
docs.text: Retro has Wi-Fi as well — see Connecting to Wi-Fi. Note that the ESP32-S3 has a single radio, so Wi-Fi and BLE cannot both be running; that page explains how to choose.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Try out the pre-installed apps
  • Write your own app → Hello World
  • Transfer apps and files from a PC → Console
  • Hardware specifications → Hardware

docs.title: Shell Commands
docs.text:
The Shell is Family mruby's command line. Open it from the launcher, the desktop icon, or by pressing S on the desktop; help lists the commands on the machine you are using.

Commands marked (development version) are on the development branch (and in Studio) but not in 3.0.0.

docs.title: Using the Shell
docs.text:
Key Effect Tab Completes a file or directory name ↑ / ↓ Earlier and later lines PgUp / PgDn, mouse wheel Scroll back through the output Ctrl + C Stops the script running in the Shell Ctrl + V Pastes the clipboard into the line

Paths are relative to the current directory unless they start with /. There is no quoting: an argument ends at a space.

docs.title: Files and directories
docs.text: Command What it does Example cd [path] Changes the current directory (cd alone goes to /) cd /home pwd Prints the current directory pwd ls [path] Lists a directory ls /app/demo cat <file> Prints a file cat /etc/system_conf.toml less <file> Shows a file a page at a time (Space / b page, q quits) less /usr/share/doc/kanji.md mkdir <dir> Makes a directory mkdir /home/games rm <path...> Removes files, and empty directories rm old.rb notes.txt cp <src> <dst> Copies a file cp hello.rb /home/backup.rb mv <src> <dst> Moves or renames a file mv draft.rb final.rb

docs.title: Writing and running code
docs.text: Command What it does Example edit [-f] <file> Opens a file in the editor, creating it if it does not exist. -f opens it fullscreen edit -f /home/hello.rb create_app <name> Writes a ready-to-edit app, /app/usr/<name>.app.rb and .app.toml (see Hello World) create_app my_clock run <script> [args] [&] Runs a script. An app starts as an app; a plain .rb runs here and prints into the Shell. & runs it in the background as a job run /home/fib.rb 20 run <script> > <file> Writes the script's output to a file (>> appends, < feeds a file to it) run report.rb > /home/out.txt open <file> Opens a file with the app its type is associated with (File Associations) open /usr/share/samples/slides/demo.md irb Interactive Ruby. $shell is this Shell app irb

docs.title: Apps, jobs and services
docs.text: Command What it does Example ps Lists the running tasks (PID, type, engine, state, name), background jobs and services. The ENGINE column says what runs each app: mruby, lua, basic, python, wasm or native (ENGINE is in the development version) ps kill <pid> Ends a user app, by its PID from ps kill 12 kill <service> Stops a service for this session kill hourly_chime kill_job <id> Stops a background job, by its JOB id from ps kill_job 1 svc list Lists the background services svc list svc start / svc stop <name> Starts or stops a service for this session svc start timesync svc enable / svc disable <name> The same, and remembered across boots svc disable hourly_chime

docs.title: Moving apps and files between machines
docs.text:
These work with apps written to be moved (movable = true; see Moving a running app) and over Asterism. A machine is named by its Asterism node ID, which anodes shows.

Command What it does Example checkpoint [-r] <pid> Writes an app to an image, /tmp/<name>.ckpt, and closes it. -r starts it again at once checkpoint -r 14 restore <image> Starts an app from its image restore /tmp/counter.ckpt amove <pid\|name> <node> Moves a running app to another machine. The name is the one ps shows. 3.0.0 has this as move <pid> <node> (development version) amove Counter fmruby-aaaaaa anodes [list] The machines on Asterism now, with their names; this one is marked (development version) anodes anodes info <node> One machine: its profile, its apps and their status, and whether it takes files and apps (development version) anodes info fmruby-aaaaaa asend <node> <file> [-o] [-s] Sends a file to another machine's /home/inbox/. -o overwrites a file of the same name there (otherwise it gets a name of its own); -s (or --sd) puts it on that machine's SD card, in /sd/inbox/ (development version) asend fmruby-aaaaaa /home/hello.rb asend -c Stops the file being sent (development version) asend -c asend -l Who may send files to this machine (development version) asend -l asend on\|off Keeps this machine on the network for sending, so the window menu's Send to lists the machines at once; asend alone says whether it is on. asend and amove work without it (development version) asend on areceive Whether this machine receives files and apps, and from whom (development version) areceive areceive on\|off Starts or stops receiving (development version) areceive on areceive allow\|deny <file\|checkpoint> <node> Lets a machine send files (file) or move apps (checkpoint) here, or takes that back. * stands for everyone on the network (development version) areceive allow file fmruby-aaaaaa

Moving an app works between machines on the same version.

docs.title: Who may send: receive.toml
docs.text:
A machine takes nothing until it is told to. Who may send is kept in /home/asterism/receive.toml; while that file does not exist, the system's copy, /etc/asterism/receive.toml, is read, which receives nothing. The first change from areceive or the Receiving app (in /app/tool) writes the /home file, starting from the /etc one:

enabled = true          # receive at all; off (or no line) takes nothing, whatever the lists say
send_enabled = false    # keep this machine on the network for Send to

[file]                  # who may put files in /home/inbox (and /sd/inbox)
from = ["fmruby-aaaaaa", "fmruby-*"]

[checkpoint]            # who may move apps here
from = ["*"]            # "*": everyone on the network

A list holds node IDs and patterns (fmruby-*). A router with access control must let the sender through as well. When the machine is a member of a console, a section the console writes into the same file adds the senders chosen there; areceive shows it but leaves it alone. Either switch on starts the transfer app at boot.

(development version) The enabled and send_enabled switches, the /etc copy, the [file] list and the Receiving app are new. 3.0.0 reads only /home/asterism/receive.toml, and only its [checkpoint] from list.

docs.title: Linux commands (the Linux program only)
docs.text:
In the Linux program a line starting with ! runs on Linux, in the Linux directory matching the current one (/mnt/host/src is ~/src). Elsewhere it answers that the machine has no Linux.

Command What it does Example !<command> Runs a Linux command; its output (with colours) comes into the Shell. Ctrl + C stops it !git status ! Opens the Linux shell; exit or Ctrl + D comes back ! Ctrl + Shift + V Pastes into the Linux command running

Full-screen programs such as vim and top are not supported (TERM=dumb).

docs.title: Other
docs.text: Command What it does Example color Shows the Shell's two colours color color bg\|text <colour> Sets the background or text colour, by name or number (0x1F). Kept in /home/colors.toml color bg navy color names / color reset Lists the colour names; goes back to the theme's colours color reset logo Draws the PicoRuby logo logo help Lists the commands help

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Default Apps
  • The Linux Program
  • Moving a running app

docs.title: Simulator
docs.text: This page has moved to Simulator, in the Tools section.

docs.title: Family mruby Studio
docs.text: The whole Family mruby machine, running in your browser. The firmware — FreeRTOS kernel, Ruby VM, desktop, editor and sound — is compiled to WebAssembly, so what boots here is the same OS the boards run, drawing the same pixels. Nothing to install, no board required.

docs.title: Starting
docs.text:
Open the following URL and click the screen — the click is the power switch, and it is also what lets the browser make sound, so you will hear the boot chord.

https://family-mruby.github.io/studio/

On your very first visit the page reloads itself once (it installs a small service worker that provides the isolation WebAssembly threads need). That is normal.

The same desktop, the same apps, in a browser tab

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A recent Chrome or Firefox on a PC with a keyboard
  • Safari is untested; phones and tablets are not supported (the machine wants a keyboard)

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Use the desktop: the top-left menu opens the launcher, the editor, the file manager and the rest; apps run side by side
  • Write and run Ruby in the editor, with Japanese input (Ctrl+Space toggles kana, typed as romaji)
  • Play the bundled apps and hear the internal sound chip
  • Install more from the App Store, which works here as it does on a board
  • Play a video: MJPEG runs in the page like it does on Modern
  • Run WebAssembly apps written in C, TinyGo, Rust or Zig, including your own: drop a folder holding <name>.app.wasm and <name>.app.toml on the page (from 3.1.0)
  • Pick a screen size up to 852x480 and a zoom — a larger screen means more room, not bigger pixels
  • Go full screen. Where the browser allows it the machine keeps Esc for itself; where it does not, Esc leaves full screen instead of reaching the app

Colours are not the page's to choose: pick a theme in Config, inside the machine, as you would on a board. The screen size is applied at boot, so changing it reloads the page.

A link can also start one app: add ?app=/app/game/blockgame.app.rb to the URL and it opens once, on that visit.

docs.title: Your files
docs.text:
What you write is kept. /home — the programs you save, your colours, your service list — and /app/usr, where installed apps live, stay in this browser between visits, and so do your settings. None of it goes anywhere else: it never leaves the machine you are reading this on.

Everything outside those two is built fresh every time. Files written anywhere else, and /tmp above all, are gone on the next reload. If you open the page twice, only the first tab saves.

The panel under the screen is how files come and go:

What it does Add — Files… / Folder… Copies them into the directory chosen beside the buttons: /home/inbox, any directory you have already made under /home, or /app/usr. Dropping them anywhere on the page does the same thing Work folder — Link a folder… Follows a folder on your disk: what you change out there arrives in the machine, and Send my work back writes the machine's copy out to it. Where the browser offers it, which today means Chrome and the browsers built on it Backup — Download Saves all of it, settings included, as one .tar Backup — Restore Puts that file back, here or in another browser Backup — Erase Clears both stores and puts every setting back to its default

Downloading is worth doing for anything you care about: a private window keeps nothing, and a browser may reclaim the space after a long absence.

A dropped folder is installed as an app when it holds an *.app.toml; anything else lands where you chose, as it is. Nothing is filed by what it looks like — a .png does not become a wallpaper on its own.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The network is the page's. FmrbNet.request fetches through the browser, so a server that refuses cross-origin requests cannot be read, and the socket side (Net::HTTP, WebSocket) is not there
  • This is the Modern-family machine; boards are still where the hardware fun is — see Getting Started

docs.title: Connecting to Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Both machines can join a network. What it gets you:

  • Remote desktop — the device's screen in a browser on your PC, driven by your PC's keyboard and mouse. Modern only
  • Networking from your apps — Net::HTTP, WebSocket and TLS
  • mDNS — the device answers to a name, so you do not have to hunt for its address

Only 2.4 GHz networks are supported.

What joining a network exposes

None of it is access-controlled. Once the device is on the network, anyone else on that network can open the remote desktop and operate the machine, and anyone in BLE range can read and write its files — no password is involved anywhere. The credentials you write below are stored in plain text on the device.

Use this on a network you trust, and read Security before putting the device on a network you share with strangers.

docs.title: Pick a network on the screen
docs.text:
The quickest way, with a keyboard attached:

  1. Click the Wi-Fi bars in the menu bar (or system menu → Network)
  2. Press Wi-Fi... in the Network dialog. The Wi-Fi page lists the networks in reach, with their strength
  3. Choose yours, type the password on the keyboard, and connect

The machine remembers up to five networks. At startup, and whenever the connection drops, it joins the strongest one it remembers among those in reach — home, a venue, a phone's hotspot. Forget removes one. What it remembers is written to /home/wifi.toml, which cannot be read over the remote desktop's file endpoints.

The simulator and the browser build have no Wi-Fi page; the Linux program's Settings app has the same page, over the PC's own network manager.

docs.title: Or write your network into /etc/wifi.toml
docs.text:
Credentials live in a file on the device. Released firmware ships without that file — your network's password is yours, not something that can be baked into a public build — so you create it once, on the device, using the editor.

  1. Start the Editor: press E on the desktop, or open it from the Launcher

  2. File → Open, and navigate to /etc/wifi.toml

    If it is not there, type the contents into the empty buffer and use File → Save as with the path /etc/wifi.toml

  3. Fill in your network:

    ```toml [wifi] enable = true ssid = "your-ssid" password = "your-password"

  4. Save, then reboot: system menu → Reset

The Wi-Fi page writes the newer form to /home/wifi.toml, which wins over /etc/wifi.toml. It holds up to five networks, newest first:

[wifi]
enable = true

[[networks]]
ssid = "your-ssid"
password = "your-password"   # "" or left out for an open network
# hidden = true              # a network that does not broadcast its name
Key Meaning enable Set to false to keep the credentials but not connect ssid / password Your network. 2.4 GHz only hostname The mDNS name, and optional — see below

docs.title: Leave hostname out and the board names itself; see below
The name the board answers to
docs.text:
Leave hostname out and the board makes one of its own: fmruby-XXXXXX.local, where the six characters are the last three bytes of its Wi-Fi MAC. It is printed in the boot log, and it is what tells two boards apart on one network.

Every board also answers to fmruby.local, which is the convenient name when there is only one of them. With two, which one replies is a race — use the board's own name then.

Writing a hostname replaces the generated one, so give two boards two different values if you do.

Another way in

If you would rather not type on the device, you can push the file from your PC over the web console, which talks to the device over BLE.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
After the reboot, open the system menu → Network.

It shows whether the connection came up, the address the device was given, and its hostname. Refresh re-reads the state.

The menu bar also carries a small Wi-Fi indicator, to the left of the clock.

From an app:

if FmrbApp.wifi_connected?
  info = FmrbApp.wifi_info
  Log.info("address: #{info[:ip]}")
end

docs.title: Retro runs one radio at a time
docs.text:
This is the difference that surprises people.

Machine Wi-Fi and BLE Modern (Tab5) Both at once. The ESP32-C6 handles them together, so the BLE web console keeps working while Wi-Fi is up Retro (narya-board) One or the other. The ESP32-S3 has a single radio

On Retro, if BLE started at boot, Wi-Fi will not start — the log says so. To use Wi-Fi there, open Config in the system menu, set ble_auto_start to off, and reboot. You can still start BLE by hand later from the system menu when you need the console.

wifi_auto_start in the same dialog controls whether Wi-Fi comes up at boot at all.

docs.title: When it does not connect
docs.text:
• Check enable = true is actually in the file
  • Check the SSID for typos — it is case-sensitive
  • 2.4 GHz only. A 5 GHz-only network will never appear
  • On Retro, check BLE is not holding the radio (above)
  • Wi-Fi starts after the desktop does, so give it a few seconds before deciding it failed. An app that needs the network should wait for FmrbApp.wifi_connected? rather than assume it
